Callie put the hook down on the stone beside her. She put her hand flat on the drift.

She knew this. She had done it on the plain every day since she was eleven, off husk lines in the silt, two fingers and then the flat of the hand, like cream off milk. But she did it the way her grandfather had shown her. Quick. Pulling.

"Don't haul," said Rook. "It isn't rope. It comes at the rate it comes. Pulling at it doesn't get you more. It gets you less." He watched. "No. No. There. There. That's it."

She felt it come.

It was not like the plain. It was slow and heavy and cold, like water finding its way into a boot. It came up into the palm of her hand and lay there. It did not want anything. There was nothing in it to want.

"Hold it high," said Rook. "It'll go down through you if you let it. Then you've got the ache tomorrow, and the road's got the money." He moved his own hand a span further. "Nothing in it to want anything. That's the whole of why you can carry it at all. Nobody home. And you're the better hole."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

They worked along the drift that way on their knees, a span at a time. What they lifted they held low and open, fingers apart, not closed.

Behind them Otto was working the other end of the track, carefully, with his tongue between his teeth. Ines was counting spans under her breath. Pell stood with the atlas and wrote.

When the track was done, Rook took his palm off the stone. Where they had worked, the drift had gone colourless at the edges, like a puddle drying. The wind came up the dip and took it.

He tipped the first jar's mouth against his palm and held it there. The ash went down out of him into the glass. It was grey again by the time it lay in the bottom.

"Now you," he said.

Callie tipped the second jar against her palm. It went out of her the same way. She watched it lie in the bottom of the glass. She had put a great deal of ash in a great many tins, and had never once watched it go.

Rook put a finger in his jar. He took it out and looked at what was on the finger, and rubbed it off between finger and thumb, slowly.

"Hand before lamp," he said. "Old saying and a true one. Nobody standing at a scale has ever once believed it." He turned the jar a quarter. "Clean. That's clean, and that's a fair Flask, and I'll say so in front of whoever's weighing."

He worked the stopper in with the heel of his palm. Then he stopped with his hand still on it.

"Thinner, though," he said. To the jar.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

"It's thinner," said Callie.

Rook turned his head and looked at her.

"I lifted husks on the plain for two years," said Callie. "A Handful off a husk line comes up like wet sand. This came up like flour." She looked at her own jar. "It's the same weight in the glass. It isn't the same in the hand."

Rook looked at her a long time.

"I thought it was me," he said. "I thought I was old and my hand was going. It was thinner at the weighbridge last week and I said nothing then either." He set the jar down against the sack. "I'd sooner it was me."

"It isn't you," said Callie.

"No," said Rook. "I don't suppose it is."

He looked up the dip at the slab by marker post six. Callie had not told him about the slab. He looked at it anyway, for a long moment, and then he looked away.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

The ditch had had most of the rest.

What was left lay along the black shallow in a smear, with the light still crawling through it. The smear was short now, and going.

Rook went down the bank into the water anyway. He put his knee in it and his hand on the bottom.

"This is the other lesson," he said. "The bad one."

His hand dragged.

"There it is," he said. "That's silt. That's four feet of ditch bottom coming up with it. It'll weigh dirty, and whoever's on the scale will write it dirty, and they'll be right." He moved the hand two inches. It dragged again. "Come on. Come on."

Up on the bank somebody moved.

It was only the day holder, shifting her feet at the south lip. Nothing else. But Rook's head turned toward it, fast, the way a head turns when it has spent eleven years turning toward things on banks.

He was a moment late with it. What he had not got yet went out from under his palm and down into the mud.

"No," he said.

He looked at the place where it had gone in.

"Thirty years old," he said, "and you turned your head like a boy."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

He came up the bank and put what he had into a third jar. It was not much. He stoppered it and set it beside the others. Then he sat down on the dry stone with his forearms across his knees and his hands hanging off the ends of them.

His hands were not steady.

He did not put them away; Callie saw that. He sat there with his hands shaking in front of everybody, and neither hid them nor said a word about them.

Toren came and sat on the stone beside him. He said nothing either. He sat on Rook's left, on the side where the hole in his back was, and looked at the road.

Callie looked at her own hands. They were steady. There was ash in the creases of them, fine and grey.

She looked up at the bank. Jab was still standing in the one door, with his dark knife. He had not moved the whole time. He was not looking at Rook's hands. He was looking at the ditch, at the place the Handful had gone into the mud, the way you look at a thing you are going to remember.

"Flask and a fair one," said Rook, to nobody at all. "And a dirty Handful, less what the ditch got."

Pell wrote it down.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

They walked back up through the north yard at the middle of the morning, the crew with the jars, and Rook very slowly with Toren beside him.

Callie walked at the back with the hook on her shoulder.

At the yard gate, the man in the long coat was standing with his hands behind his back. Callie did not know how long he had been there. He looked at the jars as they went past, and at Rook, and at Jab coming down off the bank with the dark knife gone back into the metal on its neck cord.

Then he looked at Callie.

He said nothing. He only nodded, once, as if he had seen something he had come to see.

Callie did not nod back.

"I read the ground," she said, as she went past him. "That's all I did."

"I know," said the man in the long coat. "That's what I wrote down."

Chapter 8 — Jab: Calibration

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure]

It woke him at the second hour.

At first he could not tell what had woken him. Hut twelve was dark, the stove had gone down to a red line, and Otto was asleep in the bed by the door, on his back, breathing like a big dog.

Jab lay still and listened. There was nothing to hear.

Then he felt it again. It was not a sound but a lean under his breastbone, where it lived, neither up nor down, the way a floor leans in an old house. Everything in him was sliding one way, very slightly, toward the north end of the station.

Worse, it said. That was all it ever said.

He knew what it was worth. Four times in five it was right. When it was wrong, it was wrong in the direction he wanted. So he had made a rule. He did not ask it when he wanted an answer.

He had not asked. It had come on its own.

He got up and got his boots on in the dark without waking Otto, and went out of the door and up the row, past the dark step of eleven, and turned onto the main street.

The lamps were off. They had gone off at the first hour. He walked in the dark down the middle of the street, counting paces, and stepped wide of the loose grating between the second pole and the third without thinking about it.

[Quiet, precise narration; restrained institutional pressure]

Mrs Lask was at the desk. She looked up.

"I haven't sent for you," she said.

"I know," said Jab. "I'm going in anyway."

She looked at him for a moment. Then she looked down at her list.

"Fifth on the right," she said, as if he did not know. "The nurse is already with him. She came on at the first hour and went straight there. I didn't send for you, and neither did she. So who did?"

"Nobody," said Jab.

Mrs Lask wrote something on her list. He did not wait to see what.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

The ward was dark except for a small lamp at the far end and another by the fifth bed on the right. The young nurse was there, the one who had stitched his arm on the bench. She had the blanket off Tonk's leg.

Tonk was awake. His face was red and wet. His eyes were too bright.

"Jab," he said. "The nails are hot."

Jab sat down in the chair.

"I know," he said. He did not know. He looked at the nurse.

"Fever," she said, low. "Came up about the twelfth hour. It's high. And this one's angry." She pointed without touching. The pin nearest the knee went in through a red place in the skin. The red had spread. There was a wet shine round the pin where there should not have been. "It might be only the pin. That happens. The skin gets in a temper round the metal and it'll clean up with medicine. Or it might be deeper."

"How do you tell?"

"Keel tells," said the nurse. "I've sent for her."

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

Tonk's hand found the long cord. It was still knotted round his wrist, and the other end was tied to the bed rail, the way Jab left it every night when the ward turned him out. Eight nights now. The bell on its string hung from the same rail, and Tonk had never once rung it.

Jab untied the rail end and knotted it round his own left wrist.

Tonk pulled the cord. It was a small pull. Jab was already there.

"I pulled it," said Tonk.

"I know. I'm here."

"You were already here."

"I came early," said Jab. "I had a feeling."

Tonk looked at him with his too-bright eyes.

"Is it the thing?" he said. "Your thing?"

Jab did not answer for a moment. Tonk had never asked about it before. He had not known Tonk knew there was a thing to ask about.

"Yes," he said. "It told me you were worse."

"I am worse," said Tonk, with the air of a man confirming a report. "It's right."

"It's right this time."

"Is it going to fix it?"

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

Jab looked at his brother's leg in its padded trough, with the four pins through it and the bar along the outside, and the red place at the top pin.

He had written it on the card. He had pressed hard with the pencil. It does not touch his leg. It has never gone within a hand's breadth of the bone and it never will.

He had written it because he was afraid. He knew that now. He had watched a woman with her sleeves rolled up take a dead piece of bone out of his brother, and set the leg straight, and bolt it. He had watched her do it with instruments and pictures and nine children's worth of knowing. He did not know anything. He had a thing that came when it liked and went out like a bucket going dry. If he put it into that leg and it did the wrong thing, he would not know it had done the wrong thing until it was too late to undo.

"No," he said. "It's not going to fix it. That's Keel's."

"Why?"

"Because I don't know what it does," said Jab. "And she does."

Tonk thought about that. His face was very hot.

"Can it do the other?" he said. "The warm one. From the wall."

Jab went still.

He had not known Tonk remembered the wall. Tonk had been going grey. He had not been looking at anything.

"I can try," said Jab. "It might not come. It doesn't come when I call it."

"Try anyway."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

So he put his hand flat on his brother's chest.

Not the leg. Nowhere near the leg. The chest, the way he had at the culvert, over the small fast heart.

He did not push; he had learned that much. He did not reach, or lean on it, or ask it to run uphill. He sat there in the lamplight with his hand on his brother and let go of wanting it to do anything.

It was very hard. He wanted it more than he had wanted anything since the wall.

Nothing came.

Not nothing. He could feel the bottom of the bucket, and there was something in it. A little. More than there had been on the bench on the first night. It had come back while he was busy with other things. But it lay at the bottom without moving, and it would not come up, and he did not make it.

After a while he took his hand away.

"It didn't come," he said.

"No," said Tonk. He was not surprised. "It was warm, though. Your hand was."

"That's just a hand."

"It was warm," said Tonk, and shut his eyes. "That's allowed."

Doctor Keel came at the third hour with her sleeves already rolled and her hair flat on one side from a pillow.

"Maybe," said Doctor Keel. "I'll tell you before I do. I won't sneak up on you."

At first light they took him down the slope on the rolling bed.

At the line he untied the long cord from his own wrist. Every night before this he had moved that end to the bed rail when they turned him out, so that Tonk was never tied to nothing. This time he held the loose end out.

Tonk looked at it.

Tonk took the loose end and closed his hot fist on it. He did not let go of Jab's hand straight away. Last time he had. This time he held on first, hard, for about three seconds.

Senna looked at him. Then she looked at the door.

They could not take Senna in straight away.

The grey-haired man came out and stood in the doorway and looked at the old woman in the chair. His face had the look of somebody who has been awake since the first hour doing arithmetic.

She was in there two hours.

The three of them sat outside. Nobody sent them away. Tonk had gone up the slope with Keel and the nurse and his cord, to have his pin cleaned. He had told Jab to stay and mind the old lady, because she had been rude to the machine and it might be rude back.

They did not talk much. Callie sat on the floor with the hook on her knees and did not count out loud. Jab could see her not counting. He thought she was not letting it out, because out loud it would be for Toren to hear, and it was not hers to give him.

Toren sat with his hand in his pocket, and it stayed there; he never checked. Jab had watched him do the checking at the culvert, on the road, in the ward. He had watched him stop. He did not know what had happened to make him stop, and he did not ask.

And Jab did the arithmetic, because his head would not do anything else.

Eleven days to Senna's next cycle, six to Tonk's picture, three to Callie's review and the Director's room on the second floor of the yard office, and four to his own review. Four seasons of Rook's debt, starting now. Thirteen years of Tonk coming back through those doors to be measured.

And one machine.

He had known that. Sowerby had told him on the first morning, in a corridor. There's one machine in a shed at the north end of this station that takes the picture. I don't know of another within four hundred miles. He had heard it as a fact about Meridian. Like the lamps. Like the two gates.

He had not heard it as a thing that could stop.

Tonk's fever came down a little by the evening.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

He sat on the step of twelve that night.

He had not decided to. He had come back from the ward at the tenth hour, when they turned the visitors out and he had tied the long cord's end to the bed rail, and he could not go in. Otto was inside, asleep, breathing like a dog. The stove was banked.

One door down, on the step of eleven, Toren was sitting with his back against the door frame.

[Dry, precise narration; quiet institutional pressure]

They sat on their three steps.

Jab thought about the card in hut twelve. Requested at the Director's office. All three of them, the same hour. He had thought it was about the north road. About the hounds, and the light, and people going out through a gate they had been told not to. Maybe it was.

He thought about the man in the long coat. There's a line on the register for it. It's a long line with very little written on it. He thought about Rook on this same row, in the dusk, saying I've done a thing that rhymes with it.

He thought about Callie on the floor of the corridor, reading a door by what did not come out of it. About Toren sitting outside a room he could not go into, learning the rack by heart. About himself on a bench with a hand on his chest, not asking.

None of it could make a box in a rack turn green.

"There's no other one," said Callie. "Is there. Anywhere."

"Four hundred miles," said Jab. "Sowerby said. He's looked."

"Four hundred miles is only as far as he's looked," said Toren.

Neither of the others answered that. Jab did not think Toren had meant it to be answered. He thought Toren had said it the way you say a thing to find out whether it is true, and then heard it out loud, and did not know yet.

[Dry, precise narration; quiet institutional pressure]

The lamp at the end of the row went out at the first hour.

It did not flicker. It went, all at once, the way it did every night, for its written reason. The dark came down over the three steps and the row and the whole of Yard C.

Jab sat in it.

He could not see Toren now, or Callie, but he knew they were there; he could hear the stove tick through the door of eleven, and Callie shift on her step and settle again.

He thought about a squirrel, four hundred miles north, and a heap he could not get back to.

He had told Tonk he would find a different one, somewhere in this place, for somebody, and he had thought it would be a person when he found it, and that he would know it when he saw it.

He had not thought it might be a room.

He sat in the dark with his hand on his knee. Somewhere at the north end of the station, under a long low building with a turf roof, there was a pale ring standing on its edge in the dark, and a rack of little windows behind it. One of them was yellow. All three of them were held up by it, one way or another. Senna's marrow. Tonk's picture. Whatever Callie's mother would need, the next time a fit ran long.

It was older than anybody who ran it. It was the only one.

And it was starting to wake up slow.

Chapter 9 — Toren: Test Weights

[Focused, grounded narration; keep physical instruction clear]

The lamp at the end of the row had gone out at the first hour. By the fifth, Toren was sitting on the edge of his bed in the dark of hut eleven with one boot on, listening to Rook put on his.

It took Rook a long time. He sat with his back very straight and worked the boot onto his foot with both hands, and every so often he stopped with his fingers on the laces and breathed out through his nose, and then he went on. Nobody in the hut offered to help. That argument had been had on the road, somewhere before the Level, and Rook had won it by not answering.

Toren had not slept much. He had lain on his bed with his coat on and looked at the dark, and in the dark there had been a little window in the front of a grey box, lit the wrong colour. Third row down, fourth box along. Every other light in that rack burned a steady pale green. That one was yellow, like the line painted on the floor to tell you where to stop.

He got his other boot on one-handed. His left arm lived in the sling against his chest now, and over eleven days the break under the splint had settled from a grinding, sickening ache into a dull one that he could have drawn on paper, from two fingers above the wrist to a place just short of the elbow. His right hand had come out of its wrapping three days ago with a pink seam across the palm where the Breach had opened it. The seam pulled when he made a fist. Every morning he made a fist anyway, to see how far it would close, and every morning it closed a little further than the morning before.

"You don't have to go every day," said Wyck, from the bed by the door. He said it with his eyes shut.

"I know."

"He doesn't need you out there."

"I know that too."

Rook stood up in three movements, one hand on the bed frame. "He's coming because he's got nothing better to do with his feet," he said. "Go back to sleep, Wyck."

Wyck did not go back to sleep. Toren heard him turn over, carefully, onto the side that was not strapped, and lie there listening to them go.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

The row was frozen. The wet concrete had gone white overnight and it crunched, and the air had the thin, clean bite that meant the season had turned while nobody in Meridian was looking. They went up the main street in the dark under three dead lamps, past the long building, where one window was lit at the front and a shape that might have been Mrs Lask sat behind it, and out across the north yard to the yard gate. The gate crew knew them now. A man in a grey coat opened the small door in the big one without being asked and said, "Morning, holder," to Rook, and Rook said, "Morning," and they went through.

It was two hundred paces of made road from the yard gate to the south lip of the Sag. Toren had walked it three mornings now at Rook's pace, which was the pace of a man carrying something heavy that nobody else could see, and he had stopped wanting to walk faster.

This morning the Sag was full of fog.

He had not seen it do that before. The dip lay under the fog like a bowl under milk, and the top of the fog was as level as poured milk, so that the road went down into whiteness at the south lip and came up out of it again three hundred paces away at the north. Down in the white there were the shapes of things he knew were there: the tilted slabs at the bottom, the marker posts down the east side, the black water standing in the joints. He could see the tops of the posts, the nearest three or four, sticking up out of the fog with their white paint grey in the half-dark. He could see nothing else.

"It does this," said Rook, "when the nights get cold and the ground doesn't. The ditches are warmer than the air." He looked at it a while. "It'll burn off by the eighth hour."

The day holder was at the south lip, where she always was.

She stood at the edge of the made road in a grey yard coat, with her hands out from her sides and her feet planted, facing the fog. She had been there since the night crew went off. She had held the Sag alone for two years, Pell had said, and he had said it the way he said a distance, as if it were only a number.

Toren had watched her for three mornings. He watched people's weight now; he had started on the road, with Senna in the cart and Rook's shoulders and Dessa's leg, and he could not stop. The day holder stood with her weight on her left foot. Every few minutes she moved it onto the right, very slowly, without lifting either foot off the ground, and after a while she moved it back again. He had counted, the first morning, and it was every four or five minutes. Under her right heel there was a hollow worn into the gravel at the lip about the size of a saucer.

You did not wear a hollow like that into gravel in a week.

Nobody watched her. The night crew going off watched the road behind them. The lifters coming on watched the ground in front. Rook watched the dip. She stood at the edge of all of it with her hands out and her face shut, holding a road, and the only thing Toren had ever heard anybody say to her was morning.

"Morning," said Rook.

"Morning," said the day holder. She did not look round.

[Steady, watchful narration; let distance and reserves register]

The lip path went round the west rim of the dip above the ditch, and at this hour the fog came up over it to their knees. Toren walked on Rook's left, half a step behind, where the hole in his back was. He did not know what he would do if Rook fell on that side. He walked there anyway.

It took them nine minutes to go round to the north lip. When they got there Rook stood for a while and got his breath, looking down the road into the white.

Then he put his hands out from his sides.

Nothing happened that anybody could have seen. Across the dip, at the south lip, the day holder let her own hands drop and stood where she was, resting on her feet. She did not sit. Toren had never seen her sit.

He had never been able to see the line either. Callie said it was like a sheet of clean paper laid over the ground, so that where it lay she could read nothing at all, not a track, not a crack, not the grain of the silt. Dessa said it was like somebody holding their breath in a room. To Toren it was only the set of Rook's shoulders, and the way his hands stayed out from his sides a little higher than a man's hands would hang, and the look on his face, which was the look of a man listening for a sound in another part of the house.

Somewhere down in the fog, a slab ticked as it cooled.

The lifters came down the east track in a line. Katori first, with her cap pulled down; then Ines with her bow on her back, counting something under her breath; then Otto with the sack of jars; then Callie, with the hook on her shoulder and her left arm held close against her ribs. The east track ran along the side of the dip above the fog, on dry stone, and there was a drift along it this morning where the night crew had put down whatever had come up in the small hours: a Handful, perhaps a little more, lying grey in the frost.

Callie stopped before she knelt. She stood on the track and looked down into the fog, at the place where the fourth marker post and the fifth and the sixth went down into the white, and she stayed like that for a while. Then she said something to Pell, who had come down behind them with the atlas under his arm. Pell opened the atlas and wrote.

"She's looking at that slab again," said Toren.

"She looks at it every morning," said Rook. His hands did not move. "So does Pell's book."

On the west side of the dip, halfway down, where the bank came down to the ditch in one long easy slope, Jab was standing in the only way up. He had come again. He had the fish-knife shape on his right fist, dark, with no light on it, and the fog came up round his knees like water. He did not look at the lifters and he did not look at Rook. He looked at the ditch, and at the fog, and at the one place anything could come.

Toren looked at the fog for a while, and then at Rook's hands.

"You said a thing on the step last night," said Rook.

Toren waited.

"About four hundred miles."

"I didn't know you were awake."

"The door was open. Nobody in this station's ever awake at the first hour, except everybody." Rook did not take his eyes off the dip. "It was a true thing. I'd not say it again till you've done the sums on it."

"What sums?"

"The ones you do," said Rook. "Your father's kind. With the ifs written down."

Toren thought about his father's paper. It had said nineteen days to Meridian, with three ifs written under the number, and he had carried it down the road for sixty-four days while the number broke and was crossed out and written again underneath. He had hated the ifs, afterward. He had thought they were the part of the paper that had gone wrong.

He had not thought, until now, that they were the only part of it that had been true.

"All right," he said.

Rook nodded, once. That was the whole of the conversation.

At the end of the hour the day holder put her hands out again and took the whole line back. Rook let his down. He stood very still for a moment, and then his hands began to shake, the way they did every morning now, a fine fast tremor from the wrists to the ends of the fingers that he neither hid nor mentioned.

Toren sat down on the stone on his left side.

Down on the east track, Callie and Otto were working along the drift on their knees, a span at a time, palms flat, the way Rook had shown them. Katori stood over them with her hands at her sides. The fog was going thin at the top and Toren could see down into it now, a little way, to the tops of the slabs and the black water between them and the white post with the number six on it, sticking up at a tilt out of a crack in the road.

"Go and do your sums, then," said Rook.

"You'll be all right?"

"I'll be sitting down," said Rook. "It's the same thing today."

The shed was not open on a morning when nobody was booked. Toren went down the long slope under the north end of the long building anyway, into the cool grey air where the walls went thick and the windows stopped, and he stood at the yellow line in front of the wide door and waited.

The door was open a hand's width. Through it he could hear somebody working, the small patient noises of a man with tools in a quiet room: a scrape, a click, a long breath out.

After a while the grey-haired man came to the gap and looked at him.

He had his sleeves rolled and a smear of fresh ink up the side of his hand to join the old one. His eyes were red at the rims. He looked like a man who had been awake since the first hour doing arithmetic and had not liked the answers.

"It's not a Friday," he said.

"I know."

"She's not due for ten days."

He could see the rows of little windows from here, most of them a steady green. He found the third row down and counted along. "I'm here about the fourth box."

The grey-haired man looked at him for a long moment.

"Why?" he said.

It was a fair question. Toren had walked down the slope trying to find the answer to it, and had not, and now he had to say something.

Before it stops."

The grey-haired man rubbed the ink on his hand with his thumb. It did not come off. It had not come off in some years.

He came back with a box in his arms.

It was grey steel, about the size of a loaf, with a little dark window in the front and a plate riveted to the steel beside it. He carried it the way you carry a sleeping animal, close in against his chest, and when he came to the yellow line he stepped over it without breaking stride, because nothing in the rule said a thing could not come out.

"It's dead," he said. "Row one, nine along. It died before I came here, and I came here when I was twenty. It was a reference for a kind of picture nobody takes any more. I keep it for the screws." He held it out. "Mind. It's heavier than it looks."

Toren took it in his right hand and against his hip, the way Otto took the barrow. It was heavier than it looked. It was heavier than anything that size had any business being, dense and dead and cold, and his arm dropped three inches before it understood.

"Lead," said the grey-haired man. "There's a jacket inside, all round. It keeps what's in the middle from talking to what's next door."

"What's in the middle?"

"A thing we know the true value of." He sat down on the bench against the wall, which Toren had never seen him do, and put his forearms on his knees. "Have you seen the weighbridge? In the yard?"

"I've walked past it."

"Every morning, before he weighs anything, the weighman puts the test weights on. Iron blocks, with a number stamped in them. He knows what they weigh, because somebody weighed them against something else they knew, and so on back, a long way, to people who are dead. If he puts a fifty on and the scale says fifty-one, it's the scale that's wrong. Not the weight. The weight's the one thing in that yard nobody argues with." He nodded at the box in Toren's arm. "That's a test weight. So's everything in that rack. Every morning, before the machine looks at anybody, it weighs itself against every one of them, row after row. If they all agree, it's telling the truth. If one of them's off, the machine can't tell which of them is lying. It's too honest. So it tries to agree with all of them at once."

"And the fourth box is off."

"The fourth box has started to lie. Only a hair. It's not the thing in the middle; that's as good as the day they sealed it. It's what reads it that's going, and I can't open it to find out which part, because once it's open it isn't a reference any more. It's just a box." He rubbed his hand. "So the ones either side of it try to agree with it. And they start to lie too, a hair each. That's why every run takes longer. I've been sitting at that screen telling the machine it's wrong, by hand, because I know what it ought to say. That works as long as I know."

He looked at the floor between his boots.

"I'm starting not to know," he said.

Toren stood at the yellow line with seventy years of lead against his hip and did not say anything for a while.

He was thinking about the rack. About the way the green lights had gone pale one after another when the machine walked them, left to right, like somebody going along a row of windows with a candle. About Callie on the corridor floor saying that's ten. About the yellow light.

The same makers, the same plate, the same sort of room. If I had a live one of that kind, I could set it against the ones that still tell the truth, and learn what it says, and drop it in. A month's work. Less, if I didn't sleep."

They shielded their instrument rooms the same as we are, because the same sort of people built them. It's in the manuals. I've never been in one. The last time I stood this close to one of those racks, I was fifty-three. And I'd come for the copper.

They did the bread without her that night.

She did the order. She did it the way she had done it every night: Senna's name first, and a slab set aside on a plate for somebody to carry up in the morning; then me; then Wyck; then Rook; then Tor.

The fog came again in the morning, thicker than before.

This time they went out with the lifters, because Katori's crew had come to the yard gate at the same moment, in a clump of breath and lamps. Callie had the hook over her shoulder. She looked at Toren when they came through the small door, a quick look, the way she did, and then she looked at his right hand, and then she looked at the road.

At the south lip she stopped so suddenly that Otto walked into her.

"Somebody's been here," she said.

The day holder did not turn round. Katori did.

Callie was looking at the gravel of the lip, where the made road ended and the dip began. There was nothing on it that Toren could see except the frost and the day holder's hollow and a great many boot marks, the crews coming and going, the night crew's heavy yard boots in a trampled mess where they had stood around their lamps.

"There," said Callie. She crouched, and pointed with the hook's handle without touching. "Since before the gate opened. The frost's in the heel of it, not over it. Small. Smaller than mine." She moved the handle along a line Toren could not see. "Good boots. The heels are new; there's the nail pattern, every one of them sharp. That's not a yard boot. Yard boots are all worn to the same shape, because everybody in the yard walks on the same cinders." She stood up. "They stood here a long time. Then they went round."

"Round where?" said Katori.

Callie looked along the lip path, west, above the ditch, into the white. She followed something with her eyes the way Toren had seen her follow a husk line on the plain, or a track in the dark.

"There," she said.

On the west bank, above the one door, where the fog lay thin at the rim, somebody was standing with their hands in their pockets, looking down into the Sag.

[Steady, watchful narration; let distance and reserves register]

Rook did not see her. He had already started round the lip path toward the north lip at his slow pace, looking at the ground in front of his feet. Toren went after him, on his left. When they went past the place above the one door he looked up, and the figure on the bank was a woman in a long oilskin coat, bareheaded, with dark hair cut short to her skull, standing very still.

She was not watching the lifters or the dip or the fog. She was watching Rook.

She watched him all the way round to the north lip. She watched him stand there and get his breath. She watched him put his hands out from his sides, and at the south lip the day holder's hands dropping, and the fog lying flat and white over the whole of the bottom of the Sag with a road shut underneath it that nobody could see.

For an hour she stood on the bank and watched him hold it.

Toren watched her watching. Once she took her hands out of her pockets and turned her left wrist over, slowly, the way you turn a wrist that aches in the cold, and then put the hand back. Once she looked across the dip at the day holder, for a long time, and then back at Rook. She never looked at Toren at all.

Below her, in the one door, Jab stood in the fog up to his knees with his dark knife and did not look up once. Toren was nearly sure he knew she was there. It was the way he stood.

At the end of the hour the day holder took the line back. Rook let his hands down. They began to shake.

And the woman on the bank came down.

[Focused, grounded narration; keep physical instruction clear]

She came round the lip path at a walk, not fast, and she walked the way nobody else Toren had seen in Meridian walked, as if the ground might not be where it looked and she had learned to check with her feet. Close to, she was younger than he had thought on the bank. Twenty-five, perhaps. Her face was all flat planes and it did not move much. Under the oilskin she wore the grey of the long building, and on her feet were good boots, brown, laced to the shin, with new heels.

Her left wrist, where it came out of the sleeve, had a lump on the outside of it the size of a thumbnail, where a bone had knit crooked a long time ago.

She stopped two paces from Rook.

She looked at his hands first. She looked at them for a long time, shaking in front of him at the ends of his arms, and her face did nothing at all.

Rook looked up.

Toren saw his face do something he had not seen it do, not on the step with Katori, not anywhere. On the step, Rook had looked like a man who hears a voice in the next room he has stopped expecting to hear anywhere. This was a different look. This was the look of a man who has expected to hear a voice every day for eleven years, and has been afraid of it every day, and hears it.

"Elias," she said.

And Toren knew who she was.

He had been at the fire on the lane when Rook told them. He had sat in the dark with the others while Rook said the whole of it, Homura and the wire and the long room, and he had heard the part that came after, which Rook had said quickly, as if it did not matter: I walked south for two months with a fourteen-year-old girl called Dee Wren who had a broken wrist and no shoes.

He looked at her wrist. He looked at her boots.

"Dee," said Rook.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

For a while neither of them said anything else. The fog lay in the bottom of the dip. Down on the east track the lifters had stopped, Toren saw; Katori was standing with her hand up, flat, the way you stop a crew without a word, and all of them were looking up at the north lip.

"Your line's thin on the east edge," said the woman. "You're holding it with your shoulders. I could see it from the bank."

"Good morning to you too," said Rook.

"Who cleared you to hold?"

"Nobody."

"No," she said. "Nobody would have."

She took his right hand. She did not hold it; she turned it over, palm up, and laid two fingers on the inside of the wrist, where the pulse was, and looked away over the fog while she counted. Toren had seen that before. He had seen Rook do it a hundred times on the road, to Senna, to Wyck, to Dessa after the bridge. He had never once thought about where Rook had learned it.

"Sit down, Elias," she said, "before you fall down."

Rook sat. It took him three movements. She crouched in front of him with her forearms on her knees.

He was looking at her wrist.

"It set," he said.

"It set crooked. Two sticks and a bootlace on a riverbank, and you said you were sorry for four days." Her voice had not changed at all. "It's held eleven years. I've set a hundred since. Mine are straighter."

"I don't doubt it."

"Yours held," said the woman.

Rook looked down at his own hands.

"They told me at the river," she said, after a while, "that a man came asking for me. Four years after."

"I did."

"I was here by then."

"I know. I didn't follow."

"No," she said. "You didn't." She waited. "Why not?"

Rook was quiet for a long time.

"Because I'd have had to tell you what I was doing instead," he said.

"I knew what you were doing. Everybody off the wire knew what you were doing. We used to hear it on the river road from people who'd heard it from people." She looked at his hands again, which had not stopped. "You can't get the angle on yourself. You never could."

"Dee—"

She put her palm flat against his chest, over the breastbone, the way Toren had seen Jab put his hand on his brother.

Toren watched the shaking in Rook's hands slow. It did not stop all at once. It slowed like a bell slows after it is struck, the long fine tremor going longer and finer, until it was a thing he had to look for, and then it was not there. Rook's shoulders came down half an inch. His face did not change.

"Don't," he said.

"Too late," said Dee Wren.

She took her hand away and sat back on her heels. Toren saw that her own face had gone a shade paler round the mouth, and that she pressed her hands together, one inside the other, in her lap, for as long as it took to breathe out twice. Then she let them go. Whatever it had cost her, she had paid it and put it away.

"That was yours," said Rook. "It wasn't yours to spend."

"I'll decide what's mine," said Dee. "I've been deciding it for some years now."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

Toren went down the slope.

He had stood there long enough. It was not his, and he had known it was not his since the first word; it was only that he could not make his feet move until something told them to. When he did go, he went down the east side of the north lip to the track, where the lifters had gone back to work, and knelt beside Callie at the drift. He could not lift with one hand very well, but he could hold a jar steady while somebody tipped their palm into it, and that was something.

Callie tipped her palm into the jar. The ash went down out of her into the glass and lay grey in the bottom.

"Who is she?" she said.

"Somebody he walked south," said Toren.

Callie looked up the slope at the woman crouched in front of Rook on the north lip. She looked at the boots, and then at the wrist, and then at Toren's face. She held it for a moment, the way she held a patch of ground.

Then she put her palm flat on the drift again and did not ask anything else.

He had liked her for that on the bench, the first day. He found he liked her for it more now.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

"Tor," said Rook.

Toren stood up. Rook was on his feet again, with one hand on the woman's shoulder for the last part of it, which Toren had never seen him allow anybody. The woman had stood when he stood.

"Dee Wren," said Rook. "Toren Voss."

She looked at him. She looked at all of him, from the top down, taking her time: the sling, the splint, the hand with the seam across the palm, the way he was standing, which Toren supposed was a way that said he had stitches healing at the back of one leg. She looked at him the way Sowerby looked at people, and the way Keel looked at people, and the way the woman at the north gate had looked at Tonk, for about four seconds, before anybody touched anything.

"The one who does two at once," she said.

"Once," said Toren.

"Twice, on Mr Hallet's sheet." She did not smile, but something at the corner of her mouth moved. "Hallet's sheets don't lie. They're the only thing in this station I've never caught at it."

Then her eyes went past him, across the dip, to the west side, where the fog was going thin, and where the one easy slope came down from the rim to the ditch, and where a boy of seventeen with a bandaged arm stood up to his knees in the white with a dark knife on his fist, looking at the only place anything could come.

"And that one stands in doors," she said.

"That one's why you're here," said Rook.

"I'm here for both of you," said Dee Wren. "I only found out about you last night."

She went down off the north lip and along the lip path toward the one door, not fast. Toren watched her go. She put her feet down as if the ground might not be where it looked, and he understood, watching her, that she was somebody who had once walked for two months without shoes, and had not forgotten a single step of it.

Chapter 10 — Callie: What I'll Take

[Focused, grounded narration; keep physical instruction clear]

The weighbridge was a steel plate set level into a concrete pit, as long as a wagon, with a hut beside it that had a window facing the plate and a beam scale behind the window. Callie had walked past it every morning for ten days. She had not stood on it until now, with Katori's crew and four jars of the morning's lift, waiting for the weighman to finish doing what he did before he weighed anything.

He was an old man in a leather apron. He came out of the hut with an iron block in each hand, and set them down on the plate one after the other, carefully, as if they might wake. Each one had a number cast into its face. Then he went back into the hut and looked at the beam for a long time, and moved the little weight along it with one finger, and looked again, and wrote something in a book.

Then he came out and took the blocks off the plate and carried them back into the hut, one at a time.

"Test weights," said Pell, beside her. He said it quietly, the way he said things that pleased him. "He does that every morning. He'll do it again at noon. He's done it for thirty years, I'm told, and he's never once found the scale wrong."

"Then why does he do it?"

"Because the day he doesn't," said Pell, "it will be."

Callie watched the old man go back into his hut. She thought about her grandfather at the scale house at Thistle Ford, with his hand on the beam and his head on one side, listening to it the way you listen to a horse breathe. She had been small then. She had not known that she was watching a thing that would be gone.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

There was a girl in the hut with the weighman. She was about fifteen, with a long plait down her back and a tally board on a string round her neck and a pencil behind her ear, and when the crew came up onto the plate with the jars she leaned out of the window and looked at all of them in turn, frankly, the way you look at a cart of strangers coming into your yard.

"Road lot," she said, to the weighman, not quietly.

"Road lot," the weighman agreed. "Put them on one at a time."

They put them on one at a time. Otto set each jar down in the middle of the plate, and the old man moved the weight along the beam and called a number, and the girl wrote it on her board and then read it back to him, and he nodded. There was a board on the wall of the hut, painted black, with names down one side in white paint and numbers down the other in chalk. Callie found Katori's name on it, and under it her own, which somebody had painted there without asking her.

The fourth jar was Rook's Flask, the good one off the east track. The girl wrote the number and said, "Flask," and began to put the board down.

"It's thin," said Callie.

The girl looked at her.

"It's a Flask," she said. "It's on the weight for a Flask."

"It's on the weight. It's thin."

"There's no such thing as thin." The girl said it quite pleasantly, the way you correct somebody who has called a horse the wrong colour. "There's a Handful and there's a Flask and there's dirty, and that's not dirty, because I can see it from here. A Flask's a Flask. The scale says."

"The scale says weight," said Callie. "It doesn't say thin."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

The weighman had turned from his beam and was watching them. So was Katori. Pell had his atlas open and his pencil in his hand and was not writing, which was how Callie knew he was interested.

Callie had not meant to argue. She had meant to say the true thing and let it sit. But the girl was looking at her with her chin up, the way the boys at Thistle Ford had looked at her when she told them the grade on a sack was wrong, and she found that she wanted to be right in front of this girl more than she had wanted anything in several days.

"Can I have it back?" she said. "Off the plate. For a minute."

The weighman nodded, and Otto lifted the jar off. Callie took the stopper out and put two fingers in, and brought them out grey, and held them up to the light from the hut window. Then she rubbed them together, slowly, finger and thumb, the way Rook had on the east track.

"Give me your hand," she said.

The girl looked at the weighman. The weighman nodded again. The girl put her hand out through the window, palm up, and Callie tipped a little of the ash into it off the ends of her fingers.

"Now rub it," she said.

The girl rubbed it.

"A Handful off a husk line comes up like wet sand," said Callie. "You can feel every grain of it. It sticks in the creases. It's heavy for what it is. This came up like flour. Feel it go." She watched the girl's fingers. "It's the same weight in the glass, because you fill the glass. You'd need more of it to fill the glass. So it's the same weight and there's more of it, and each grain of it's got less in it than it should." She put the stopper back in. "Somebody who paid for that at a Flask would get less out of it than a Flask. Not much. A tenth. Maybe more. They'd notice at the end of a long night."

The girl was looking at her own hand.

"Rook said it on the track," said Otto, going red. "Before she did. He said thinner."

"He said it to the jar," said Katori. "She said it to the scale."

The weighman came out of his hut and took the jar and unstoppered it and put his own finger in. He looked at the finger for a long time. Then he rubbed it between finger and thumb, the way Callie had.

"Write it Flask," he said to the girl. "And put thin in the margin. And whose call it was."

"Whose call was it?"

"Hers," said the weighman, and went back into his hut.

[Dry, precise narration; quiet institutional pressure]

The girl wrote it. She wrote thin, and then she looked up at Callie with the pencil still on the board.

"What's your name, then?" she said. "For the margin."

Callie told her, just the first part. The girl wrote a C. and looked at it.

"C.'s call," she said. "That's what the old man with the book does. I've seen him at the window." She jerked her chin at Pell. "He writes concur after, with letters. Like a ledger."

"I do," said Pell, pleased.

"It's a daft way to write." The girl said it with great satisfaction, as if she had been waiting to say it to somebody for a week. Then she looked at Callie's hook, on her shoulder, and her expression changed.

"Is that the one?" she said. "The one that does two?"

Callie did not answer.

"Everybody in the yard knows," said the girl. "You're on the register with two doors. The man in the long coat went up the stair with your card and came down again without it." She put the pencil behind her ear. "Nobody I know's got two. I've got one."

She held up her right hand, flat, out of the hut window. Then her fingers closed, and something came out from between them.

It was a blade. It was grey and straight and plain, about the length of her forearm, with a clean narrow edge that caught a line of pale light along it as it came, like frost along a wire. It came out all at once, the whole of it, in about the time it took to breathe in, and it stood out of her fist exactly level, and it did not shake.

It was the proper blade, the one Callie had wanted on the wagon bed, shorter and straight, the one she had tried to make and watched gutter out like a lamp in a draught.

"Ember," said the girl. "Since thirteen. It's the only shape it does, and it's never done anything much, because there's nothing in the weighbridge wants cutting." The blade went back into her fist as neatly as it had come. "So they put me on the tally."

Callie looked at the place where it had been.

"It's a good shape," she said. She meant it, and she heard herself mean it, and did not like how much.

"It's a boring shape," said the girl. "Everybody on the register's got one like it. Yours is the one they talk about." She leaned out of the window a little further. "Is the grey mare yours? At the south stable. With the bad leg."

"She's the crew's."

"She's the best horse inside the berm," said the girl. "There's nine. I know all of them." She said it as if it were the most important thing about her, and Callie thought it probably was. "Tell whoever does her leg she wants the poultice changing twice a day, not once. The stable man does it once because he's lazy."

"Tell him yourself," said Katori.

"He doesn't listen to me," said the girl. "Nobody at the stable listens to me. I'm the tally."

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

They went back to fourteen at the middle of the day.

Callie's mother was sitting up on the edge of her bed by the stove with her boots on and a stick across her knees. It was a new stick. Pell had cut it out of a length of ash from the wood pile behind the long building and shaved the handle down with his knife to fit a left hand, and he had done it in the night, and told nobody, and left it leaning against the end of her bed.

"I've been practising," said her mother. "Eleven steps to the door. I went to the door and back four times and nobody saw me, and I'd have got away with it if the door didn't creak."

"I heard it creak," said Ines, from her bed. She did not open her eyes.

"You hear everything."

"I do."

Callie sat down on the floor with her back against the bed frame. She could feel her mother's leg through the blanket, the right one, which lay a little further out than the left, the way it lay now, as if it had been put down by somebody else and left.

"Tomorrow," she said.

"Tomorrow," said her mother.

"The review's at the ninth hour. On the first floor. The man at the window said it's three people and a table." Callie had asked. She had gone and stood at Hallet's window yesterday afternoon, and he had told her, in order, the way he told everything. "I'll go. I'm the household for the window. You don't have to climb a stair to hear them read your sheet out to you."

Her mother was quiet for a moment.

"No," she said.

"Mum."

"You're the household for the window," said her mother. "The window can call you what it likes. I've no argument with the window. It's a very good window." She put her left hand on the stick. "But I'm going to that room, and I'm going to sit in front of whoever's sitting there, and they're going to look at me while they do it."

"You'll have to climb a stair."

"Then I'll climb a stair. I climbed a scarp."

"You drank a Handful to climb that scarp."

"I did. And I'm not going to drink one to climb a stair, because a stair's got a rail." Her mother looked down at her. "Love. They're going to say household and contribution and head of, and all of it's going to be about me, because I'm the one in the bed. I'd like to be in the room when they say it. I've been in the back of a wagon for a month while people decided things about me over my head. I've been in a bed for two days while a very kind man with a folder told me things. I'd like one room in this place where I'm the one doing the talking."

Callie looked at the stove.

"All right," she said.

"Thank you."

"I'll count the stairs."

"Don't you dare," said her mother.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

"What do they want?" said her mother later, to the hut. "At a review. From a woman with one hand."

"Contribution," said Pell. He was sitting on the floor by the door with the atlas on his knee. He had a sheet of paper inside the cover with columns ruled on it, and he had been writing in the columns all afternoon. "That's the word they'll use. Contribution. They'll read out what's on the sheet, and what's on the sheet is three Handfuls lifted, less station, and a sponsor line in Katori's name, and the girl's wages off the Sag. Which are a day's pay a day, when she's fit to kneel."

"It's not a key," said Katori, from the window. "The sponsor line. The man said so at the gate. It's a line."

"Then what's the key?"

Nobody answered for a while.

"They don't have keys," said Pell at last. "They have columns. You put enough in the columns and it opens, and nobody ever tells you how much is enough, because it changes." He looked at his paper. "I've been trying to work out the number. I can't. It's a sum with half of it written on the other side of a door."

Callie's mother sat with her hand on the stick.

"I grew up in a scale house," she said.

They looked at her.

"At Thistle Ford. My father's name was on the door. He weighed grain for the elevator for forty years, and I sat in the window from the time I could see over the ledge and read the beam for him when his eyes went." She moved her left hand on the stick. "I can read a beam. I could read a beam when I was seven. I can read one with my left hand and catch a short weight with my eyes shut, because you hear a short weight before you see it. The beam comes up too fast."

"Mum—"

"The girl at the weighbridge is going to the Director's yard," said her mother. "I heard it at the pump this morning. The woman with the red scarf said the tally girl's on the list. So they'll be short a tally." She looked round the hut. "I'd like somebody to tell me why that's not a contribution."

Nobody told her.

Pell looked at her for a long moment. Then he bent his head over his ruled sheet and wrote, and when he had finished he turned it round and held it up so she could see. There was a new line at the bottom of the contribution column, in his small neat hand.

T. — tally, weighbridge. Her call. Concur — P.

"There," said Pell. "That's in the book."

[Dry, precise narration; quiet institutional pressure]

Callie did not count the stairs.

It was the hardest morning she had spent in Meridian. The yard office was a long concrete building on the north side of the yard with a door at the front and a steel stair up the outside to a second door on the floor above, and the review room was on the first floor, at the top of an inside stair with a rail on the left. Her mother went up it with her left hand on the rail and the stick in her right, which did not work, and then with the stick hung on her wrist by its cord and her right hand doing nothing at all, which did. Callie walked one step below her with her own hands at her sides. Not holding. Only there.

It was fourteen steps. She knew that without counting. She knew it the way you know how many fingers you have. She did not say it.

At the top her mother stood for a while and got her breath, with her hand on the post of the rail.

"You counted," she said.

"I didn't."

"You're a terrible liar, love. It's the only thing I've ever been sorry about in you."

The room had a long table and three chairs behind it and two chairs in front of it. There was a window, and a stove that was not lit, and a jar of water on the table with three cups. The man in the long coat sat on the left, with his coat on. On the right was a woman of about fifty with a red face and a ledger. In the middle was an old man with a white moustache and very pale eyes, who looked at them when they came in and then looked at the window and did not look at them again.

"Please," said the woman with the ledger, and waved at the chairs.

Callie's mother sat. It took her a while. Nobody hurried her.

"Household review," said the woman, and opened the ledger. "Yard C, second row, hut fourteen. Conditional admittance, fourteen days, reviewable, fourteen days being today." She ran her finger down the page. "Household, two. Head of household, for the window, the daughter, aged thirteen, the mother being a clinical admission—"

"Strike that," said Callie's mother.

The woman looked up.

"Ma'am?"

"The window can have its column. I've no quarrel with the window." Her mother sat very straight, with the stick across her knees and her left hand on it. "But this isn't the window. This is a room. And I'm sitting in it with my own mouth, and I'm the head of this household, and she's my daughter." She paused. "She's thirteen. It's on your sheet. I'd like it read out as that and nothing else."

The woman with the ledger looked at the man in the long coat.

"It's noted," said the man in the long coat.

[Dry, precise narration; quiet institutional pressure]

The woman read out the sheet.

It was very short. Callie had known it would be short and still it was shorter than she had thought. Three Handfuls, lifted, less station, weighed at the south gate on the day of admission. A sponsor line, in a name the woman read out carefully, in full, which Callie had not heard before and which made Katori, standing at the back of the room by the door with her cap in her hands, go very still. Wages on the Sag crew, for the daughter, two days out of the last four. A fee against the ash for a horse's leg.

"And a line," said the woman, and turned the page, "this morning, from the weighbridge." She frowned at it. "T., tally."

"That's me," said Callie's mother.

The woman looked at her.

"I grew up in a scale house at Thistle Ford," said her mother. "My father weighed grain on the elevator scale for forty years. I read the beam for him from the time I could see over the ledge." She said it without any hurry at all. "I can't use my right hand. I don't need it for a beam. I can read a beam left-handed, and catch a short weight before the man on the plate knows he's done it. Your weighbridge is short a tally from tomorrow. I heard it said at the pump."

"It is," said the man in the long coat.

"Then I'd like to be your tally."

The old man in the middle turned from the window and looked at her. It was the first time he had looked at anything but the window since they came in. He looked at her for a long time with his very pale eyes.

"And the fits, ma'am?" he said. His voice was thin and dry. "It's on the long building's note. Fits. What does the weighbridge do if you have a fit on the plate?"

"It waits," said Callie's mother. "Forty-one seconds, last time. Nearly three minutes the time before, on the plain, before I had any pills. I've had four since the winter. The pills have made them shorter and further apart. My daughter counts them." She did not look at Callie. "If I have one on the plate, the old man in the apron can sit down and have a cup of tea, and when I've finished I'll read him his beam. I read it better than the girl does. I've watched her. She's quick and she's careless and she writes her sevens like ones."

The old man looked at her a moment longer. Something moved under the white moustache. Then he turned back to the window.

"And the—" said Callie's mother, and stopped.

Callie saw it happen. She saw her mother's mouth move on nothing, the way it did now sometimes, going down into the dark for a word the way you reach into a bag for a tool you know is there and find everything but the tool. One second. Two. Nobody in the room spoke. The woman with the ledger opened her mouth to help and the man in the long coat put one finger on the table, very lightly, and she closed it again.

Three.

"The contract," said her mother. "The paper with the seasons on it. That the man in eleven signed. I want it written down that nobody in my household is signing one. Not for this. Not for an address." She let out her breath. "That's all."

"It's noted," said the man in the long coat.

He told her.

He had told it once on a card and once to a man on a step. He had never told it out loud to somebody who wrote it down while he talked, and he found it came out differently. It came out in order.

The lean. How it lived under his breastbone, a finger's width behind it, and leaned, neither up nor down, like a floor in an old house. How it leaned toward his brother when his brother was worse. How he had first felt it on the road, three nights running, with his hand on Tonk. How it was right four times in five, and when it was wrong it was wrong in the direction he wanted.

"No."

She wrote.

The warmth. He told the snow shelter: four stones in the fire, and the four stones packed round his brother's back and feet, and pushing at the thing, pushing like a man leaning on a door, and nothing; and then stopping, and it coming. Tonk turned his head and looked at his brother, sitting on the floor of the corridor with his back against the wall.

"Myself," he said to him, with enormous satisfaction.

"Yourself," said Jab. His voice did not work very well. "Can you get up now?"

"No," said Doctor Keel.

"When?" said Tonk.

"Spring," said Doctor Keel, and went back up the slope as fast as she had come down it.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

The grey-haired man was still in the doorway. He was looking at Callie, not at Jab.

"You counted," he said.

"Ten, four times in twenty-two runs," said Callie. "Same as the tenth day."

The man looked at her for a long moment.

"Same as the tenth day," he said. "That's the first good news I've had off that rack in a month." He rubbed the ink on his hand with his thumb. "It doesn't mean it's getting better. It means it's not getting worse this week."

"I know," said Callie.

"I'd like you to count it on the twenty-first day," he said. "When the old woman's in. If you're able."

Callie looked at Jab, sitting on the floor. Then back at the man.

"I'll be here," she said.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

At the tenth hour the ward turned the visitors out.

Jab tied the end of the long cord to the bed rail, the way he had every night since the second, and checked the knot, and checked it again. Above Tonk's bed there was a frame now, two tall legs and a crossbar, and hanging from the crossbar on a chain there was a short smooth bar, like the rail of a gate, at the height of a small boy's reach. Tonk had pulled on it twice before he fell asleep. He had not got his shoulders off the pillow either time. He had said, both times, "That's further."

In the next bed, Senna lay on her back with her hands folded on the blanket and her eyes on the ceiling.

"Milo Faust," she said.

She said it to the ceiling, not loudly, in the voice of somebody stating a fact they have stated before and will state again. Jab had heard her do it last night, and the night before, at about this hour. He had not asked. It was not his.

Tonk was not asleep.

"Who's Milo?" he said, into the dark.

Senna did not answer at once. Jab stood by the bed with the knot under his fingers and did not move.

"A boy with a lamp," said Senna.

Tonk thought about this.

"Where is he?"

"He's what I say every night," said Senna. "So he's somewhere."

It was quiet for a long time in the ward. Down at the far end a nurse turned the small lamp lower. Jab thought his brother had gone to sleep.

"Can I say it?" said Tonk.

Senna turned her head on the pillow and looked across at the small shape in the next bed, under its frame, with the bar hanging over it like a rail.

"Yes," she said. "You can say it."

"Milo," said Tonk, to the ceiling, the way she had. And then, in a smaller voice, because he was four and it was dark and he had had his picture today: "Milo Faust."

"There," said Senna. "That's two of us."

Jab went out past Mrs Lask at her desk, who did not look up, and out into the frozen street under three lamps that would go out at the first hour. He walked home in the lit bits. At the loose grating between the second pole and the third he stepped wide without thinking about it.

On the step of twelve he sat down, and after a while he went down, under his breastbone, to look at the bucket. There was a hand of dark in the bottom of it, and a finger up from the bottom, scratched on the inside, a line.

Not for anybody, she had said.

He looked at the line for a long time. Then he came back up, and sat on his step in the cold with his hands on his knees, and did not decide anything.

Chapter 12 — Toren: From the Ground Up

[Focused, grounded narration; keep physical instruction clear]

By the third morning the yard had a shape.

Toren could see it from the corner of the east shed, where he left the chair for Senna, out of the wind with its back to the stove pipe. He saw it the way he saw everything now, as weight, and where it went. The first lane ran along the shed wall for sixty paces, and Rook had spent two afternoons putting things in it out of the scrap bins: three posts sunk in the cinders at uneven distances, a length of old rope strung between two of them at the height of a man's hip, a timber frame at the far end made from two uprights and a crossbar and four iron brackets that did not match. Nothing in the first lane was straight, and nothing was where you expected it. Rook said that was the point.

The second lane ran to the sand heap by the berm. It was old ballast sand, grey and coarse, dumped there when the wagon lane closed and never moved, and Wyck had claimed it the way a dog claims a step. He sat on top of it most of the day with his bar across his knees and his strapped arm across his chest, and told people how to stand, and how to fall, and where they were putting their weight, and why that was stupid. There were four straw sacks at the foot of the heap and a post wrapped in old blanket. Otto spent most of his mornings there, falling over on purpose.

The third lane was the shed. It was not a lane at all, but Rook had painted a line to its door anyway, so that it would have one. Inside it was the stove and the cot and the table with the brass scale, and at the far end the bucket under the drip, going tick. Dessa's table stood against the wall outside the door, where the light was, with the big book open on it and a stone on each page to keep the wind off.

That was all of it. Three lines of whitewash on the cinders, some scrap, a heap of sand and a shed that leaked. Toren had been in it for two days. He had already found that he walked differently when he crossed from one lane into the next, and that he could not have said why.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

"Two," said Dee. "Know how much of yours there is."

She had a glass in her hand. It was small, the height of her palm, with a brass frame round it and grey sand inside, and when she turned it over the sand began to run through the waist of it in a thin grey thread.

"One turn's a minute," she said. "Near enough. I've had it since I was fourteen. It's the only thing I took off the wire that wasn't on my back."

Toren saw Rook, on the shed step, look at the glass and then look away.

"This isn't a Reading," she said. "Elias has taught some of you Readings. That's how much of the room's lit. It's a good question. This is a different one. This is how much oil's left in the lamp, today." She set the glass on Dessa's table. "Everybody does the smallest thing their door does, and holds it, from wherever you are now, down to your floor. You feel for the floor. You don't go through it. When you feel it, you stop, and I write down how many turns of the glass that took. Tomorrow we do it again. It's not a race. The numbers don't compare between doors. They compare between days."

"What's a floor?" said the weighbridge girl.

"The last place you can stop," said Jab, before Dee could answer. "And still walk home, and still do it again tomorrow."

The woman looked at him. Then she nodded, and did not say anything else about it.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

Callie went first, because she was nearest. She stood in the first lane with her feet planted and her hands at her sides, and a shine came up over her like old glass, a skin's width off her coat, and she stood in it. Her lips moved. Toren knew she was counting. The woman watched the glass.

At thirty-eight, by Callie's lips, the shine went off her.

"Floor," said Callie.

"Thirty-eight seconds, standing," said the woman, and Dessa wrote it. "That's today."

The weighbridge girl did her blade, lit. It stood out of her fist straight and level with its frost-pale line along the edge, and she held it very still and did not look at it, and her face got whiter and whiter, and at a turn of the glass and most of another she said, "That's it, I think, is that it?" and the woman said, "You tell me," and she said, "That's it," and the blade went.

Jab lit his knife and held it. He held it through one turn of the glass, and two, and three, standing easily in the lane with the amber line lying along the edge of that fat ugly blade, and at the fifth turn he yawned.

"That'll do," said the woman. "I believe you. Put it out before you fall asleep."

"I can do it all day," said Jab. "If it's only the light."

"I know. I read your card." She turned to Toren. "You."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

Toren took the stone out of his pocket.

He had been waiting for this since the morning before. He had lain awake in hut eleven for part of the night waiting for it, with his hand in his coat pocket on the stone and not closing on it, which was the only way he had found to keep his hand there at all.

The stone was warm. It had been warm for fifteen days, since a night on a step when he had stopped checking. It came and went under his fingers like something breathing, the least impressive thing anybody had ever felt. He did not know how full it was. He had not asked. He had been afraid, every day for fifteen days, that asking would be the same as checking, and that checking would put it out, and that this time it would stay out.

"It's not a question you can ask me," he said.

The woman waited.

"The last time it went out," said Toren, "I didn't know when it was coming back. The time before that, it was two days. I asked it, every forty steps, for two months, if it was still there. And the asking put it out." He stopped. "Rook says so. Callie says so. It's the one thing I've learned in this place that I know is true."

"Checking puts it out," said the woman. "Yes. I'm not asking you to check."

"What's the difference?"

"Checking's asking every forty steps whether it's still there," she said. "Because you're afraid it isn't. It's asking the same question over and over and not listening to the answer, because the answer isn't what you're asking for. You're asking to be told you're not going to lose it." She did not say it unkindly. "Measuring is asking once, properly, and writing the answer down, and then leaving it alone. You don't have to believe the answer. You only have to write it."

Toren looked at the glass on the table.

"One," said the woman. "The spike. Dark. Not lit. Not the other thing with your legs, and not both, and I know about both, and Dessa's told me she told you not this year. Just the spike, dark, until you feel the floor. Then stop. And don't look at the stone. Look at the glass."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

He held the stone in his right hand, with the seam across his palm, and let the spike come.

It came the way it always came, not the way he wanted it. It came up out of his fist crooked and ugly, as long as his forearm, thick at the root with a bad heavy heel to it, grey and blunt and dark. Garrick had looked at it on the day it first came, in a stone cut with husks coming up the road, and said keep the ugly shape, stop trying to be good at it. Rook had looked at it for two months and not let him improve it. It sat on his fist now like a thing that had been dropped there, and he held it.

The woman turned the glass.

He did not look at the stone. He looked at the sand. It ran through the waist of the glass in a grey thread, and piled up in the bottom in a little grey hill, and the hill got taller.

Holding the spike cost something. He had never let himself notice what. He noticed it now, because he was looking for it, and it was a small steady draw from somewhere behind his breastbone, like water going out of a barrel through a pinhole. It was not frightening. It was only a thing that was happening.

The woman turned the glass again.

Somewhere in the second turn, he felt it. It was not the stone going cold. It was not a door closing. It was a thinning, the way a rope thins when you feel the strands begin to go under your hands before it parts, and he knew the way you know you have been walking too long that there was a place a little way below here where he would not be able to get up again.

"There," he said.

He let the spike go. It went back into the stone. The stone was warm in his palm. It was still warm. It was exactly as warm as it had been before he started, which was to say it was faint, and breathing, and there.

"Two turns and a quarter," said the woman. "Dark." Dessa wrote it. "That's today."

It was not much. Toren knew it was not much. Callie's thirty-eight seconds had been standing in a Ward, which cost everything, and the weighbridge girl's turn and three-quarters had been lit, and Jab had yawned at five. Two and a quarter, dark, was the smallest number anybody had said, for the cheapest thing anybody had done.

He stood in the first lane with the stone in his hand and found that he did not mind.

He had asked it how much. He had asked it once, and it had answered, and it was still there. For the first time since the Breach he had put a question to it and it had not gone out.

"Thank you," he said to the woman.

She looked at him over the glass for a moment. Then she wrote something in her own book, not Dessa's, and Toren did not see what.

"Write why," said Senna, from her chair by the stove pipe.

"Because tomorrow," said the woman, before Dessa could look at her, "you'll need to know whether today was a good day."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

"You fall like a dropped plate," said Wyck.

He said it from the top of the sand heap, in the flat voice he used for things that were simply true. Toren was lying at the bottom of the heap on his good side, in the sand, where Wyck had told him to fall.

"I fell like you said."

"You fell like you'd been told to fall. That's different. You went down like a plate off a shelf, all at once, and you put your hand out." Wyck pointed with the bar at Toren's right hand, which was flat in the sand where it had landed. "You put your hand out and that's how people break their wrists. I know. I've done it." He did not say which time. "You fall on the road every time you do the thing with your legs. Dessa says eleven times since you started it. She counted. So you might as well learn to do it properly."

"How do you do it properly?"

"Like a sack," said Wyck. "A full sack. You don't reach for the ground. You let the ground come and you give it something round." He thought about it. "Tuck the chin. Round the back. Take it on the meat, not the points. Roll the way it wants to go. Don't put your hand down, ever, for any reason, even if your mother's at the bottom of the heap."

"And you know how to fall."

"I don't fall," said Wyck. "I've had a lot of time to watch other people do it."

Toren fell eleven more times. The last three he did it like a sack, or like something that had once seen a sack, and Wyck said "Better" once and "That'll do" once and said nothing at all the third time, which Otto told him afterward was the best thing Wyck said to anybody.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]
