He was still at the strut with the husk on it. He looked at the carrier on its board by the heap of boxes, with one box in it and the lid lying on the board beside it.

"Lid on it," said Dee. "Leave the box. Out."

Toren let the strut go. The husk fell forward onto the floor where the strut had been, and began to get up. He did not wait for it. He took the lid off the board with his good hand and dropped it into the groove on the carrier, where it went in with a soft heavy sound, and he turned.

"Out," said Dee. "Stair. Toren last."

Jab went.

Chapter 36 — The Door That Opens Toward You

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build urgency without rushing]

They came out of the room in the order Dee had said and turned east, toward the stair.

Jab went first, with the frame on his back and the lantern swinging from it, walking fast and holding his right hand away from his side. Dee went behind him with the open jar in the crook of her arm and the glass in her fist, and Callie behind her with the hook. Toren came last. They kept to the room side of the corridor, along the wall with the doors in it, away from the tray, and the steel door stood open twelve paces ahead of them with the stair beyond it.

Nobody ran. Running was how you went down on a floor like that, and Toren had one arm.

Behind them, in the room, the short husk had got up off the floor, and they heard it come out after them, the dry soft sound of it on the concrete.

Toren did not look round for it. He knew where it was the way he knew where the others were.

He looked west instead, once.

The heap was at the second door now. It filled the corridor from wall to wall, grey, higher than his waist, with the rope in the tray going down into it from above like a rope going into a well. It came on. It was slower than a man walking, and faster than he had thought anything that size could be. At the three the line of light opened in the middle of it, the colour of the edge of the sky, and stayed open for three breaths, and shut.

Toren turned his back on it and walked east.

"Door," said Callie, ahead of him.

They had all stopped. Jab was standing a pace short of the steel door with his lantern held up, and he was not going through.

There had been a heap on the corridor side of that door since before any of them was born: twenty years of grey come under the gap in threads. It had lain against the steel a hand deep all afternoon while its threads went west. It was not lying now. It had swelled. It had drawn itself up into a hump against the wall beside the door, between them and the doorway, the way the corner in the room had drawn up. Toren came up behind the others just as the push came. At the three the hump cracked along the top, and something came up out of it.

"Husk," said Jab. "In front."

It stood up in the corridor a pace from the steel door, faceless, between them and the stair, and it turned toward the lantern on Jab's frame.

Toren looked back. The short husk was coming along the wall behind him, and the heap was coming behind the husk, past the second door, toward the first.

He did the sum, and it was not a long one. A husk in front and a husk behind, and a thing he did not have a name for behind that. And every one of them, if it was killed, would lie on the floor for ten breaths and stand up again.

"Callie," he said. "Hold the front one."

She did not ask him how. She put the back of the hook's curve down on the concrete in front of the husk, still, and it went pale, and the husk came at the lantern and walked into the hook and stopped.

"Holding," said Callie.

"Jab. Dee. Round it. Through the door. Up."

There was room. The hook stood across the corridor at a slant, from Callie's hands down to the curve on the floor, with the husk pushing against the curve, and between the curve and the open doorway there was a gap a pace wide along the tray wall. Jab went through it sideways, with the frame scraping the concrete, and the husk turned its blank front toward him as he passed and did not come, because the hook was in its way. Dee went through behind him with the jar. Then the two of them were in the flat place at the foot of the stair.

"Callie," said Toren. "Now you."

"If I let go, it comes."

"Let it come." He had the spike on his fist, and he did not light it. "I'll hold the door."

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

Callie let go. She lifted the curve off the floor and went through the gap sideways past the husk, and the husk came after her, to the doorway, to the steel frame she had just gone through.

Toren went past it on the other side.

He did not go past it the way Callie had. He went the way he had gone past the husk on the strut in the room, close, on its blind side, the side away from where it was turning, and he came through the doorway into the flat place a breath after it did. It was in front of him now, going for the lantern on Jab's frame at the foot of the stair.

He lit the heel.

It turned. It came at the light on his fist, because the light on his fist was nearer than the lantern. He put the lit hook into it low, and dragged it round against the steel of the door, and put the point in. It came apart against the door, and the grey fell at the foot of the steel in a heap.

He did not look at the heap. He knew what it would do.

"Up," he said. "All of you. Don't wait."

"Toren—" said Callie.

"Up," said Toren. "I'll shut it."

He put his good hand flat on the steel of the door, at the edge, and pushed.

It did not want to go. It had opened toward them. It had come off its stick with a shriek and swung toward them as wide as a man, and stood there. Now it had to go back the other way, away from him, into the corridor, and it was heavy, and it was stiff, and he had one arm.

He put his shoulder to it, and it went a hand's width and stuck. He set his feet and leaned his whole weight on it the way he had leaned on the rack in the north yard, and it went again, and it swept the heap of the husk he had just killed along the floor in front of it, into the corridor.

Through the narrowing gap he saw the short husk at the door of the first room, coming. Behind it, filling the corridor at the first door now, there was the heap, and at the three the light opened in the middle of it.

He put his shoulder to the door, and it shut. It went the last hand's width with a sound like a great weight set down, iron on iron, in the frame.

He stood with his shoulder against it, breathing. Above him he could hear the others on the stair: Jab first, his boots slow and heavy with the frame, then Dee's quick steps, then Callie's. They were at the landing. They were going on up.

The door moved.

It moved against his shoulder. It did not open. It moved a finger's width in its frame, the way a door moves when somebody on the other side of it puts a hand flat on it and leans.

The husk.

He understood it with his shoulder against the steel. He had forgotten it until now. The door had opened toward them, which meant it pulled from this side. So from the other side, from the corridor, it pushed. Anybody in the corridor who leaned on it would open it.

It moved again, a finger's width, and came back.

He did not decide anything. There was nothing to decide. He took his shoulder off the door and stepped back from it, and put the foot of a strut down on the concrete of the flat place two paces from the door. He let it come up at its slant from the floor to the steel, at the height of his chest, the way you set a plank against a door you want kept shut.

It met the steel just as the door began to open. The door stopped. It stood a finger open in its frame, with the strut against it and something on the other side pushing it, and the push came down the strut into the floor and not into him, because he was soft.

"Holding," he said, to nobody.

It was the husk. He could feel what it was: a husk's weight, a steady blank push with nothing behind it, the same as it had been on the strut in the room. It pushed, and it pushed, and he paid for it by the breath.

"Toren!" Callie's voice came down from the landing. "Toren, where are you?"

"The door," he said. "It opens from their side. I'm holding it. Go up."

"Toren—"

"Go up. When you're at the top, say."

He heard her go.

He counted breaths. He looked at the steel in the light of the lantern on his belt, and he counted, and once he went down to look. The stone was less than half. It had been less than half when he came out of the room, because he had held the husk on the strut in there for the whole of Jab on the rope, and Jab on his knees, and Dee drawing. He had not been able to think about it then. He thought about it now. There was less than half, and it was going.

Then the push changed.

It did not get stronger all at once. It got heavier, the way the weight had got heavier on the strut at the wash when the crown went. Something else had come up against the other side of the door, behind the husk, and it was not a husk's weight. It was slow and enormous, and it did not push the way a husk pushed. It leaned. It leaned the way the whole cart had leaned on him over the arch.

He felt the strut take it. He felt it go down into the concrete of the flat place, and the concrete hold it, and his stone go out from under it like water out of a basin with the plug pulled.

Every breath there's a wheel on it, I pay for.

This was not a wheel.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

At the top of the stair the square of grey light from the hall lay across the last three steps. Jab came up into it first, with the frame, and then Dee, and then Callie, and Callie turned round on the top step and put her voice down the stair as hard as she could.

"We're up!" she said. "Toren! We're up!"

"Out of the hall," said Dee. "To the door. Now."

Callie did not go to the door. She crouched on the top step instead and laid the hook across the top of the stair, from the wall to the yellow rail, with the curve down flat on the concrete. They watched it go pale.

"He's got a light on his belt," she said, without looking round. "If anything's behind him, it's coming at that."

Dee looked at the hook, and at her, and did not say out again. She stood back against the wall of the hall with the open jar in the crook of her arm and the glass in her fist. Jab stood beside her with his right hand held away from his side and his left hand on the frame's strap, and the three of them listened down the stair.

Below them, at the door, Toren felt the stone go.

He had felt it go before, at the wash, at the ring stone, and he knew what it was. There was nothing at the bottom of him now but his own, two turns and not the bit, and the strut was on that, and the weight on the other side of the door did not care whose it was.

He counted three more breaths. He did not know why. So that it was a number.

He let go.

He was on the fourth step when the door opened behind him. He heard it. It came off the strut's place and swung toward the flat place with the shriek it had made the first time, all the way, and hit the concrete wall at the end of its swing with a sound he felt in his teeth. He did not look round. He went up the stair. He went up it the way he had gone up the loose bank at the wash on his own strut-steps, only these were real steps, concrete, and he took them two at a time with his left arm against his chest and his right hand on the yellow rail.

The lantern on his belt swung and knocked against his hip and threw his shadow up the stair in front of him, enormous.

Husks come at a light.

He heard it behind him on the stair. It was the dry soft sound on the concrete, coming up, not fast, but faster than him.

At the top the others heard it too. They heard the door hit the wall, and Toren's boots on the stair two at a time, and under his boots the other sound, and Jab's lips moved without anything coming out of them.

Toren came round the landing and up the second flight. At the top, in the square of grey light from the hall, there was Callie, crouched on the top step with the hook laid across the stair from the wall to the rail, the curve pale on the concrete.

"Over it," she said. "Step over. It's only the steel."

He stepped over it.

The husk came up the last of the stair behind him, and walked into the hook, and stopped.

It stood on the top step of the yellow stair with the pale curve across its front, and pushed, and pushed. Its grey went on up the stair behind it in the light from the hall. Toren stood in the hall with his back against the wall and looked at it.

"Kill it," said Callie. "Against the hook. It'll go down the stair."

He lit the heel. He did not have much to light it with. He lit it anyway, off his own, a hand's width of thin white-grey along the hook of the spike, and came round the end of the rail and put it into the husk from the side, low, and dragged it round against Callie's curve, and put the point in.

It came apart against the Ward, against the still steel of the hook.

The grey fell. It fell down the stair behind the hook, down the steps, in a long slow slide toward the landing and the door and the dark, and none of it came over the curve.

"Down," said Callie. She lifted the hook, and the Ward went out.

They stood in the hall of the long building, all four of them, in the light from the door, and breathed. Nobody said anything for a while.

"It opens toward you," said Toren at last. His voice was not steady. "From the other side, it opens away. It pushes." He looked at the stair. "Gran never said."

"Your gran was never on the other side of it," said Dee.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

They went out of the long building and down the road with nothing to drag.

It was the middle of the afternoon. The sun was over the drum behind them, going down into the wrong sky, and the light on the yard below had gone yellow. The wind had not come. The grey lay in its combed lines going up the road, and they walked down beside them on the inside, along the pipes, the way they had come up.

At the top of the road Callie stopped and turned round and looked up, because she had said she would. Toren stopped with her and took out the paper.

She counted, and they watched her lips. Ten. Three. Ten. At the end of the fourth ten, as the edge thinned, the long grey veil came down out of the bottom of the dark over the drum and went down behind the broken rim.

"One," said Callie.

She counted on. At the ninth count there was another.

"Two," she said. "In twelve." She looked at Toren. "It was one in twelve going in."

He wrote it. Coming out: 2 in 12.

"Is that more?" said Jab.

"It's two," said Callie. "It's not enough counts to say more. It's what I saw."

Rook was where he had said he would be. He was sitting at the foot of the first post at the near end of the bridge, with his coat over his shoulders and his face grey and wet. He had seen them come out of the long building at the top of the road, and he watched them all the way down the Z, and across the yard along the pipes, and through the gate.

At the gate Toren stopped. The green copper wire was hanging on the fence where he had left it. He took it down, and brought the gate round on its hinges, scraping, and put the chain twice round the frame and the post. Then he twisted the wire through the two ends of the chain, round and round, one-handed, with Callie holding the chain so it did not swing. It took a long time. He did not tuck the ends in. He left them so they would come.

"Why?" said Callie.

"Because we're coming back," said Toren.

They crossed the bridge on the outside planks, not the middle one. At the near end Rook looked up at them from the foot of the post, one after another, as they came off the planks onto the gravel. He did not get up. He counted them out loud, which Toren had never heard him do.

"Dee," he said. "Jab. Callie." He looked at Toren last, and longest. "Toren."

"Four," said Toren.

"Four," said Rook. "In." He looked at Jab's hand, held away from his side, and he looked at it for a long time. "Wash," he said. "Then tell me."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

They washed. Coat off. Shake it. Wash at the river below the pump house, the hands and the face and the hair, before you eat.

Toren did it one-handed, on his knees at the edge of the water, with Callie's counter going along each of them afterward. Jab did it with his right hand held flat on the surface of the river and not put into it, because Dee had said not to put the white place in anything cold until she had looked at it again.

Toren took the canvas bag off his shoulder. The two vent jars in it were stoppered and heavy and hot, and one of them was the jar from the rope. Callie held the counter to the other one, the jar from the first lift, at a hand.

"Forty," she said. "Out here, where the river reads seven."

Dee carried them both to the far end of the gravel herself, away from the water, and stood them beside the flat stone with the chalk cross on it where the rag was buried.

"They're not going on the cart," she said.

Then the three of them stood in a row on the gravel by the cold fire, and Dee drew them.

She did all three. Jab could not work, but he could watch, and he did. He stood at her side with his left palm out and his right held against his chest like Toren's arm, and said vent before she needed it, and when she had finished the three of them he took the leftovers out of her hands with his left palm only.

"Callie," said Dee.

Callie weighed the jar.

"Three out of two," she said. "For the four of us at the stair, and here, and Jab's arm again." She set it down. "Five in it. Three whole." She did not wait to be asked for the rest. "Twenty-nine. One over today's line."

"One over," said Dee.

She measured their floors.

"Your stone's gone," she said to Toren. "Your own's a turn. And a bit." She looked at him. "You held that door on your own."

"I held it on the stone," said Toren. "Then I held it on my own. Then I let go."

"When?"

"When they said up." He looked at the hill. "Three breaths after."

Dee wrote it.

Callie's stone was a quarter. Her own was where it had been in the morning. Dee's stone was half, where the watch had taken it. Jab's floor was a finger, and his own was less than a hand, and his arm was warm from the elbow down, and the heel of his right palm was white and shiny and would not feel.

Dee held his hand in both of hers, turned up, in the last of the sun.

"It's fixed," she said. "You know it's fixed."

"I know."

"It'll not come back." She did not let go. "It might go red. It might blister. If it blisters, I'll do what Sowerby would, and keep it clean, and it'll close. But it'll not feel, there. Not that bit." She looked at him. "Can you draw with it?"

Jab put his right palm flat on his own left forearm and shut his eyes.

"Yes," he said. "Round it. Not with the bit."

"Then it's a mark," said Dee. "Not a hand." She let him go. "It's the first one the work's put on you that I can't take off. It won't be the last." She wrote it. "Vell had one. On the heel of his hand. The same place."

Pell had been counting since noon.

He was sitting on the cart with his back to the rack and his leg out and the atlas open on his knee. Beside it lay a sheet of Senna's route paper, and on the back of the sheet Pell had made marks: strokes in rows, some of them with a cross through them. Callie looked at the rows of strokes for a moment longer than anybody else did.

"I counted it on my own heart," said Pell. "I've no glass. It's sixty to a turn if you sit still, near enough. I sat still." He held out the sheet. "It never missed. Ten and three. From noon, when you went through the gate, till you came out of that door at the top. Every count."

"And what came out of it?" said Toren.

"Grey." Pell put his finger on the strokes with the cross through them. "Out of the bottom. At the three. Down into the round one. It's like watching rain a long way off, over there, when it isn't raining here." He looked up. "Seven. Seven that I saw, from noon till you came out at the top. That's two hours and more." He tapped the sheet. "I missed some. I'd look down to mark one, and look up, and not know if I'd missed the next. And you can't look at that edge long. It gets in your eyes."

"Callie saw one going in," said Toren. "In twelve. And two coming out."

"Then she saw more than I did," said Pell. "She was looking up, and I was looking down at my marks half the time. It's more toward the end than the start. I'd not swear to it." He folded the sheet. "Write it. I'll count it again tomorrow. Somebody will want to know if it's more."

Toren wrote it. Pell's count, from the cart. Ten and three, every count. 7 falls of grey seen, gate (noon) to the top of the road coming out, 2 hours and more. He missed some, looking down to mark. More toward the end (Pell's not sure).

He looked at what he had written. It was the Director's count. It was the thing she had asked for, count what comes out of it and write it down, and it was the first thing on the paper that was hers.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

They told it at the fire.

Dee lit it with the last of the wrack from the morning and put the pot on for Rook's back, and they sat round it in the dusk on the gravel outside the fence, on the right side of the river. Toren said it. He said it the way he had said the evidence at the edge of the water on the forty-third: in order, all of it.

The yard. The lines going up the road. The door at the top, and the stair, and the yellow rail. The door at the bottom that opened toward you, and pulled open in thirty breaths. The corridor going west. The tray, and the rope in it, crawling. The first room, and the boxes on the floor, hundreds of them, the way Gran had said, with the rope gone in among them like roots. Three live ones, and one of those open. One in the carrier.

"One in the carrier," said Pell.

"In the room," said Toren. "With the lid on. Where we left it."

He told the rest. The heap in the corner, and the husk that stood up out of it, that he had killed and that had come back. The same one. The cut in the strands, and how it had mended in the three. Callie's lee across the door, and how it had stopped the floor and not the rope. Jab's palm's worth, into a vent jar, and the husk coming back a hand short.

He told them about the rope. He did not look at Jab while he told it. He told it the way Jab had said it on the floor of the room with his arm in Dee's hands. It thought I was a hole in it. It thought I was a wound, and it was mending me. He told them what Dee had done.

Rook, on the canvas by the fire, did not say anything. He had his eyes on Jab's hand.

Then Toren told them about the thing on the rope: the heap as high as a waist, coming along the corridor, pulling itself along its own rope with nothing to pull with. The light that opened in it at the three. The red. The door, and what the door did from the other side.

"It came along the rope," he said. "From the west. From the round one, or from somewhere between. It came to where we were. To where the husk had been killed, and the grey was lying. And to him." He did not look at Jab. "It came to us."

"It came to you," said Rook.

He said it quietly, from the canvas, with his eyes half shut.

"If it comes to you," said Rook, "you do what you have to do and you come home." He opened his eyes. "You came home."

"We came home with one box," said Toren. "In a room, under a hill, behind a door that opens away from it."

"What is it?" said Pell.

For a while nobody answered.

"It's lifting," said Jab.

He was sitting by the fire with his right hand on his knee, palm up, and the white place was catching the light. He had not said anything since the river.

"It lifts like we lift," he said. "Flat. At the rate it comes. It draws for ten, and it vents for three. Only it vents where it wants a thing. Into a heap, and a husk stands up. Into a cut, and the cut's not there." He looked at the hand. "Into a hand, if the hand's drawing on it."

"Then it's a lifter," said Rook.

He said it with the corner of his mouth moving, the way it moved when he was going to laugh and was not sure it would be allowed.

"It's got my job," he said. "Four seasons, on the worst of the north yard. And there it is, doing it for nothing, on its own hill, better than me." He looked at the fire. "A lifter."

Nobody laughed. But Callie's mouth moved, and so did Pell's.

Toren wrote it on the paper. The lifter. Jab had said what it did, and Rook had said what that made it, and nobody had a better word.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

"You've a box," said Pell.

He said it after Dee had changed Rook's pad, in the dark, with the boiled water cooling in the pot and the fire going down. He had said nothing all through the telling. He had sat on the cart and listened, the way he listened to a hub.

"You've one box," he said, "in a lead box of its own, in a room, under a hill. You've twenty-nine inside. Sixteen's the line. That's thirteen to work with. You've a road home that's cut, and a man with a fever, and a man with one leg." He was not looking at anybody. "And in the room with the box, there's a thing that mends what you do to it, every thirteen breaths, and came along a rope to see you, and had its hand in Jab."

"I know," said Toren.

"I know you know," said Pell. "I'm saying it so it's been said by somebody who's not going in." He was quiet a moment. "A box and a half short, and all of you alive, is a thing I'd take back to that woman's office and put on her table. I'd not be ashamed of it."

"The box is in the room," said Callie.

"Then it's in the room."

"Then we go home with nothing," said Callie. "And that thing's got it. And the ash that went in the door today. And everything lying on the whole of that hill, going up it, ten and three." She said it flat. "And Senna's on the narrow bed on the fifty-fourth with a man guessing."

"She is," said Pell. "And she'd say the same as me."

Toren did not know if that was true.

He thought about his grandmother on the pillow with her eyes shut, saying pull the door. She had been saving that. She had not said come back without it, and she had not needed to. She had known his father, and his father's father, and she had told him where the boxes were anyway, knowing what he would do: I know what every man in that line does with a number once he's got it. He goes and gets it, she had said. With a paper and three ifs.

He looked at the five of them round the dying fire. At Pell on the cart with his leg out, who had said it so it had been said. At Rook, hot, on the canvas, not asleep. At Dee with her book on her knee and her hands still. At Callie. At Jab with his hand palm up on his knee.

Everybody back.

He had written it, and he had meant it. He had not known, when he wrote it, that it might one day mean leaving behind a thing that everybody at home needed, so that everybody could come home.

"Tomorrow," he said.

They looked at him.

"Tomorrow we decide," said Toren. "Not tonight. With the light." He had said the same thing on the forty-sixth, and it had been right then, and he did not know if it was right now. He said the rest of it anyway. "Tonight we think about what it did. All of it. Every time it did something, and what we did, and what happened." He looked at Jab. "It mends in the three. You said. It vents where there's a hole. That's the whole of what we know. If there's a way in that, we find it tonight. If there isn't, we go home in the morning with nothing."

"And if there is?" said Dee.

"Then we go back for the box," said Toren. "And I'll say before we go what we'll pay for it. And if it costs more than that, we come out, finished or not."

Dee looked at him across the embers for a long time.

"Write that," she said.

He wrote it, under the day, under the lifter, under Pell's count.

47th. The pump house. In: 4. One box in the carrier, left in the first room, lid on. J.'s right palm: a white place on the heel, fixed. It mends in the three.

And under that, because it was true, and because there was nowhere else to put it:

Gran's door pulls. From the other side it pushes.

Chapter 37 — The Flap

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build urgency without rushing]

The pump was still in the pump house.

Callie had not looked at it the night before. She had been too cold, and too tired, and the wall had been something to put a fire against and nothing else. Now she got up from the fire and took a lantern in through the gap where the door had been, because she could not sit there and think about a rope any more, and everybody at the fire could see that she could not.

The pump stood in the middle of the stone floor under the open sky. It was iron, and it was bigger than the cart. A long iron drum lay on its side on a stone bed, and at one end of the drum there was a wheel as high as Callie, with spokes, and a rod going from the wheel into the drum. A pipe as thick as her body came up out of the floor on the river side and went into the bottom of the drum, and two more came out of the top of it and went through the wall toward the river, toward the broken pipes lying in the water.

It was all rust. It had not moved in a long time, and when Callie put her hand on the wheel, it did not move now either.

"It's a pump," said Pell, from outside.

He was on the cart, which they had drawn up against the outside of the wall so close that its rack stood a pace from the gap. When Callie held the lantern up, he could see in. He was sitting with his back to the rack and his leg out along the boards, the way he had sat all day.

"I know it's a pump," said Callie.

"I know you know," said Pell. "Ask me what you came in to ask me."

She stood by the wheel with the lantern.

"How does it work?" she said.

Pell told her. He told her the way he had told her about the wheel, sitting back with his hands on his knee, not looking at her, looking at the thing.

"It lifts," he said. "And it pushes. That's all a pump does. Two strokes." He nodded at the drum. "There's a plunger in that. The wheel goes round and the rod goes in and out. When it comes out, it lifts: it pulls the water up out of the river through that pipe in the floor, into the drum. When it goes in, it pushes: it pushes the water out of the drum, out through the top, up those pipes, over the river, up the hill. Wherever they wanted it."

"It lifts and it pushes."

"Lift, push. Lift, push." He moved his hand in time with it. "Only there's a thing in between. There's a flap."

Callie waited.

"In the bottom of the drum, where the river pipe comes in," said Pell, "there's a flap. Leather, on a hinge, like a door. When it lifts, the flap opens and the water comes up past it into the drum. When it pushes, the flap shuts, because the water's pushing on it the wrong way. So what it lifted can't go back down the pipe to the river. It's got nowhere to go but out of the top." He looked at the drum. "My father had a little one, on the farm, for the trough. A hand one. The flap went every spring. When the flap goes, you can hear it."

"What does it sound like?"

"Like it's working," said Pell. "That's the thing. It lifts, and it pushes, and it sounds like it's working all day. But it pushes the water straight back down the pipe it came up. It lifts it up and pushes it down again, the same water, all day, and nothing comes out of the top." He shook his head. "You'd not know. You'd pump for an hour and go to the trough and it'd be dry."

Callie stood very still with the lantern.

She was thinking about the heap in the corner of the room under the hill. She was thinking about the ten, and the heap drawn out into threads and gone into the rope, and the three, and the corner swelling. She was thinking about Jab with his hand on the rope by the door, saying nothing, it's going past, and then the three, and the push, and his face.

"If you wanted to stop it," she said. "The pump. If you were in the drum."

"I'd not be in the drum."

"If you were. If you wanted it to stop pushing water up the hill."

Pell thought about it. She could see him do it, the way he thought about a distance.

"You'd not do it on the lift," he said slowly. "On the lift it's got the whole river behind it. You'd stand in front of that pipe in the floor and it'd lift the river at you, and you'd not stop the river." He looked at the pipe going down into the stone. "You'd do it on the push. On the push it's only got what's in the drum. What it's just lifted. That's all it's got. A drum's worth."

"And if you took the drum's worth," said Callie. "On the push. Every time. So it pushed and nothing got up the pipe."

"Then it'd lift the river again," said Pell. "And push it at you again. And you'd take that." He was quiet. "Till the river ran out. Or you did."

"And if somebody shut the river?"

Pell looked at her properly then.

"Then it'd have a drum's worth," he said. "And no more. And it'd push it at you, and you'd take it, and it'd lift nothing, because there's nothing to lift. And it'd push again. Less." He was quiet for a long time. "It'd pump itself dry. It doesn't know how to do anything else. A pump doesn't stop because the water's gone. It stops when somebody stops the wheel."

Callie put the lantern down on the stone bed of the pump.

"Nobody stops its wheel," she said.

"Then it'd go on," said Pell. "Pushing nothing. Into whatever was taking it."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

She went out to the fire.

They were all there. Dee had changed Rook's pad and was sitting with her book. Jab was sitting with his right hand palm up on his knee. Toren had the paper. Rook lay on the canvas with his eyes open. Nobody was talking. Nobody had talked since tomorrow we decide.

"Pell," said Callie. "Say it again. The pump."

Pell said it again from the cart, while she stood by the fire with her hands open. Lift, and push, and the flap, and the river. On the lift it's got the whole river. On the push it's only got what it's lifted.

Jab had looked up at the push, and he did not look away from Pell until Pell had finished.

"On the push," said Jab.

"That's what I did wrong," he said. He said it to his hand. "I put it on the rope in the ten. On the lift. And it went past, because it had the whole hill behind it and it was going somewhere. And then the three came, and it pushed, and I was a hole." He turned the hand over. "And there was nothing shut. The whole hill was behind the push. So it kept pushing."

"If somebody shut the river," said Callie.

"The lee," said Toren.

He had put the pencil down.

"The lee stopped the floor," he said. "At the door. It stopped everything crawling in. It didn't stop the rope." He was looking at the fire, not at her. "But the rope's a thing. It's a rope. It's lying there. If the rope's cut—"

"It mends in the three," said Jab.

"It mends in the three if it can reach." Toren looked up. "If it's cut at the door, and Callie's lee is in the door, in the cut, it can't reach. It can grow up to the lee. It can't grow through it." He stopped. "Then what's in the room's all there is. That's the drum. The river's on the other side of Callie."

Nobody said anything.

Dee had opened her book, and she was not writing in it. She was looking at Toren.

"Say it in order," she said. "All of it. From the stair."

He said it in order. He said it the way he had said everything since the forty-third, the siding and the wash: not with the answers, because he did not have them, but with the questions in the right order where everybody could see them and see if they stood.

It would be in the room. Everybody agreed with that, and Rook said it from the canvas: "It goes where the grey is." The grey had been lying in the first room all afternoon, and the heap in the corner, and the husks killed and killed again. And the carrier was there. None of them thought it wanted the carrier, but it would be there.

Dee said the rest of it, so that it was said.

"It's in the first room," she said. "The room she sent us to, and the box she sent us for. It came at us there." She did not look at the hill. "So we go to the first door and no further. Not the second, not to look. Nowhere near the round one. We're not going hunting for anything. If it's not in the first room in the morning, we don't go looking for it. We come out."

There were two ways into the room from the corridor for the rope. One was the floor, through the door, where the rope would lie across the threshold. The other was the ceiling, through the hole above the door and down the wall.

"I cut both," said Toren. "The ceiling first, outside, before it goes in the hole. Then the floor at the threshold. The heel. In a ten. Before it pushes."

"And me in the door," said Callie. "On the threshold. In your cut." She held her hand out flat and tipped it back. "The lee off the curve, standing up into the corridor. And leaned back. Up the wall over the door. Over the hole. Like a lean-to, the wrong way up."

"Can you?" said Toren.

"It's a door," said Callie. "And a bit. It's still. It's on concrete." She thought about it with her lips moving, the way she did a sum. "A door's the cheapest thing I know. A door and a bit's more. And if there's husks in the corridor, and there will be, they'll come at it, and that's more again." She looked at Dee. "I want two. Settled. Tonight."

Dee did not answer at once.

"Two's more than you've ever carried," she said.

"I settle well. You said. It's the only thing I do better than Toren."

"It's not the only thing," said Toren.

"It's the only thing tonight," said Callie.

Dee looked at her for a long time. Then she wrote it.

"Two," she said. "You'll settle it slowly, and I'll sit with you, and if it slops I'll stop you at one and a half." She looked up. "And you'll be in the room."

"I'll be in the door."

"You'll be in the room," said Dee. "With your back to it. You'll be facing the corridor with the lee in front of you, and everything that's in that room will be behind you. You'll not see it. You'll not see any of it."

"I know," said Callie.

"Jab," said Toren.

"On the push," said Jab. "Not the lift. When you cut it, it'll mend. That's all it does. It'll push into the cut at the three. I put my hand on the cut, on the room side, at the three, and it pushes into me, and I take a drum's worth. And I put it in a vent jar, and stopper it. And I take my hand off." He looked at Dee. "Before the ten. Every time. Off before the ten."

"I'll say off," said Dee. "At the end of every three. Every one. You'll not wait for me to say it twice."

"I'll not wait."

"And what's in the room is all it's got," said Toren. "And every three it pushes some of it into Jab, and Jab puts it in a jar. And every ten it lifts what's lying in the room. And it's less." He stopped. "Pell said. It'll pump itself dry."

"It'll not stand there and let you," said Rook.

He said it from the canvas. He had not moved, but his voice was clear.

"It had a husk on your strut all afternoon," said Rook. "It'll make more. It'll put them in your way. It'll throw what it's got at whatever's worked, and Jab's hand is worked, and so is Callie's back. And so is you." He looked at Toren. "You'll not be cutting. You'll be keeping it off them."

"Then I'll keep it off them," said Toren. "And cut when I can." He looked at the paper. "Every rope it's got in the room is a way it moves. Every one's a way it throws. I cut them, one at a time. Every cut's a hole. Every hole, it pushes, at the three. And Jab's there."

"And when it's got nothing left to push with?" said Dee.

"It opens," said Jab. "At the three. In the middle. The light." He did not look at anybody. "I saw it open. It opens every time it pushes. That's where the push comes from."

"Then that's where I'll put the point," said Toren.

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build controlled urgency]

"Say what it costs," said Dee.

Callie said it.

"Twenty-nine," she said. "Inside. One jar open, with five in it. Three whole." She did the sum out loud, because Dee would want it out loud. "Settling tonight. Two in me, that's a Handful and three quarters more. A Handful and a half in Toren, and that's more than he's carried too. Half in you, Miss Wren, to make you one. That's three and three quarters." She stopped. "Twenty-five and a quarter. The line's sixteen. Nine and a quarter to work with."

"Nine and a quarter," said Toren.

"It's not twelve," said Callie. "It's less than today cost us."

"It's not twelve," said Toren. "It's nine and a quarter. That's what I'll pay." He wrote it. "If it's not done at the line, we come out, finished or not."

"And if it's nearly done?" said Dee. "At the line. If it's lying there with nothing left and you've got the point up."

Toren did not answer at once. The others waited for him, and nobody filled the gap.

"Then I'll say it," he said. "Then. Out loud. What we're doing, and what it costs, and how long. And you'll write it. And it'll be mine."

"It'll be mine as well," said Dee. "It's my line." She wrote. "And the rule's still the rule, after. Two Flasks left inside, everybody out. If you say it, it's once. It goes in front of her at home with both our names on it."

"And the home three don't cross that bridge," said Toren. "Whatever happens. Whatever it's lying there with. They're for the road." He looked at the cart, at the rack behind the driver's bench, where the three jars stood grey to the shoulder in the dark. "Say it, somebody who's not going in."

"The home three don't cross the bridge," said Pell. "I'm sitting on them."

Callie settled by the fire with Dee beside her.

It was the most she had ever taken. Dee weighed it out of the open jar onto the square of paper on Callie's knee, a Handful and three quarters, grey and fine, and Callie put her palm flat on it and let it come.

It came. It always came well for her. It came up into her palm slow and cold, and went down, and lay at the bottom of the well on the quarter that was there, and she felt the stone get bigger. She did not haul. She let it come at the rate it came, and she tried to think about nothing, the way Dee had taught them at the long table.

She did not think about nothing. She thought about the door.

She thought about standing in it with the hook on the threshold and the lee up, facing the corridor, with the room behind her: Toren behind her, and Jab, and Dee, and the lifter. She would not see any of them.

She had always held what she could see. That was what Rook had taught her on the forty-fourth. Watch who's inside. Put your eyes on the people and hold them there. She had held Jab's shoulders on the old line. At the wash she had held Jab and Pell under the lee, and taken Toren in and out of it with her eyes. The lee went where she looked. It had always gone where she looked.

Tomorrow she would be looking at a corridor.

The lee would not be over anybody. It would not be shaped like where they were. It would be a wall across a door, keeping a corridor out of a room. Nobody would be inside it. Everybody would be behind it, doing things she could not see, and she would not know how they were until one of them said so.

You can't have all of us, Dee had said on the forty-fourth. You'll have to decide who's worth the lee.

She did not know who that was, tomorrow. She did not know what a lee was for, if it was not over anybody. She had never held anything she could not see.

Stop holding so hard. Let what's been built hold.

Her mother had said that with her words half gone, on the edge of the bed, with Callie's fingers round her wrist. She had opened Callie's fingers off her wrist, one at a time. Callie had not known then what she meant, and she did not know now.

"One and a half," said Dee quietly. "It's lying still. Go on."

Callie went on. The last quarter came up into her palm and went down and lay there.

"Two," said Dee. "Is it still?"

Callie went down to look. The stone lay big at the bottom of the well, bigger than it had ever been, and it was still. It was not slopping. It was not in the hall. It was lying where she had put it.

"It's still," she said.

"Then it's yours," said Dee. She wrote it. "Road, none. Inside, twenty-five and a quarter. One open, with a Handful and a quarter in it. Three whole." She looked up. "Say it back."

Callie said it back. Everything above the line was what tomorrow could cost. The line itself was for getting out.

She had the first watch with Pell, because Pell was awake.

He sat on the cart with his back to the rack and the atlas shut on his knee, and she stood by the cart wheel with the hook and the counter. The fire was down. Toren had settled his Handful and a half at the fire for most of two hours, with his palm flat and his face shut. It was half as much again as he had ever carried. Dee had sat with him through the last of it, the way she had sat with Callie, and at the end she had put two fingers on his wrist and said it was lying still. Then he had lain down by Jab and counted them. Jab had fallen asleep at once. Dee had not.

Across the river the fence stood black against the dark, and the hill went up beyond it. Over its flat top there were no stars, and round the place with no stars there was the light the colour of the bottom of a pond. It thickened and thinned.

"I'm counting it," said Pell. "In case anybody asks."

"Can you see the falls?"

"No. It's too dark. I can see the edge." He was quiet. "I'd like to see the falls. I'd like to know if it's more at night."

They watched it together.

"I said what I said at the fire," said Pell, after a while. "About a box and a half short. About the woman's table."

"I know."

"I'd say it again."

"I know you would."

"I said it so it had been said," said Pell. "By somebody who wasn't going in. Somebody has to say it, on a road, or you go in without anybody having said it, and then you don't know you chose." He looked across the river at the hill. "It's said now. It's written down. So now you can go in and do it properly."

Callie looked at him.

"That's all," said Pell. "That's what saying it's for."

She stood by the wheel and did not say anything for a long time.

"Pell," she said. "Your father. With the pump."

"What about him?"

"Did he mend the flap? Every spring?"

"Every spring," said Pell. "Cut a new one out of an old boot and put it in. Took him ten minutes." He was quiet. "Took me a year to learn how, and he let me do it wrong for most of that year. He'd stand there and watch me pump water down the pipe for an hour and not say anything. Then he'd say now go and look at the trough."

"That's cruel."

"It's a good way to learn about flaps," said Pell. "You never forget which way they go."

In the morning Rook was cooler.

He was not cool. Dee had her fingers on his wrist at first light, and her face said so. But the sweat had stopped, and his eyes were clear, and when she lifted the pad the red round the stitches had not gone any further out in the night. It had not come in either.

"It's holding," she said.

"Like the post," said Rook.

"The post was in lead," said Dee. She gave him the second of the four papers in boiled water, and he drank it and made the same face.

Then Rook got up. He did it in three movements, with a hand on the cart wheel and a hand on Pell's good knee, and Pell said "Mind the leg," and Rook said "I'm minding it." He stood with his coat over his shoulders and walked slowly down the gravel to the near end of the bridge, and sat down at the foot of the first post with his back against it. He had not asked anybody.

"Sitting's allowed," he said, when Dee looked at him.

She measured the rest of them at the cold fire. Toren's own had come back in the night to two turns, near enough, under the stone he had settled. Callie's own was three parts. Dee did her own last and wrote it without saying it. Then she took the last three vent jars out of the straw on the cart and put them in the canvas bag.

They ate. They drank the boiled water, and a little of the full skin. They said the rules at the bridge end, and pull the door at the end of them.

Rook said the rules with them from the post. At the end he looked up at Callie.

"You'll have your back to them," he said.

"I know."

"When I shut the road at the Sag," said Rook, "I never once looked round at the people lifting behind me. Not once, in six weeks. I looked at what was coming up out of the bottom." He was looking at the hill. "If I'd looked round, I'd have dropped it. You can't hold a thing and look behind it. You hold what's in front. They'll hold what's behind." He looked back at her. "You'll want to look. Don't."

"I'll not look," said Callie.

"You will," said Rook. "Once. Everybody does. Then you'll not do it again."

"One in twelve," she said. "The same as yesterday going in."

Toren wrote it.

The lanterns in the hall. The yellow rail. The stair. The long grey slide of the husk's ash lay down the steps from the top, where Toren had killed it against the hook, in a streak going down the stair in threads, and they went down beside it. The door was open.

It stood against the concrete wall of the flat place where it had swung the day before, wide, as far as it would go. Toren looked at it as he came off the last step, and then he looked at the place on the floor two paces from it where his strut had stood.

"Open," he said.

"Good," said Dee. "That's thirty breaths we don't have to spend."

The corridor had changed.

The tray was bowed all along the tray wall. The rope in it was as thick as a leg, grey and heavy, crawling, and it had bent two of the brackets so that the tray hung down at a slant between them. Where the small trough crossed the ceiling toward the first door, the rope in it was as thick as an arm.

It had not been there yesterday. It came out of the dark from the west, along the floor, as thick as Toren's thigh. It lay along the foot of the wall with the doors in it, heavy and grey, and it turned in at the first door and went over the threshold into the room.

Callie read the floor. The threads came along it from the stair the way they had all day yesterday, and they went into the big rope on the floor and into the one in the tray, and everything in the ropes went west. But the big rope on the floor went east into the first room.

Two paces short of the doorway Callie stopped, and Toren unhooked the lantern from his belt and held it out past her shoulder, and they looked in.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

It pushed.

Jab felt it before he put his hand down. He felt the whole grey hump behind the rope do what it did at every three, the thing he had felt through his palm on the rope by the door. It drew breath. It vented. It pushed out into every place in the room where there was a hole, and the cut was a hole.

He put his palm flat on the end of the rope, round the white place, on the fingers and the side of the hand.

It came. It came up the rope at him from the hump like something shoved down a pipe, all at once, warm and gritty and loose, and into his palm. The clean cold came in at his left hand from the jar, and went through him, and held it off his wrist, and he held it high. It was not the hill. It was not the whole of everything lying where it fell, the way it had been on the rope by the door. It was one push. It was a palm's worth, and a little more, all at once.

Then it stopped. It stopped because there was no more behind it. That was the thing he had not known until he felt it. On the rope by the door the push had come and come, and this came once, and it was all there was, and it stopped.

In the same three, the rest of the room moved.

There was a long heavy dry sound from the boxes, like a wet rope lifted off a floor. "It's up," said Toren, and Jab, with his palm on the stump, said "Busy," in the same breath. One of the arm-ropes had come up off the boxes, heavy and slow, the way a wet rope comes up when somebody lifts the end of it, and it swung across the room at the door. It swung at the worked thing standing in the doorway with its back turned.

Toren's strut was already there. It went up from the concrete beside his boot at a slant over Callie's shoulders, the way you lean a plank over a door, and the arm-rope hit it at the height of her head with a sound like a sack hitting a wall. It stopped there, draped over the pale line of the strut, and began to slide off it slowly, the way a wet rope slides off a rail.

"Holding," said Toren, through his teeth.

Callie felt it through the floor under her boots, and she felt her whole body start to turn round. It started the way Toren's arm had started to go out when he fell in the stream, without asking her. She stopped it. She stood in the doorway with the curve on the threshold and her hands open on the conduit, and she kept her eyes on the corridor.

The corridor was pushing too. At her boot, the cut end of the big rope pushed out from its cut toward the threshold, to mend, the way the strands had pushed toward each other on the floor of the room the day before. It came up against the pale foot of the lee where it stood on the curve, and could not go through, and heaped. She felt it heap. It was like somebody leaning a sack against the outside of a door she was holding shut. Over her head, the cut end of the ceiling rope pushed out of its trough toward the hole, and met the lean of the lee, and stopped, and heaped against it there.

At the far edge of the lantern light, by the stair door, the heap swelled, and cracked, and something stood up out of it the colour of an old wasp nest, and turned toward her.

She did not turn round.

"That's the three," said Dee, behind her. "Jab. Off."

Jab took his hand off. He took it off with the grey held high and open in it, and turned, and Dee had a vent jar out of the bag with the stopper out. He put its mouth to his palm and tipped his palm, and the grey went down out of him into the glass, and Dee put the stopper in with her thumb.

"One caught," she said.

The arm-rope slid the rest of the way off the strut, onto the floor behind Callie, and lay there.

"Letting go," said Toren, and the strut went.

Jab looked at the cut.

The end of the rope lay on the floor a pace from Callie's heels. It had not grown. It had not reached for the threshold. It lay where Toren had left it, with its spill, and the spill was going away from the threshold in threads, back along the rope toward the hump, because the ten had begun.

"It's where it was," said Jab.

"It's where it was," said Dee. She wrote it with the vent jar under her arm. "Jab. It's where it was."

In the door, with her back to all of it, Callie did not look round. She held the door.

Chapter 38 — Off Before Ten

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build urgency without rushing]

"Husks," said Dee. "Two."

The corner heap had stood up in the same three, and so had the heap at the far end of the cabinets, three cabinets along from the frame. There were two husks in the room now, grey and faceless, the colour of old wasp nests, and they turned toward the worked things in it: toward Toren's hands, with a strut just gone out of them; toward Callie's back in the doorway; toward Jab's palm, which had been worked a breath ago and was open now.

"I've got the cabinet one," said Toren.

He went at it, and he did not go at it with the heel. He set a strut from the floor in front of it, slanting back toward the cabinets, and the husk walked into the strut and stood against it, pushing, pinned between the pale line of the strut and the steel of the cabinet door behind it. Toren stood behind the strut, soft, and paid by the breath.

"And the corner one?" said Dee.

It was coming along the heap of boxes toward Jab.

Jab let the knife come. It came on his left fist the way it always came, dark, heavy in the spine and fat in the belly: the fish-knife, the one shape he had lived inside for four years. He did not light all of it. He lit the last inch, the hook, and felt the draw of it behind his breastbone.

The husk came along the boxes at him, low.

He did not want to kill it. Every one you killed lay on the floor, and then it was in the air, and then at the three it was standing up again; he had watched it happen five times the day before. But it was coming at his hands, and Toren was on the strut, and Dee had the jar, and Callie had the door, and there was nobody else. He killed it. He put the hook into it low as it came, the way he would have cut a rope, and it came apart, and the grey fell on the boxes and the floor at the foot of the racks in a heap.

"A hundred and twenty," said Dee, with the counter.

Jab let the knife go dark. He crouched by the heap and did not try to lift it, because there was no time, and because he knew now what lifting against the lifter was like. He watched it instead. For ten breaths it lay there, and then it drew out into threads and went into the strands at the foot of the racks, and along them into the corner, into the heap the husk had first stood out of.

He went after it. He went along the foot of the racks at a crouch with his right hand out, all the way to the corner, and he put his left hand up behind him without looking. Dee was there. She had followed him, and she put the mouth of the jar against his palm.

"Three," said Dee.

The corner swelled.

Jab put his hand flat on it, on the top of the heap where it swelled, where the husk was going to stand, and it pushed into him. It was the same as at the cut: one push, a palm's worth, warm and gritty and loose, all at once, and then nothing behind it. He held it high. The clean cold came into his left palm from the jar to hold it off his wrist, and it came thin, like the pour at the bottom of the jug.

"Jar," said Jab.

He said it before the jar was dry. Under his hand the heap did not crack and did not stand. It sank back a little, like a loaf that has been knocked.

"Off," said Dee.

He was already off. The vent jar, and the grey going down into the glass, and the stopper.

"Two caught," said Dee.

The corner heap lay in the corner. It was smaller than it had been, and it did not stand up.

For a moment Dee did not answer the jar. She looked at the empty in her hand.

"That's jar two done," she said. "The open one. It went on the first two catches, and they were the biggest." She turned the empty over. "They'll not all be that big. It's less every time."

She crossed to the frame on the cabinet top, and Jab watched her hand go to it. There were three full jars in it, and three empties, and the broken socket. She put the empty in beside the others, which made four empties, and then she stopped with her hand on the neck of the first full one.

"That's the last one above the line," she said.

Nobody said anything. Toren was behind his strut with the husk against it and his face wet. Callie was in the door. The lifter lay over the carrier.

"Open it," said Toren.

"It's the last above," said Dee again. "When it's done, it's the line. I'm saying it now so it's said."

"It's said," said Toren. "Open it."

She opened it. She lifted it out of the frame by the neck and pulled the stopper, and came back to the corner, and put the mouth of it against Jab's left palm.

"Jar three," she said. "Open. Eight in it. Two whole behind it, and that's sixteen. The line." She looked at the hump. "Say it, Jab."

"Eight above the line," said Jab. "In this one. Then it's the line."

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

"It doesn't matter where," said Jab.

He said it to Dee, crouching in the corner with his hand held away from him. The lantern was behind him on the cabinet, and one side of Dee's face was yellow with it.

"It doesn't matter where I take it," he said. "The cut. The corner. Wherever it pushes. It's all out of the drum." He looked at the hump over the carrier. "Every time I take one, there's a palm's worth less of it. Anywhere."

"Then take it where it matters," said Dee.

She said it at once. Jab thought she had known it before he said it, and had been waiting for him to find it.

"Where it's going to stand up," said Jab. "Where it's mending something Toren did. Where it's going to hurt somebody." He looked at Toren behind the strut with the husk against it. "There."

"Then that's the order," said Dee. "You'll not get all of them. It pushes into every hole at once. You'll get one." She looked at the glass in her fist. "Pick the one."

It learned.

Jab felt it learn. Afterward he did not know how else to say it, and he did not try. It had nobody in it and it did not want anything, but it did what it did, and when what it did stopped working, it did something else. The way water does.

At the next three it did not push into the corner. It pushed into the husk on Toren's strut.

He felt it go out of the hump across the floor along the strands, not to the corner but to the thing pinned against the cabinet at the end of the row, and he saw the husk get bigger. It swelled against the strut like a sack being filled, taller and thicker, and the strut had to take more of it, and Toren made a noise through his teeth.

"It's feeding it," said Jab. "The one on your strut."

"I can feel it's feeding it," said Toren. "It's heavier."

Jab went along the cabinets fast, crouching, with his hand out behind him for the jar. But the three was over before he got there, and the ten had begun, and the husk on the strut was as big as a man now, and it leaned.

"I'm paying for that by the breath," said Toren. "It's more than a wheel."

"Next three," said Jab. "I'll be on it."

"On what? On the husk?"

"On whatever it pushes into."

He crouched at the foot of the strut, at the husk's feet, with his right hand an inch off its grey where it stood on the floor. He did not touch it. You did not touch a husk. But it was not only a husk now. It was a place the lifter pushed into. It was a hole in the lifter, walking about, and the lifter was trying to fill it.

"Clean in," said Dee, behind him, with the jar at his left palm.

"The three," said Jab, before she did.

It pushed. He put his palm flat on the foot of the husk where it stood on the concrete, and the push came into him instead. It came along the floor from the hump and up into the husk, and at the husk's foot it found his palm drawing, and came into his palm, warm, a palm's worth. The husk did not grow. It shook against the strut the way a sack shakes when you pull something out of the bottom of it.

"Off," said Jab, and came off. The vent jar. The grey. The stopper.

"Three caught," said Dee.

The husk leaned on the strut. It was as big as it had been, and no bigger.

"It's not heavier," said Toren. "It's not getting heavier."

[Taut, spatially clear narration; controlled urgency]

Toren began to cut.

He did it on the tens, and he did it one thing at a time, because he could not keep a strut up and light the heel together. For Toren it was one or the other. So at the top of a ten he let the husk's strut go, and the husk fell forward off the cabinet onto its front, the way they did when the thing they were leaning on went out from under them. It would take it a breath or two to get up. He went to the hump.

There had been three arm-ropes, and there were still three. One lay where it had slid off the strut behind Callie, on the floor between the hump and the door. The other two lay across the boxes, out from the far side of the hump, toward the corner.

He went to the near one first. He lit the heel and put it across the arm-rope a pace from the hump, low, and dragged it through. It came apart. The long end lay on the floor toward the door, spilling, and the short end stuck out of the hump like the stump of a branch.

He let the heel go dark. The husk was getting up by the cabinets, and he set the strut in front of it again as it came, and it walked into the strut and stood against it, pushing.

"The three's in four breaths," said Dee.

Jab went to the stump.

He was learning the room. He did not know that he was doing it until he was doing it: where the lantern light fell and where it did not; where the boxes were, and the carrier under the hump with its iron handle sticking out, and the cabinets; where Callie's heels were, and the curve on the threshold, and Toren. He went round all of it at a crouch with his right hand out in front of him and his left hand back, and Dee came behind him with the jar and the bag. She was always there when he put his hand back.

He put his palm an inch off the stump.

It pushed. The stump grew at him, the way the cut strands had grown toward each other on the floor the day before, a finger, two fingers, to mend. He put his palm on the end of it, and it came into him instead of growing.

"Off."

The jar. The grey. The stopper.

"Four caught," said Dee. "That's the first vent jar full. Near enough." She put it in the bag. "Two vent jars left. They'll hold more than that one did. It's giving less every time."

The stump stuck out of the hump, short, a hand long, and it did not grow. The long end of the arm-rope lay on the floor by the door with its spill going away from it in threads.

Toren looked at it.

It learned again. At the next three it threw.

It did not push into a hole. It lifted the second arm-rope, the one that lay across the boxes toward the corner, and swung it, and it swung it at Jab.

Jab did not see it come. He had his hand an inch off the stump of the first arm-rope and his eyes on it, and Dee's jar at his left palm, and all his attention down under his palm in the grey. He heard the long heavy dry sound of the rope coming up off the boxes. He heard Toren say "Jab."

Something went over his head.

It went over him the way a roof goes over you: pale and hard, a line of light going up from the concrete at a slant beside his knee and on over the top of him and Dee, like a plank leaned against a wall with the two of them under it. The arm-rope hit it. Jab felt it hit through the concrete and up through his boots, with the sound of a sack hitting a wall, and the strut took it and stood over him and Dee, pale, while the rope lay over the top of it and began to slide.

"Holding," said Toren. "Both."

Jab looked round.

Toren was standing between the hump and the cabinets with his left arm against his chest, and he had two struts up. One went from the floor to the husk at the end of the cabinets, pinning it. The other went from the floor over Jab and Dee. He was soft behind both of them, and his face was grey and wet in the lantern light. He had held two at once on the arch at the wash for as long as it took to walk a cart onto a post, and Jab had heard him say what it cost. Two struts while it moves. That's twice the price.

"Toren," said Jab.

"Get the stump," said Toren. "I've got the roof."

The arm-rope slid off the strut onto the boxes. The ten had begun.

He came off late once.

It was the seventh. He had his palm on the corner heap, which the lifter was trying to stand a husk up out of again, and the push came into his hand, a palm's worth, and he held it high. The ten began. He felt it begin under his palm. It was held high and open in his palm, and it was not his, and it was not in a jar.

Not his hand: the drawing. The part of him that was reaching down into the grey went after the threads toward the hump, toward the middle, the way you lean after a rope that is being pulled away from you.

For a breath he was going.

"Off," said Dee.

He took his hand off.

He crouched in the corner with his palm up and empty. Half the palm's worth had gone back into the heap. He could feel where it had gone, and he could feel where he had nearly gone after it.

"Off before the ten," said Dee. "Not at the ten. Before."

"I know."

He did not come off late again. At every three after that he said off himself, before she did, and was off, the way he had said vent before she did at the mouth of the cut. And every time, as he lifted his palm, he felt the ten begin a breath behind it. It was like stepping off a step just as it gives.

[Steady, watchful narration; let distance and reserves register]

He looked at Callie once.

He could not help it. He was crouched by the stump of the first arm-rope, near the door, waiting for a three, and she was a pace and a half from him with her back to him. He had not looked at her properly since they came in. He looked now.

She was standing in the doorway with the curve on the threshold and her hands on the conduit, and the lee stood up out of the curve on the corridor side. He could see it past her: a pale sheet standing up off the threshold and leaning back up the wall over the door, like a lean-to the wrong way up. It was grey on the outside. The grey of the corridor's cut rope had heaped against its foot in a long ridge as high as Callie's knees now, piled against the outside of the pale wall, and up by the hole the cut end of the ceiling rope had heaped against it too.

And there was a husk against it. It stood in the corridor on the other side of the lee, pushing. It had come from the stair door, at the worked thing in the doorway, and walked into the lee, and it stood pressed against the pale wall a foot from Callie's face, pushing, with no face of its own. Every time it pushed, Jab saw Callie's shoulders take it.

She was holding it off her stone, her whole stone, two Handfuls: the husk on the outside, and the heaps, and a door and a bit.

There was blood on her lip.

She turned her head.

She did not turn round. She turned her head a little, over her shoulder, the way you turn your head at a noise behind you, and for a breath her eyes found him: Jab crouched on the floor with his hand out over a stump, and Dee behind him with the jar, and the room behind that.

He did not know what she saw. He did not know what her own face did. He looked at her and said the only thing he had.

"Busy," he said.

Callie looked at him a breath longer. Then she turned her head back to the corridor, and she did not turn it again.

It was smaller.

Jab saw it as he went round the hump for the eleventh catch. He had been too near it to see it before, the way you do not see a heap of sacks going down while you are lifting off the top of it. The hump had been as high as Callie's waist. It was. The husk on Toren's strut had been as big as a man. It was the size of a boy now, pinned against the cabinet, and it pushed with less.

And the three was different. Jab felt it before he knew what it was. The line of light opened along the top of the hump at the three, the colour of the edge of the sky, and it stayed open longer. It opened at the three and did not shut at the end of the three. It shut at the end of four. Then five.

It could not find its floor either. There was nobody in it to find it. There was nobody in it to say off.

The difference between him and it was one word, and Dee.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

The lifter moved.

It had not moved since they came in. It had lain over the carrier like a dog over a bone. It had thrown its arm-ropes and pushed into its holes and stood its husks up, and it had not moved.

At the seventeenth three it moved.

It pulled itself, the way it had come along the corridor the day before, drawing itself along its own rope. But the only rope it had now that went anywhere was the cut end of the big one: the stump that ran from the hump across the floor to the threshold, to the curve of the hook, to Callie's heels. Jab knew what she was asking. It was not the counter, and it was not the jar. It was Rook's question, the one Rook had asked at the ditch, and at the pen with his hand on Jab's shoulder doing nothing. What's there? She was asking him what she could not measure.

He put his palm an inch off the edge of the lifter, where it leaned on Toren's strut, and shut his eyes.

And under the draw, at the middle of it, where the light opened at the three, there was a place. It was a hole, and nobody had made it. It was the place the push came from, the vent, and it was open wider every time. It was a hole in the middle of the lifter that the lifter was pushing out of, and it had nearly nothing left to push.

Dee looked at him for a long moment. Then she looked at the counter on her shoulder.

"A hundred and thirty," she said. "Not red."

Then she looked at Toren.
