[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

Toren said it.

He said it from behind his one strut, with the lifter leaning on it and his own reserve going under it. He said it with his teeth together, flat, in order, the way Pell said a distance.

"We cross it," he said. "The line. Now. On purpose. Inside two turns of the glass. Not three. If it's not open for the point inside two turns, everybody out, finished or not, and it has the door." He breathed. "It's mine. I'm saying it. Write it. And the rule's still the rule. This is once."

"It's mine as well," said Dee. "It's my line."

She did not write it, because she had no hand for the book. She said it instead, out loud, to the room, so that it was said. "Inside two turns under the line, and not a breath more. His call and mine. Written tonight, and put in front of her at home with both our names on it." She turned the glass in her fist. "The glass is running."

She reached back to the frame on the cabinet and took the fourth jar out by its neck, one of the last two whole ones. She pulled the stopper and put the jar against Jab's left palm.

"Jar four," she said. "Open. One whole left behind it. That's under." She looked at him. "Holding on an open's not a catch, Jab. It'll pull on this the whole time you're on it. A Handful and a half a turn, near enough. Three, for two turns. Not a grain more."

Jab felt the clean cold come in.

It was the fence's. It had been for the stair, and the rooms, and the road home. It was under the line, where it was never supposed to be opened except to get somebody out. He knew that. He knew what it cost. Every Handful that came out of this jar was a Handful that nobody would have. He felt it come in at his left palm and go through him, and wait.

"Callie," said Toren. "Two turns."

"I heard," said Callie, from the door. She did not turn her head. Her voice was flat and thick, the way it was with a nosebleed. "My stone went at the fifteenth three. I'm on my own. I've got two turns. I've not got three."

At the next three the light opened, and stayed open.

It opened along the top of the lifter where it leaned on Toren's strut, the colour of the bottom of a pond, and it opened wide. Jab could see into it, and there was nothing in it. There was only the light, green-grey, pushing out like breath out of a mouth, with nothing behind it.

It pushed at every hole in the room at once. Jab felt it go: at the stumps; at the corner; at the husk's grey by the cabinets, which shivered and did not stand; at the cut arm by the door. He did not go to any of them.

He put his palm on the lifter.

He put it flat on the edge of the grey where it leaned against Toren's strut, a hand from where the light opened. He had never put it on the lifter itself. He had been on its ropes and its holes and its stumps the whole fight. He put it on the thing now.

It was not warm. That was the first thing. It had been warm all the day before, warm all through, with the whole of the hill in it. It was not warm now. It was grey and loose and cool and thin, like flour in the bottom of a sack.

It pushed into him. It pushed into him because he was drawing, and he was a hole, and it had never known anything else to do with a hole. It pushed what it had, and it had very little.

He held it high. The clean cold came in at his left palm hard and fast, faster than it had come all the fight, to hold the push off his wrist, and he could feel the jar going down under it. He did not let the push into his wrist. He held it in his palm, the last of what the lifter had, and felt it go on pushing, five breaths, six, with nothing, into his hand. It was like breath going out of a man who has no more breath.

Off before the ten.

He did not take his hand off. Not yet. He knew he had to. He knew the ten was coming a breath behind the three, and that it would draw, and that what he had in his palm was loose and would be drawn back, and him after it. He knew all of that.

But the light was open, a hand from his palm. It was open because he was on it, taking the push, so that there was nothing to shut it with. If he came off now, the ten would come, and it would draw what little was lying in the room, and at the next three it would have something to push, and it would shut.

"Toren," he said.

Toren was there. He was standing over the lifter with his one strut still under it, soft, and the spike on his fist, dark.

"It's open," said Jab. "It's open and I'm on it. It's got nothing to shut it with."

"How long?"

"Till the ten," said Jab. "Then I'm off. Whatever you've done."

Toren did not light the spike. Not with the strut up. He looked past Jab at Callie's back.

"Callie," he said. "I'm giving you the lean. It's coming onto your hook. A pace. Then it's on your steel till I'm done."

"Give it me," said Callie. She did not turn her head.

"Letting go," said Toren.

The strut went out. The lifter slid the last pace along its stump, low, the whole thin grey of it, and came up against the curve of the hook on the threshold, on the room side, and stopped as if it had come up against a wall. Because it had. Jab went with it, crouched, with his palm flat on it and the jar at his other hand, and he did not come off.

In the door Callie made a small sound.

"Mine," she said.

Toren lit the spike.

Chapter 39 — The Point

[Taut, spatially clear narration; build urgency without rushing]

The light Toren asked for was at the very end of the spike, a finger's length of it, and nowhere else.

He did not light the heel. He had nothing to light the heel with and the point both, and the heel was for hooking, and there was nothing left to hook. He asked it of his own, because the stone was gone, and he felt the draw behind his breastbone, thin, like the last of the water going out of a barrel through a pinhole.

It lit: a finger of white-grey at the end of the ugly crooked thing on his fist.

Everything else in the room was where it was.

The lifter lay against the curve of Callie's hook on the threshold, knee-high, grey. Toren was holding nothing now. It had to be one thing at a time, because there was only one of him. Jab crouched beside the lifter with his right palm flat on the edge of the grey, a hand from the light, and Dee crouched at Jab's back with the fourth jar against his left palm, under the line, and the glass running in her other hand. The husk Jab had killed was a heap on the floor by the cabinets, and it had not stood up again. In the doorway Callie stood with her back to the room, with the lee standing out into the corridor off the curve, and the lifter leaning on the room side of the same steel a foot from her heels.

The light was open. It was a line along the top of the lifter, the colour of the bottom of a pond, as wide as two fingers now. It had opened at the three and had not shut, because it had nothing to shut with, and Jab was taking what came out of it.

Toren could see all of them. He could not see the lee from where he stood, but he could see Callie's shoulders, and they had taken the lean when it came and had not moved since. He could see Jab's palm, held flat, and his face, which was very still. It was the face Toren had seen on the step of eleven, when Jab put his hand on a drift in his sleep. He had been able to see all of them since they came in. It was the only thing he had been able to do the whole time that was not holding.

"Six," said Dee, very low. "Seven."

The ten was coming. Jab would take his hand off at the ten. He had said so.

Toren put the point in.

He did not stab. He put it in the way you put a knife into a loaf you are cutting at the table, point first, down, into the line of light, a hand from Jab's palm. He put it in slowly, because there was nothing to be quick for. There was no hide and no bone. There was only grey, and light.

The point went into the light, and the light went out.

It went out the way a lamp goes out when you pinch the wick, all at once, with nothing after it. There was a sound. Afterward Toren did not know whether it had been a sound. It was more like the air in the room changing, the way the air in a house changes when somebody who was in it has gone out and shut the door.

Then the lifter came apart.

It came apart the way husks came apart, all at once, into grey. But it was not a husk. It was all of it. The whole long low hump went, from the end that lay against Callie's curve back to where it had lain over the carrier, and it did not burst, because there was no wind. It fell. It fell in on itself like a heap of flour when you take away the board that was holding it up, and it spread out across the floor, over the carrier and the boxes and the concrete, and over Jab's boots and Toren's. It lay there in a long low slope of grey, knee-deep in the middle, loose.

Callie's curve had nothing against it now.

Toren let the point go dark. At the end. Not after.

"Off," said Jab. He had taken his hand away. He held it up, open, with a palm's worth of grey in it, and turned, and Dee had the last vent jar out, and he tipped the grey into it. "It's off."

"Ten," said Dee.

They counted. For ten breaths nothing moved. The grey lay on the floor where it had fallen and did not draw out into threads. It did not go anywhere. It lay there, loose, and was only grey.

Three.

Nothing.

Toren looked at the ropes.

The stumps of the arm-ropes had been sticking out of the hump, and they were gone; they had fallen with it. The long end of the first arm-rope lay by the door where he had cut it, and it was not a rope now. It was a line of grey on the concrete in the shape of a rope, lying there the way a snake's skin lies. The strands at the foot of the racks were lines of grey. The rope that came down the wall from the hole was a streak of grey down the concrete.

Callie did not turn round. She did not need to. She was looking at it.

The ridge against the lee isn't going anywhere." She breathed. "The husk's come apart. The one on the outside. It just came apart. Nobody touched it."

Jab had gone down onto his knees when the lifter fell, and he did not seem to know it.

Nobody answered him.

Toren looked at the floor of the room: at the long slope of grey that had been the lifter, and at the carrier's iron handle sticking up out of it.

It was still fixed.

She went forward onto it.

She went down onto the conduit of her own hook, with the steel still fixed in the air in front of her like an iron bar set in a wall. It took her across the ribs on the left side, the side she had walked into it on the forty-fourth. She made a sound. It was not loud.

"Same place?" said Dee. She had not moved from Jab's back. She could not.

Dee measured them where they were.

Nobody said anything.

Three turns of lifting puts us back over sixteen. If it doesn't, we go at the third, with what's in the jars." She did not look at Toren. "It doesn't make the crossing right. It's the same once, and it goes on the paper with the rest."

They lifted.

There was no other word for it, and Toren would not have used one. It was the east track, and it was Rook's drift, and it was the old north road on Callie's first morning with her grandfather's flat palm. It was the most ordinary work any of them knew, done on the floor of a room under a hill, beside a thing that had tried to fill Jab's hand with the whole of the world.

The empties were in the frame on the cabinet top: the three fence jars that had been opened that morning and the day before, and the two that had been empty since the cut at the wash. Five. Dee lifted them out one at a time and pulled the stoppers and stood them in a row on the cabinet top.

"Nobody kneels," said Dee. "Jab. Up off your knees. You crouch. You don't put a knee down."

Jab looked down at himself as if the knees were somebody else's, and got up onto his heels.

"I'm on my knees," said Callie, from the door.

"You're hurt," said Dee. "You're allowed your knees. You're not allowed to lift."

"I can lift," said Callie.

She came across the floor on her knees with one arm across her side, to the edge of the slope of grey by the door, where the ridge had spilled in over the threshold. She put her right hand flat on it.

"I've been lifting since I was eleven," she said. "Off husk lines, in the silt. Lifting's what I'm for." She did not look at Dee. "It doesn't come out of me. It comes up into my hand. I don't need a stone for it."

Dee looked at her for as long as it took to breathe in.

It came up cold.

Pell had them tip the cart.

He told them from the boards, sitting with his back to the rack and his leg out. Lift the shafts, all of you that can, till the tail comes down. It's a cart, not a house. When the shafts go up, the tail goes down, and the tailboard's gone anyway, so the bed's a ramp to the ground.

"Four in," he said. "Six. And a horse."

He wrote it.

48th. The pump house. In: 4. The lifter's stopped. T. put the point in, at the open, with J. on the push and C. in the door, holding the lean at the last. Under the line on purpose, inside 2 turns: 3 Handfuls (jar 4). T. and D. W.'s call. Once. For the Director. Still under after the kill; back over by the third turn of lifting. 2 boxes in the carrier, in lead, on the cart. The third left (open). C.'s ribs cracked (left, the same). D. W. at her floor (once). T. at his. The sky's lost the count.

He looked at it for a while. Under it, in the same hand, he wrote: Everybody back.

Chapter 40 — Graded

[Measured, lucid narration; give every name, number, and ledger turn room to land]

Jab drew them at the river, all of them, alone.

There was nobody else to do it. Dee was at her floor. Rook was off, and hot, and lying on the canvas with his eyes open. So Jab stood on the gravel below the pump house in the last of the sun, with a jar of the lifter's ash against his left palm and his right hand flat on one chest after another, and drew. He had Toren's jar first, the half one. When it went thin he said jar before it was dry, and Callie took his own second jar out of the frame and pulled the stopper for him.

Callie held the counter for him too. She held it in her right hand, because her left arm would not go out from her side without the ribs saying so, and she held it at arm's length to each chest in turn and said the number, and Jab drew until she said a smaller one.

"Ninety," she said, at Toren. And later, "Twenty." And later, "Twelve. Off."

He did Toren. He did Callie, with his palm flat on the inside of her wrist, because the ribs were where the rest of it would have been. He did Dee.

He did Dee longest.

She stood in front of him with her hands at her sides and let him. Her face was white, and for the first time since the gate it was not steady. It had been steady the whole time under the hill, over the jar and the glass and Jab's back, nineteen times. It had stopped being steady on the bridge.

"A hundred and ten," said Callie, at Dee's chest. "Ten breaths."

Jab did not say anything. He drew. He held it high and vented it into the gravel downstream of the pump house, away from the water, onto the road's ground and not the river's, and went back on.

"Sixty," said Callie, after a long time. "Thirty. Fourteen."

"Off," said Dee. Her voice was thin. "That's enough. That's the room."

Jab came off.

Then he stood with his hands held out a little from his sides, the way he had stood in the cut at the wash, and nobody took them. There was nobody to take them.

"I'll vent," he said. "Long."

He went down the gravel to the far end, past the stone with the chalk cross on it and the two hot jars from the day before standing beside it, and knelt there, and put both palms flat on the stones. He stayed like that while the sun went down behind the hill.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

Callie graded the jars at the fire.

Nobody asked her to. She took the counter and went to the frame where it stood against the pump house wall on its two flat stones, and she held the counter to each jar in the rack at a hand's width, one at a time, and waited ten breaths for each. And she said each one out loud, because that was what you did with a number.

"The fence's last whole one," she said. "Eight. The room. It's clean. Eight in it." She moved along. "The fence's fourth. The one under the line. Eight. Clean. Five in it."

She weighed it on her palm. Five, near enough.

Then the lifter's.

"Jab's first," she said. "Nine. Clean. Full. Eight." She moved along. "Jab's second. Eight. Clean. Six in it. He's drawn two out of it at the river."

"Mine," said Toren, from the fire.

"Yours is empty," said Callie. "It went on the four of us first. It was only a half." She moved along. "Mine. The first." She held the counter to it for ten breaths, and then for ten more, because she wanted to be sure. "Ten. It's clean. Full. Eight."

She came to the last one.

"My second," she said. "Nineteen."

She held it up to the fire and looked through the glass at the grey in the bottom. It was grey. But there were darker grains in it, fine, like pepper in flour, all through.

"It's dirty," she said. "There's grit in it. The hill. It came up with the rest. I felt it come, and I didn't know it was coming." She put it in the rack apart from the others, in the socket at the end where jar B had been, with the broken glass taken out of it now. "Four in it. Dirty. It'll burn wrong."

"It'll burn wrong," said Dee, from the canvas by Rook. "It'll not go on anybody's back unless there's nothing else. Write it dirty."

Toren wrote it.

Callie stood by the frame and said the whole of it. She said it the way her mother said the store book, flat, for somebody else, the way she had said it at every halt on the old line and every night since.

"Inside," she said. "The fence's, thirteen. Five in the fourth, eight in the last. The lifter's, twenty-two, clean. Four, dirty. Thirty-five clean. Four dirty." She stopped. "Home, twenty-four. On the cart. Not touched. The road jar's empty. The vent jars are under the hill, and two by the stone."

"Say what we went in with," said Toren.

"Forty," said Callie. "Clean. On the forty-seventh."

Nobody said anything for a while.

"Thirty-five and four," said Pell, from the cart. "Against forty." He was quiet. "Five short, clean. For two boxes."

"And three under the line, inside two turns," said Dee. "That goes in front of her with our names on it. Not as a thing we'll do again. As a thing we did." She did not stop there. "And my floor. And his." She nodded at Toren. "And her ribs. And his hand." She did not look toward the far end of the gravel, where Jab was still kneeling. "And the rest of it on the floor of that room."

"How much is on the floor of that room?" said Pell.

Callie thought about it. She thought about the long slope of grey from the carrier to the threshold, knee-deep in the middle, and the bank of it along the corridor wall in the shape of a rope, and the tray full of it the whole length of the corridor into the dark, and the stair.

"More than we lifted," she said. "Four times. Five." She shook her head. "I don't know. It's not a number. It's more than we could lift in a day, with nobody hurt."

"Then write that," said Toren. "More than we could lift."

"What was it?" said Pell.

He said it to Rook. He said it the way he would ask the weighbridge about a jar, not unkindly. Rook was lying on his side on the canvas with his face to the fire and his eyes half shut.

"The Director'll want a word for it," said Pell. "On the paper. They grade them. A Flask, or a Barrel. She'll want to know which." He looked across the river at the hill in the dusk. "It came along a rope and had its hand in Jab. It mended everything anybody did to it every thirteen breaths. It had the whole hill." He looked at Rook. "That's a Barrel, surely."

Rook opened his eyes.

"A Barrel's a thing on its own," he said.

He said it slowly, because he was hot and his mouth was dry. Dee held the cup for him, and he drank, and went on.

"A Barrel comes out of a tear all by itself, and it's big on its own account. What's in it is its own." He looked at the fire. "That wasn't big. That was a Flask. Maybe. A Flask with its hand in everybody's pocket." He shut his eyes again. "All that grey on the floor wasn't it. It was everybody else's. The husks'. The hounds' at the wash. The jar that broke on the rail. Twenty years of whatever came out of that sky and fell on the hill and lay there. It went and got it all, and put it on, like a coat that's too big." He was quiet. "Write it a Flask. Write the rest as what it had."

Toren wrote it. Its own: a Flask (R.). What it had: more than we could lift.

"You'd know," said Pell.

"I'd know," said Rook. "It had my job."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

Dee was sick in the night.

Callie heard it before she saw it. She was on the first watch with Pell, because Pell was awake and Callie could not lie down without the ribs, and she was standing by the cart wheel in the dark with the hook for a stick. Somebody got up off the gravel by the wall, fast, and went down toward the river and was sick, and it went on for a long time.

Jab was already there. He had not been asleep either. He went down the gravel to Dee in the dark, and Callie could see the two of them against the grey of the water: Dee on her knees with her hand on a stone, and Jab crouched beside her.

"It's that room," said Dee, when she could. Her voice carried along the water. "It's twenty turns in that room after, at a hundred and thirty, with nobody drawing me. It's that room coming out." She was sick again. "It'll be that room for a day."

"Hold still," said Jab.

"I'm holding still."

"You're not. You're shaking."

"I'm allowed to shake," said Dee. "I'm not allowed to be drawn at my floor. There's nobody to draw you after."

"There's nobody to draw me now," said Jab. "You're busy. I can feel it from here. Hold still."

Callie did not hear what Dee said to that. She saw Dee sit back on her heels on the stones, and she saw Jab put his palm flat on Dee's back, between the shoulders, and his other hand on the jar he had brought down with him, and bend his head.

Callie watched them for a long time. Then she looked away, because it was not hers to watch.

Pell was counting the sky.

He sat on the cart with his back to the rack and his leg out, the way he had sat for all three days, with the sheet on his knee that he could not see to mark in the dark. He was looking across the river at the hill. Over its flat top there were no stars, and round the edge of the place with no stars there was the light the colour of the bottom of a pond.

"It's not ten and three," said Pell.

"I know," said Callie. "We saw it at the top of the road."

"I've been counting it since dusk." He did not take his eyes off it. "It's not anything. Eight, and five. Then twelve and two. Then fourteen and nothing, and it goes again. It's thickening and thinning, the same as it was, but there's no count to it. It's like a man breathing in his sleep who's having a bad dream." He was quiet. "It had a count for three days. Every one. I'd have put my name to it."

"It had the lifter," said Callie.

"Or the lifter had it," said Pell. "Jab doesn't know which. I don't. I'd like to know which." He moved his leg on the boards and made a small sound. "Write it down. Tomorrow. That woman'll want it more than the boxes, I think. Or as much."

"She'll want the boxes."

"She'll want the boxes," Pell agreed. "And she'll want to know why a thing that counted to thirteen for three days stopped counting the afternoon somebody put a point in a heap of grey under it." He looked at Callie in the dark. "I wouldn't like to be the one who has to decide what to do about that. With a Sag held and a machine that can see."

Callie looked at the sky over the hill. It thickened for a long time, and thinned, and thickened again at once. She did not count it. It had nothing to count.

[Steady, watchful narration; let distance and reserves register]

She thought about the door.

She had not let herself think about it all afternoon. There had been the stair, and the road, and the bridge, and the river, and the jars. Now there was only the dark and Pell and the cart wheel, and she thought about it.

She had held it. She had stood in it with her back to the room for twenty turns and more, with the stone going out of her into a door and a bit until it was gone, and then her own, and a husk pushing against the pale a foot from her face. She had never once seen what was happening behind her. She had heard it. She had heard the sack hit the wall. She had heard Toren say holding with his teeth together, and Jab say busy, and Dee say off, over and over, and the glass going over. She had heard the line said. She had heard two turns, and said I've got two turns, I've not got three, and she had not known, saying it, whether two would be enough. And she would not have been able to do anything about it if they were not.

She had looked round once. Rook had said she would.

She had turned her head and seen Jab on the floor with his hand out, and Dee behind him with the jar, and the room behind that, grey. And Jab had looked at her and said busy. Just that. It was the word he said to tell you he was working and how long you had to hold.

And she had turned her head back and held.

She had not carried them. That was what she understood, standing by the cart wheel in the dark with her arm across her side. She had carried people all her life. She had carried her mother across four hundred miles in her head, every breath, every step, counting her. She had held a wagon on a hook with her mother in it. On the lip at the wash she had held a lee off her own stone over two bodies and taken a third in and out of it with her eyes. She had thought that was what it was for: holding people.

Under the hill she had held a door, and the three of them had done the work behind her back. She had not been holding them. She had been holding the edge of them. And they had held the rest.

Stop holding so hard. Let what's been built hold.

When her mother said it, she had thought it meant letting go. It did not mean letting go. It meant choosing what to hold, and holding that, all of it, and trusting the people on the other side of it to hold their own.

She had not known it would feel like this. It did not feel like forgetting. It felt like the ache in the palm after lifting, when you have put down a thing that was worth carrying.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

In the morning Dee measured them.

She did it sitting on a stone by the cold fire. She was not inside a fence, so she was allowed, and her legs would not have done it standing. Her face was grey, and there were marks under her eyes like bruises, but her hands were steady again, and they all watched the hands go to each wrist in turn.

"Your own's back," she said to Toren. "A turn. Not two. It'll be two by tonight if you do nothing."

"I'll do nothing."

"You'll carry a wheel," said Dee. "But not today." She did Callie. "Your own's back. Half. You slept?"

"No."

"You slept an hour," said Dee. "Jab said. Your own's half." She put her palm flat against Callie's side, over the coat, not pressing. "And that's cracked. Two, I think. The same two." She took her hand away. "I'll strap it. You'll not lift anything heavier than a counter for a week. You'll not lean on that hook."

"I'll lean on it to walk."

"You'll lean on it to walk," Dee agreed. "That's what it's for this week."

She did Jab. She held his palms in both of hers, turned up. The white place on the heel of the right one was red round its edges now, and shiny, and there was a small blister at one side of it.

"They're warm," she said.

"I vented half the night."

"I know you did. I watched you. I was being sick, and I watched you." She put her palms flat on his, palm to palm, and they saw her find it. She drew. It was the watch taking it off the one who had worked, the way she had done it in the cut at the wash, and her face went quiet while she did it. "There," she said. "Cool."

"You're at your floor," said Jab.

"I'm a finger over it," said Dee. "I slept too. After you'd finished with me." She let go of his hands. "That's enough for a watch. It's not enough for anything else. Not today."

She did her own last, with two fingers on the inside of her crooked wrist.

"A finger," she said. "Over." She wrote it.

Rook was holding. That was Dee's word for it, and she said it the way she had said it about the post on the arch. The red round the stitches had not gone further out, and it had not come in. He was hot, but not as hot as he had been on the first morning, and he drank the third of Sowerby's papers in boiled water and made the face.

"One left," said Dee.

"Keep it," said Rook. "For whoever's worse."

"You're the worst."

"Then keep it for when I'm worse than this," said Rook. He looked at her across the cup. "You were sick."

"I was the watch," said Dee. "Nobody watched me." She took the cup. "I'll not do it that way again."

"Yes you will," said Rook. "If it's the same thing again, you'll do it the same way." He shut his eyes. "I'd like it written down that I said so."

"I'll write that you said so," said Dee. "I'll not write that you were right."

He laughed. It was the low careful laugh of a man with a hole in his back. Dee's mouth moved at the corner, once, and stopped.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

They decided at the cart.

Pell had the atlas open on his knee, and Toren had the paper. Everybody else stood, or sat on what they were allowed to sit on, round the tail of the cart, where the carrier sat on its board behind the home jars with two live boxes in it and the lid in its groove.

"Say the clock," said Toren.

"The forty-ninth," said Pell. "Today. The cycle's the fifty-fourth. Five days." He put his finger on the atlas. "It was six days from the gate to here, with the siding. With the road whole."

"It isn't whole," said Callie.

"It isn't whole," said Pell. "The crown's gone into the wash, and the post, and the arch. There's a gap in the embankment four paces wide, with the wash running through the bottom of it and the drifts heaped on both sides." He looked at the three of them. "North round the head of the drifts, toward the hill. Or south through the marsh to the river and down this bank. Two days more, either way, and there's no bed for the cart on either. That's what I said on the forty-sixth. It's still true."

"That's the fifty-seventh," said Toren. "Home."

"Or later," said Pell. "With me on the cart and not walking."

"And the other thing?" said Toren. "What you said at the fire. That it'll take people across the bottom on foot."

"On foot," said Pell. "Through the drifts. Quick, and wash after. It won't take the cart." He looked at the cart under him, and the carrier on it, and the three home jars. "Nothing takes a cart across that."

He was quiet for a long time.

"Nothing takes a cart across that," he said again, slowly. He put his hand flat on the boards of the cart bed. "A cart's not a thing. It's a lot of things. Two wheels. An axle. A bed. Two shafts. Pins." He looked up. "A cart in pieces goes across in pieces."

Nobody said anything.

"The wheels roll," said Pell. "You roll them, down one side of the gap and up the other. They're as high as her shoulder." He nodded at Callie. "The axle's two men. The bed's four, or two and a horse with a rope on it. The shafts are one each. The carrier's on its board, and a board slides on a drift. It's flour." He looked at Toren. "And there's a bank on each side of the gap, loose. And you set steps on a loose bank at the wash. On stones."

"I set them on my own," said Toren. "The last of it."

"You'll have a day's worth by tomorrow," said Pell. "Miss Wren says two turns by tonight. And there's a jar of that thing's ash to settle, if it's clean."

"And you?" said Toren.

"I'm a bed and two poles and a bit of canvas," said Pell. "Two of you. I'll not say anything about the camber."

"Price it," said Toren.

He said it to Callie. She stood by the tail of the cart with her arm across her side and the counter in her other hand, and she priced it out loud, because that was the rule, and because saying it was how she found out whether it was true.

"The drifts were eighty, ninety at the foot of the bank," she said. "In the wind. With no wind, lying still, they'll be less. Sixty, seventy. Where the crown went in, where it's turned over, more. A hundred." She looked east, toward the ridge and the cut and the wash behind it, a mile off. "An hour. For all of it. Down, across, up, the pieces, and Pell, and the horse, twice over for the wheels. An hour at eighty. All of us, and the horse."

"How much?" said Dee.

"Ten," said Callie. "Maybe twelve. For the drawing after, in the cut on the far side. And the settling for Toren's steps." She looked at the frame against the wall. "Out of the lifter's."

"Out of the lifter's," said Toren.

"Out of the lifter's," said Callie. "It's got twenty and a half clean. A Handful and a half went on Miss Wren in the night." She did not look at Dee. "It'd have ten and a half left, and the fence's thirteen, and the dirty four. And home, twenty-four, not touched." She stopped. "That's half the lifter's, for one hour in the wash. The rest is for the road." Then she went on. "We'd be on the old line east of the gap by the fiftieth, with the cart back together. And it's five days from there, on the road we know. With the siding." She did the last sum. "The fifty-fifth. Home."

"Not the fifty-fourth," said Toren.

"Not the fifty-fourth," said Callie. "Nothing's the fifty-fourth. The fifty-fourth was gone before we crossed the bridge."

Toren looked at the paper for a long time.

"It's the fifty-fifth, or the fifty-seventh," he said. "Or later." He looked up. "That's Sowerby dosing her off her blood, badly, a day past the cycle. Or three. And whatever the fifty-fourth does, with a man guessing." He did not say Gran. "And ten Handfuls of that thing's ash, and an hour in the drifts, and Callie's ribs, and Dee a finger over her floor."

"The wash," said Toren. "In pieces. Tomorrow, first light, if the wind's down. Not today. Nobody carries a wheel through a drift at their floor."

"Not today," said Dee, and wrote it. "And if the wind's up?"

"Then we sit at the cut and wait for it to drop," said Toren. "And I'll write what it costs."

Pell shut the atlas.

"Then today we go to the cut," he said. "It's a mile. The cart'll do that whole. It's this side of the gap." He looked at Duchess, tied to the wheel with her rope halter, eating. "She'll pull it to the cut. And tomorrow she'll walk through a drift, because somebody she knows is walking in front of her. And then she'll hate every one of us for a week."

"She'll be right," said Rook, from the canvas.

"She's always right," said Pell. "She's a horse."

They loaded the cart.

The frame went on the cart this time, in the rack behind the driver's bench beside the home jars, because Jab's palm was blistered and Dee said he would not carry a frame of jars a mile on a blister. Rook went on the cart on the canvas, on his side, with his back off the boards. Pell stayed where he was. The carrier sat behind them on its board with the lid in its groove.

Toren went round the cart once, the whole of it, and counted what was on it. Then he counted them.

"Pell," he said. "Dee. Rook." He stopped on Rook the way he always did, longest. "Jab. Callie." He looked at the mare. "Six. And a horse."

He wrote it on the back of the signed paper, standing at the pump house wall.

49th. The pump house. Out: 6. To the cut. The wash tomorrow, in pieces (Pell's). Home the 55th, if the wind's down.

He looked at it.

"Dessa left six lines," he said. "At the foot of the page. For back."

"I know," said Callie.

"I'll not write in them yet," said Toren. He folded the paper and put it in his coat beside the plate.

Callie went out in front. She did it without being asked, the way she had done it on the first morning on the old north road: twenty paces in front of Duchess, with the hook for a stick and her left arm strapped across her side under her coat. She began to read the road for the wheels.

It was the road they had come on, three days ago, at dusk: the old line going up from the river on its long bare slope to the ridge, and the cut through the ridge, and the wash behind it. She knew it. She read it anyway, for the wheels. She read the loose stones on the bed, and the place where the frost had heaved it, and the mark where the cart had come down it on the forty-sixth with Pell on it and his foot on a coil of rope.

At the top of the slope, at the mouth of the cut, she stopped and turned round.

She looked back once. Everybody does.

The river lay low and dark in its stony bed, with the pump house on its near bank, roofless, and the two broken pipes going into the water. The footbridge went across on its posts, with two grey poles of wrack wood still lying along it over the crack. At the far end stood the gate, with a twist of green wire through its chain, left so it would come.

Beyond the gate there was the yard, and the road going up the hill in its long Z, and the long building standing along the rim with its windows black. There was the drum behind it with its broken top. And over the whole of the top of the hill there was the sky.

The edge of it thickened. She did not count it. It thinned, and thickened at once, and thinned for a long time. It had no count. It was a thing breathing in its sleep, having a bad dream.

Under it, in a room under a hill, there was more ash lying on a floor than she could have lifted in a week. There were hundreds of boxes, and a third live one talking to the room, and three stoppered jars with a chalk cross beside them. She would put the number of every one of them on the Director's table.

In the cart behind Duchess there were two.

It was the forty-ninth day. At home it would be the ninth hour, near enough. Her mother would have walked to the ward for her pills at the eighth hour, with Katori on one side of her and Ines on the other, not holding. Senna would be on the fourth bed on the right, with five days to the narrow bed and the machine that sang flat. Tonk would be in the fifth bed, with a cord round his fist. They were all breathing without her. They had been breathing without her for eight days, and nothing had happened to any of them because she was not there counting.

She did not know what would happen on the fifty-fourth. She did not know if the wind would be down tomorrow.

She knew what was in the cart, and what was in the frame, graded. She knew who was on the cart and who was walking. She knew the road to the cut, and she knew the wash.

She turned round and went on into the cut, twenty paces in front of the horse, reading the road for the wheels. Behind her Duchess came on with the cart, with Pell and Rook riding on it beside the boxes and the home jars, and Jab and Dee walking at the wheel. At the back, where he always walked now, Toren was counting them.

Chapter 41 — Jab: In Pieces

[Warm, intimate narration; keep emotion earned and restrained]

Jab woke in the dark at the mouth of the cut and knew where everybody was before he opened his eyes.

He had not always been able to do that. He could now, if they were near and he knew them. Pell was on the cart, awake, and trying not to move his leg. Dee was sitting up. Callie was standing, the way she stood every night now because lying down hurt more. Toren was asleep with his face in his good arm. Rook was on the canvas by the wheel.

Rook was hot.

Not the way he had been at the pump house on the first morning. Less than that. But it had come up in the night, the way a fire you have banked comes up again when the wind turns. Jab could feel it from where he lay. It was all through Rook, not in bits. It was him, fighting.

It was not a thing Jab could draw. He lay and felt it anyway, because he could not stop himself.

Then he felt for the other thing. He put his left hand flat on his coat, over the left side, and felt the shape through the cloth. The body. The tail. The place where the fin had been.

He got up.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

The wind was down.

Callie said so before anybody asked. She was standing at the mouth of the cut with her arm strapped across her side under her coat and the hook in her other hand for a stick, looking east along the embankment. The sky over the marsh was going grey at the bottom. There was no sound at all from the reeds.

"It's down," she said. "It's been down since the middle of the night. I've been watching the reeds. They've not moved."

"And the drifts?" said Dee.

"Still." Callie did not look round. "I watched them too. They were still all night. Then about an hour ago the one nearest the gap slid. A hand's width. Not at a ten. Not at anything." She was quiet. "Then it lay still again."

Dee came and stood beside her.

"Once?"

"Once that I saw."

Dee looked at the drifts for a while. They lay along the north side of the embankment in the grey light, long and soft and pale, heaped against the bank like snow against a wall. Nothing moved on them.

"Write it," she said. "Then measure yourself. Then come and be measured."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

She measured them at the cart, two fingers on each wrist.

"A hand and a bit," she said to Jab. "Floor's a finger." She turned his right hand over and looked at the heel of it by the first light. The white place was the size of a coin. The red round it had gone darker in the night, and the blister at its edge had filled. She had put a square of clean rag over it the evening before and tied it with thread. The rag was still clean. "Can you draw round it?"

"I did last night. On Duchess."

"I know you did. I was watching." She let go. "Round it. Not with it."

She did Callie, and told her three parts, and told her the ribs were not a thing she could measure with two fingers. She did Toren.

Toren had settled a Handful at the fire the night before, out of the lifter's second jar. Jab had watched him do it. He had sat with his palm flat on the square of paper for most of an hour, with his eyes shut, and let it come at the rate it came for him, which was slow. It had been full dark when the paper was clean.

"Stone's full," said Dee. "Your own's two turns. You've the bit back."

"I did nothing yesterday."

"You carried nothing yesterday," said Dee. "That's not the same thing, but it's near enough." She did her own last and did not say it, and wrote it.

"Say it," said Toren.

Dee looked at him.

"You said we'd say everything," said Toren. "Yours as well."

Dee was quiet for a moment.

"Two fingers," she said. "Over my floor. I can watch. I can draw leftovers off one person, once. I can't work." She shut the book. "That's what there is, Toren. It's not what I'd like."

"Then that's what we price," said Toren.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

The gap was seventy paces from the mouth of the cut.

They walked out to look at it in the grey light, all of them but Pell, who looked at it from the cart. The embankment ran east from the cut, four paces wide on top, packed stone, with the drifts heaped up against its north side and the marsh standing black and still against its south. Iron posts stood along the north edge every twenty paces. Most of them leaned.

Then the embankment stopped.

It stopped the way a loaf stops where somebody has cut a slice out of it. The bed ran to an edge, and past the edge there was air, and then, four paces off, the bed began again. Between the two edges the bank went down on each side in a slope of loose stuff, stone and earth and grey, to the bottom. At the bottom the wash ran through, shallow and quick, from the drift side under where the arch had been, out to the marsh side. The arch was down in it. The stones of the crown lay in the water in a heap, and the water went white round them.

Lying across the bottom of the gap, half in the water and half out, was the iron post.

It had gone down with the crown. It lay at a slant from the foot of the near bank to the foot of the far one, with its lead collar still round it like a ring on a finger. The water ran under it.

Callie held the counter out over the edge at the length of her arm and waited ten breaths.

"Forty," she said. "Here. On the lip." She moved along the edge and held it out again, lower, over the slope. "Eighty. The bank. It's got grey drifted into it." She moved again. "A hundred. There. Where the drift comes into the gap from the north side. Where the crown went in."

Jab looked where she was looking. On the north side the drift came right down to the water. It had spilled into the gap when the crown fell, and it lay against the foot of both banks in a soft grey bank of its own, knee high, running up into the great heaps beyond.

"Seventy," said Callie. "At the water. The water's running. It takes it down."

Toren stood at the very edge with his left arm in its cuff against his chest and looked at all of it. He looked for a long time. Jab watched him look. It was the way he had looked at the rack in the north yard when Rook first put it in front of him, as weight, and where it went.

"Pell," said Toren, without turning round. "Say it again. How it goes."

Pell said it again from the cart, the way he had said it at the pump house. Wheels, axle, bed, shafts, the carrier on its board. Down one side on a rope round something that doesn't move. Up the other on a rope. Nobody below it.

"And the horse," said Pell. "The horse is the thing that lifts. Not you. None of you can lift anything this morning, and she can lift the lot. You put her on the top of the far side with a rope, and she walks away from the gap, and whatever's on the other end of the rope comes up. That's what a horse is for."

"And the near side?"

"The near side lets it down," said Pell. "Round a post. Slow."

Toren looked back along the embankment at the posts.

"Eight paces back," he said. "That one. It's standing straight." He looked across the gap. "And that one over there. Eleven."

"That'll do," said Pell.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

Toren said who did what.

He did it at the cart, standing by the wheel with the paper in his hand, and he said it slowly, one name at a time, the way Dee said the rules at a gate. Jab listened to him do it. He had heard Toren give orders before. He had not heard him do this.

"I go first," said Toren. "Down the bank on steps, across on the post, up the other side on steps. I take the long rope over. I tie it round the post on the far side. Then there's a rope across, for hands."

"You'll be in the bottom," said Dee.

"I'll be in the bottom the most. That's mine. Somebody has to put a strut under things at the post, and that's me." He did not look at her. "Callie reads the banks for me. From the lip. Stone, soft, hollow. I don't set anywhere she hasn't said."

"Stone, soft, hollow," said Callie.

"Then Callie goes over with Duchess. Once. She leads her. Duchess knows her." He looked at Callie. "You don't come back. You stay on the far side with the horse and the counter, and you read the far bank for the loads. You don't lift. You don't take the rope."

Callie opened her mouth.

"I'll not lift," she said.

"Then Jab," said Toren. "With the frame. All the ash goes over on Jab. He stays on the far lip. That's where everybody comes up, and that's where everybody gets drawn." He looked at Jab. "You're the jar and the work. Dee's the watch. From here."

"From here?" said Jab.

"She can't be drawing and drawing," said Toren. "She's got two fingers. She stays on this side and lets the loads down round the post, and calls the glass. Nobody's in the bottom longer than she says." He looked at Dee. "And when the loads are over, she comes across with Rook. Last. And draws your leftovers. Once."

Dee did not say anything for a moment.

"That's right," she said. She wrote it.

"Rook," said Toren.

Rook was lying on the canvas with his eyes open.

"You're off," said Toren. "You come over at the end with Dee, on the steps, on the rope. You don't hold a load. You don't hold a rope. You don't help."

"I could sit on the post and count," said Rook. "Counting's not helping. It's counting."

"Then count," said Toren.

"And me," said Pell.

"You come over on the shafts," said Toren. "Like you said. On the canvas between them, with the horse pulling." He looked at the cart, at the rack behind the driver's bench. "And the home three with you. In your lap. You're sitting on them."

Pell looked at the three jars in the rack, grey to the shoulder.

"I'm sitting on them," he said.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

Taking the cart apart took most of an hour.

Pell told them how from the boards. They set the axle up on two stones from the edge of the bed, one under each end, and knocked the linchpins out. Pell took the linchpins himself and put them in his coat pocket and buttoned it. "There's no finding a pin in grey," he said. They got the wheels off.

A wheel was as high as Callie's shoulder. It was ash wood with an iron tyre round it, and it was heavier than it looked. Jab walked the first one along the bed with his hands on the tyre, rolling it, and felt it try to go its own way at every stone.

They had the bed off the axle with Duchess on a rope, sideways, the way Pell said, and it came off with a groan and lay upside down on the embankment like a boat on a beach. The axle lay on its stones. The shafts came off their pins.

Pell watched them do all of it. He had his leg out on the canvas and his hands flat on his knees. When they lifted the shafts off, he took the canvas from under himself and folded it in four on his lap. Then he told Jab and Toren how to lash it between the two shafts, at the wide end, with the long sides round the poles and a rope through the eyelets.

"There," he said. "That's a bed and two poles and a bit of canvas. I said so."

"You said you'd not say anything about the camber," said Rook.

"I'll not," said Pell. "There's no camber on a drift."

They got him onto it. It took Jab and Toren and Dee, with Pell holding his own leg by the splint and saying easy and easy and there. When he was down, Toren brought the three home jars out of the rack one at a time. He put them into Pell's hands.

Pell set them round himself, one on each side of his hips and one between his knees, and put a rope round all three and round himself, and tied it.

"If I go in the wash," he said, "they go with me."

"If you go in the wash," said Dee, "I'll write it."

The carrier sat on its tailboard sledge on the embankment, with the lid in its groove. Jab stood and looked at it. Two boxes in it. The whole reason for everything.

"That comes after me," said Pell. "Not before. If something goes wrong on the first load, it wants to be me that it goes wrong with." He looked at the carrier. "Not that."

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

Toren went down first.

Jab watched him from the lip. He watched Callie crouch at the edge of the bank with the counter in her strapped arm and the hook's end out flat over the slope, pointing, the way she pointed at the ground in the north yard.

"Stone," she said. "There. Under a hand of grey. It's the edge of the old bed, where it was built up." She moved the hook. "Soft. Soft. Not there." She moved it again. "Stone. That's a block off the crown. It's sitting on something."

Toren set.

He put the foot of a strut down on the stone she had pointed at, under its hand of grey, and let it come up flat, a step, pale and hard, at the height of his knee. He put his boot on it. He stood on it for one breath, and it held him, and he stepped down onto the next one, which was already there, because he had set it while he stood on the first.

Set. Step.

He went down the bank that way, on steps nobody else could have stood on, with the long rope over his good shoulder, paying out behind him from the post. Each step went out when he left it. At the bottom he stepped off the last one onto the iron post where it lay across the water, and stood on the post, and the water ran under him.

"Eighty," said Callie, reading him from the lip. "A hundred, if you go to the north end of the post. Don't."

He did not. He walked the post to its far end, one-handed, with the rope going across behind him. Then he set steps up the far bank on the stones she called for him across the gap, and went up them, and stood on the far lip.

He tied the rope round the far post. He did it one-handed, slowly, with his teeth for the knot at the end.

Then he looked back across the gap at them. Jab could see his face. It was grey, the way it went when he had been paying.

"There's a rope," said Toren.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

Callie took Duchess over.

She did not lead her down the steps. There were no steps for a horse. There was the bank, and it was loose, and Duchess put her front feet on it at the top and stopped, and put her ears back, and blew through her nose at the grey.

"She'll not," said Pell, from the shafts.

"She will," said Callie.

She stood below the mare on the slope. She did not pull the rope. She had her strapped arm across her side and the rope loose in her right hand, and she talked to Duchess. Jab could not hear what she said. It was low and flat, the voice she used for a number.

Duchess put one foot down. Then the other. Then she came down the bank the way a horse comes down a bank it does not like, sitting back on her haunches, in a slide of stone and grey. Callie went down in front of her, backward, reading every step, and did not once let the rope go tight.

At the water Duchess stopped again.

It was not the water. Jab saw that. It was the drift. The grey came down to the water on the north side of the post, a pace from her nose, and at the moment she reached it the edge of it slid. A hand's width, toward the water, and stopped. Not at a ten. At nothing.

Duchess threw her head up. The rope came tight all at once, and Jab saw Callie's arm go out after it, the right one, and her body turn with it.

She let go.

She opened her hand and the rope went out of it, and she stood in the bottom of the gap with her empty hand in front of her and her strapped arm across her side, and did not grab again.

Duchess stood with her head up and the rope hanging. She did not run. There was nowhere to run in the bottom of a gap. She stood and blew, with her eyes white.

"Let it run," said Callie, to nobody. "Lead's cheaper than you."

"Horse," said Pell. "She's a horse. Not lead."

"It's the same rule," said Callie.

She picked the rope up out of the water slowly, and talked to the mare again. After a while Duchess put her head down and followed her across the post-side stones and up the far bank in a scramble of hooves. Toren stood at the top with his good hand out, not on the rope, only there.

Callie came up after her on Toren's steps. At the top she stood with her hand on the mare's neck. She had her other arm tight across her ribs, and her face was the colour of the drift.

"I let go," she said to Toren. Jab heard it across the gap. "It pulled, and I let go."

"Good," said Toren.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

Jab went over with the frame.

He went down Toren's steps with his hand on the rope. They came up one at a time in front of him, pale and hard, and went out behind him. Toren was on the far lip setting them, calling step for each one. Jab put his boot on them and they held him, and he did not look down at the grey.

He felt the bottom as he came into it.

It was not like Caul Hill. There was no pull in it. There was nothing under the grey drawing at anything. It lay there, the whole soft heap of it on the north side of the post, loose and cold and busy with the hill, and did nothing. It did not want him. It did not want anything.

He was glad of it. He had not known how much he would be.

On the post he stopped for a breath. He did not know why. He stood on the iron with the water running under him and the frame on his back, with every jar they had in it, and looked north along the wash at the drifts going away toward the hill, and at the edge of the sky over it.

It was thickening and thinning. It had no count.

"Jab," said Toren, from above. "Step."

He went up.

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

The far lip was the station.

That was what Toren called it, and Jab did not argue. He stood on the embankment at the top of the far bank, four paces back from the edge, with the frame on his back and nothing to rest it on. The tailboard was on the other side of the gap under the carrier. So he stood.

Callie read the ground under him. "Forty," she said. "Clean enough. It's the road's."

"Then I vent into the road," said Jab.

"Not into my floor," said Callie. Somebody had to say it. Dee was on the other side.

He had the lifter's second jar, and the first. He took the second out of the rack by the neck and pulled the stopper and held it in the crook of his left arm, against his palm. Three and a half in it. It was the lifter's. It was cold, all of it, with nobody in it.

He drew Toren first.

Toren came and stood in front of him on the lip with his arms at his sides, the good one and the cuffed one, and Jab put his right hand flat on his chest, round the white place, and felt.

"Busy," he said. It was the bottom, and the steps, and the bank. It was in the chest and a little in the legs, where the grey had come up off the bank as Toren walked in it. Warm grit. The hill.

He drew. It came up into his palm. The clean cold came through him from the jar into his left hand and held it off his wrist, and he held it high, and turned, and put his palm flat on the stones of the road and let it go down out of him.

"Clean," he said.

"How much?"

Jab weighed the jar on his palm, the way Callie did.

"A quarter," he said. "And the vent."

"That's one crossing," said Toren. He looked back across the gap at the carrier on its board and the bed upside down and the axle on its stones and the two wheels and Pell on his canvas between the shafts. "There's nine more."

The wheels went first, because Pell wanted to see how a load behaved before it was him.

Dee let them down. She had the long rope round the near post twice. Jab could see her across the gap, standing back from the post with the rope over her hip and her feet set, the way she had stood at the rail's post on the landing with the ramp going down in front of her. Rook sat on the embankment beside the post with his knees up and his coat over his shoulders.

"One," he called. Jab heard it across the gap. "One wheel. Going down."

The wheel went down the bank on the rope, rolling, with Dee paying out slow. At the bottom it came up against the post, and Toren was there. He had gone back down his steps to the post, and he stood on it and put a strut under the rim of the wheel where it met the iron. It came up at a slant, a short ramp, and the wheel went up it and over the post and down onto the stones on the far side.

"Rolling," called Pell.

Then Callie walked Duchess away from the far lip along the embankment, east, with the other end of the rope on the mare's collar, and the wheel came up the far bank behind her. It came up the whole slope, bumping, rolling where it could and sliding where it could not, with Jab at the top guiding the rope off the edge. It came over the lip onto the bed. Callie stopped the mare.

"One," said Jab.

It had worked. He saw Toren see that it had worked, down in the bottom on the post. He saw him breathe out.

The second wheel went wrong.

It went wrong halfway down the near bank. The rim hit a buried stone that Callie had called stone and meant for a boot, not a wheel, and it jumped. It came off the ground and turned in the air and came down on its edge, and the rope jerked round the post, and Jab saw Dee go forward a step with it and set her feet.

The wheel twisted on the rope. It came round broadside. Its weight went sideways off the line of the rope, and the rope slipped up the post, off the stone it had been sitting on.

"Let it run," said Pell. He said it loud.

Dee let it run.

She opened her hands on the rope, and it went out round the post with a hiss, and the wheel went down the rest of the bank on its own. It went fast. It came off the bottom of the slope and hit the stones of the fallen crown, and bounced, and went over the water and over the end of the post. It went into the drift on the north side.

It went in three paces, and fell over on its side, and lay there in the grey with half its spokes showing.

Nobody said anything.

"A hundred and ten," said Callie, beside Jab, with the counter held out over the edge. "Where it's lying."

Toren was on the post.

Jab saw him look at the wheel. He saw him look at the grey round it, knee deep and soft, and at the far end of the post, and at his own boots.

Then he saw Toren look up at the far lip. At Jab.

"It's a wheel," said Toren. "We can't go home on one wheel."

"No," said Pell.

"Who goes in?" said Toren.

He did not say I'll go. Jab heard him not say it. He heard it the way he heard Callie not say a number when she did not like it. Toren stood on the post and asked it, out loud, to everybody.

"You're in the bottom already," said Dee, from the near lip. "You're the one that's in it."

Callie crouched on the far lip. She held the counter out, and looked for a long time at the grey on the north side of the post, the way she looked at a floor. Jab watched her read it.

"The water's in it," she said. "At the edge. Look." She pointed with the hook's end. "Where the drift comes down to the stream, it's dark. It's wet. The stream's been running into the foot of it all night. The wet grey doesn't lift. It's like wet flour. It lies." She moved the hook along. "There's a line of it. Wet. From the end of the post along the water to where the wheel is. A pace wide. If you walk in the wet, you're walking in the stream's side of it, not the drift's."

"How much?" said Toren.

"Eighty on the wet," said Callie. "A hundred and ten on the dry. Don't touch the dry."

"How long?"

"As long as it takes you to put a rope through a wheel with one hand," said Callie.

Toren looked at the wheel.

"Jab," he said. "Throw me the other rope."

Jab threw it.

It was the back rope off the carrier's sledge. Pell had had them take it off. It went out over the gap and Toren caught the end of it one-handed against his chest and looked at it.

Then he stepped off the post into the stream.

Jab watched him walk the wet line. It was a pace wide, as Callie had said, a dark band along the foot of the drift where the stream had soaked it. He walked in the water where he could and in the dark grey where he could not. He did not touch the pale grey above it. He went slowly. At the wheel Toren stopped. He was in the stream to his shins. The wheel lay on its side a pace from him, half in the wet grey and half in the dry. He bent. He could not kneel. It was. It was more than the first time. It was in the chest and the belly and the legs to the knee. The drift had come up off the wet edge onto him after all, the way it always did, a little, however careful you were.

"That wheel's the way home," said Toren.

"Two and a quarter in it," he said. "Out of three and a half."

The axle went down and across and up. Then the bed, upside down, on two ropes, with the horse pulling it up the far bank like a sledge and its planks grating on the stones. Then the carrier.

Pell came last of the loads.

He came down the near bank on the shafts with the canvas slung between them and the three home jars roped round him. Dee let the shafts down on the rope, butt end first, and the canvas went down the slope behind them with Pell in it, holding his splinted leg up off the stones with both hands, and saying things.

Dee and Rook came over at the end.

They came down the near bank on Toren's steps, with Toren standing on the post calling step up to them one at a time. Rook came first. He came down very slowly, with one hand on the rope and the other at his side, and his face grey and wet under his hat. He did not touch anything that was not the rope or a step. He stopped the way Jab had stopped, with the water running under him. He stood on the iron and looked down at the stream, at the heap of stones that had been the crown, and at the lead collar round the post under his boots.
