And at the south lip, on a crate, with her bad leg out straight and a book in her lap and her eyes shut, there was Dessa.

Jab could see her. It was three hundred paces across the bowl. He could see the crate, and the book, and the small straight shape of her on it, not moving. Behind her, on the gravel of the lip, there was something new. A table. It was a board on two trestles, with jars on it, and a canvas on the ground beside it with somebody lying on it.

A yard lifter. One of the big quiet men. He was lying on his side on the canvas behind the lamp-line, and somebody was kneeling beside him.

"He's sick," said Jab. He could feel it. "That one. It's in his belly."

He looked at the rest of it. He could not help looking, the way you look at a room you have come back to after a long time, to see what has moved.

The lamps had moved. There were more.

There was a rope along the lip path now, knotted to iron stakes, for hands. It had not been there on the forty-first.

The weighbridge girl's left arm had no plaster on it. It had a leather binding from the wrist to halfway up the forearm, laced tight.

Wyck was on the lip above the lamps. He had the bar. He had it in his left hand, the way he had since the gate, and his right arm was still strapped across him. He was standing where he could see everybody's feet. Jab watched him turn his head and say something down the line to Otto, and saw Otto shift his weight back into his heels.

The day holder's hollow at the south lip was empty.

The long building stood beyond the berm, low and white, with the windows of the ward along its side. Somewhere behind those windows there was a fifth bed on the right.

Jab put his hand flat on his coat and felt the fish.

Three hundred paces. And a Sag.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

She turned her head and shouted something. It came across the bowl thin and flat, the way voices do over water.

It was not loud. It did not have to be. It was flat, and it carried, the voice nobody argued with, and it came across three hundred paces of grey fog in the still afternoon as if she were standing beside them.

"I know," said Dessa. "I can hear you. Stay on the lip. Don't come down."

Toren stood at the edge of the north lip with his good hand at his side.

Toren had not moved.

Jab looked at him. Toren was standing at the edge of the north lip with his face doing a thing Jab had seen it do once before. That had been in the long room on the thirteenth day, when the Director read out what he had done at the Breach and he heard it said by somebody else.

"She's using it," said Toren.

"Using what?"

"Everybody back." Toren did not take his eyes off the far lip. "It's the call. For a push. Everybody back behind the lamps. And let it come to the light." He was quiet for a moment. "I wrote it on the step of eleven. The night before we went."

"Pell wrote it under his," said Callie. "In the book. Under everybody out."

"And she's made it a call," said Toren.

"She's made it work," said Pell, from the cart. He had pulled himself round on the boards to see. "That's a different thing. You wrote a thing. She made it a call. That's better than yours."

"I know," said Toren.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

He turned round.

Jab saw him do it. He turned his back on the Sag and looked at them, the six of them, on the north lip with the cart. Pell on the high side, with his leg out. Rook on the canvas, up on one elbow now, looking at the bottom. Dee with the glass. Callie with the hook. Duchess in the shafts, with her ears back at the fog. And Jab.

"Dee," said Toren. "Measure us."

"Now?"

"Now," said Toren. "Before I say anything. I need to know what there is."

Dee did it fast, two fingers on each wrist.

"Your stone's full," she said to Toren. "The Handful last night. Your own's two turns and the bit." She did Callie. "Half settled. Your own's all back." She looked at Callie's side. "The ribs are what they are."

"They're what they are," said Callie.

Dee did Jab. "A hand and a bit. Floor's a finger and a bit. It's not come down." She turned his palm over. "That's still a blister. And it's hot."

"I know."

She did Rook, and said nothing, and wrote it. She did her own, last, and said it, because Toren had asked her to at the wash.

"A hand," she said. "Over my floor. I can watch. I can draw leftovers. Every time." She looked at him. "I've slept five nights. I'm a watch again."

"And the jars," said Toren.

Callie said it, flat.

"The lifter's first, a quarter. My first, seven and a half. The fence's thirteen. Dirty, four. Home, twenty-four." She stopped. "Not touched."

"Not touched," said Toren.

He looked at the cart. At the rack behind the driver's bench, where the home jars stood grey to the shoulder beside the frame.

"They go back on the board," he said. "Whatever that is down there. They go back to Tilda, not touched. They're the store's." He looked at Jab. "Anything that gets drawn today comes out of the lifter's. Then the fence's. Not those."

"Not those," said Jab.

Toren turned back to the Sag.

"Jab," he said. "When does it push?"

"I don't know when," said Jab. "I can feel it gather. Under everything. Then it pushes." He shut his eyes. "A breath, mostly. Sometimes I don't get it. Callie's counter gets it after."

"Then you call the gathering," said Toren, "and Callie calls the number. And when you miss it, she's there." He looked at the fog. "A breath's enough to say everybody back."

Jab could feel him doing the sum. It had the cart in it, and the walking wheel, and Pell who could not walk and Rook who should not, and the boxes in lead, and three hundred paces of fog. It had forty husks since the fourth hour and four sick. And on the far side, a girl with a bad leg on a crate who had held the whole of it since first light with her eyes shut.

"I'm not going to tell her what to do," said Toren.

"No," said Dee.

"I'm going to tell her what we've got," said Toren. "And ask her what she wants. And then I'll tell you who does what." He looked at Dee. "Is that right?"

"You know it's right," said Dee. "You're asking me so it's said."

"I'm asking you so it's said," said Toren.

He stepped to the edge.

"Dessa!"

"I'm here."

"We've six!" He said it slow, flat, so it would carry. "Pell can't walk. Rook's off. Callie's ribs are cracked. Dee's a watch. Jab's a hand and a bit, and Jab can feel it gather before a push. Most times. A breath." He stopped. "I've a stone, and two turns." He stopped again. "And the boxes. In lead. On a cart with a wheel that walks."

There was a long pause from the far lip.

"Most times?" said Dessa.

"Most times. Callie's counter's on it after."

Another pause.

"What do you want?" said Toren.

Jab watched the small straight shape on the crate. It did not move. It sat with its eyes shut and its book in its lap, three hundred paces off, and he could feel it, not busy, the one person in the whole of the Sag who was not.

"I want you over," said Dessa. "All of you. Without anything following you up." A pause. "And I want my watch drawn. They've been in it since the fourth hour. I can feel it on them."

"Both," said Toren.

"Both."

"Then say where you want us."

Jab felt the field start to gather, the small hard load under everything.

"Now," he said.

"Pushing," said Toren, across the bowl.

"Everybody back!" said Dessa.

The line went back. The fog came up. The things stood up out of it and went up the slope at the lamps, into the light. Ines killed one. The girl killed one. Katori, at the top of the dark lane, did not move.

"Down," said Dessa. And then, in the same flat voice, as if nothing had happened: "I want you on the made road with the cart. Callie on the ditch side, from the corner where the post was. Not before. The top half's quiet. Toren where the wheel needs him. Jab calling." A pause. "Nobody stops in the bottom. If Jab says it's pushing, you stand still where you are, and we'll take what comes up. You don't fight it. You stand."

"And then?"

"And then Jab draws my watch," said Dessa. "Behind the lamps. And you do what I tell you."

Toren stood at the edge of the north lip.

Jab looked at him. He looked at Toren's face and saw something go out of it, some weight, the way weight goes out of a strut when the wheel comes off it. And something else come into it that Jab did not have a word for.

"Yes," said Toren.

He turned round.

"Pell," he said. "The high side. Dee, Duchess's head. Rook stays on the canvas and doesn't get off it whatever he sees. Callie—" He stopped. "You heard her."

"From the corner," said Callie. "Not before."

"Jab. At the tailboard. With the frame on, not in the rack. Call every push you get." He looked past Jab at Callie. "And you call every one he doesn't."

"Every one I get," said Jab.

He took the frame out of the rack. He backed up to it on the cart, the way he backed up to the tailboard at every halt, and slid his thumbs into the chest band and stood up under it. It was lighter than it had ever been. Four jars with clean ash in them, and the dirty one, and two empties. The home three stayed in the rack.

He put his left hand flat on his coat, over the fish.

Three hundred paces of grey fog that heaved when it wanted to. And beyond it the gate, and the long building, and a ward, and a fifth bed on the right.

He did not know if Tonk was asleep. He did not know if he was awake and ordering the nurses about. He knew he was there.

"Ready," said Toren.

"Ready," said Jab.

Pell lifted Duchess's rope off the rail and handed it down to Dee. Dee took the mare's head.

"Coming down," said Toren, across the Sag.

"Come down," said Dessa.

Chapter 45 — Everybody Back

[Urgent but grounded narration; keep movement and consequence sharply clear]

The top half was quiet, the way Dessa had said.

From the made road they could see all of it. The Sag lay below them like a bowl of smoke, three hundred paces from lip to lip. On the far side the lamps stood along the upper edge of the east track, with the watch between them and a second line below, two of its lamps dark. Ines was a small shape on the west rim. At the top of the dark lane a grey blade lay lit and flat, with Katori behind it. On the south lip Dessa sat on her crate with her eyes shut.

They went down toward all of it with the cart.

Toren walked beside the walking wheel with his good hand an inch off the rim. The made road went down the north slope in a long straight line, cracked and tilted, with grass in the cracks. Dee had Duchess's head. Pell sat on the high side of the cart, leaning, with his leg out and his hands on the rail. Rook lay on the canvas behind him on his side, not asleep, looking at the fog. Jab walked at the tailboard with the frame on his back and his left hand flat on his coat.

Callie walked behind the cart, not in front of it. Dessa had said from the corner, and the corner was at the bottom. She read the road over the tailboard with the counter held out, and said the numbers.

"Thirty," she said. "Forty. Fifty, at the edge of it."

The fog began a third of the way down.

It did not have an edge the way a wall does. It had an edge the way water has one on sand, thin at first and then not thin. Toren walked into it beside the wheel, and it came up round his boots, grey, and then round his shins. It was not wet. It was not anything. It was dust that had not decided to lie down.

"Sixty," said Callie. "Seventy."

"Jab," said Toren.

"Nothing," said Jab. "It's lying there."

The walking wheel knocked at every turn. In the bottom of the Sag it sounded very loud, like a man tapping on a door.

"Now," said Jab. "Pushing."

Toren put his hand up without looking. Dee stopped Duchess, and the cart stopped with her.

"Pushing," said Toren. He did not shout it. It went across the fog.

"Everybody back!" said Dessa, from the far lip.

On the east slope the lamp-line moved. From down here the lamps were a row of yellow blurs, and the dark shapes between them stepped back from the blurs, all together, and stood.

The bottom heaved.

It came up under the fog all round them, not a sound, a movement, and they all felt it through their boots. The grey round their shins rose to their knees and sank back. And off to the left, east, beyond the road, where the slabs dropped away toward the ditch and the joints, something stood up.

It stood up out of the fog twenty paces off, grey on grey, and turned.

Nobody moved. That was the rule, and all six of them had heard it said across the bowl. You stand still where you are. Toren kept his good hand an inch off the rim. He had a full stone at the bottom of him, and he did not reach for it. Jab's knife stayed off his fist. Nothing on the cart was worked. Nothing on the cart was lit.

The husk turned toward the lamps.

It went up the east slope at the yellow blurs, away from them, through the fog, into the light. Something came down off the west rim, thin and fast, across the whole width of the Sag. The husk stopped. It came apart.

"Down," said Dessa.

"Go," said Toren.

They went on.

The bottom was slabs.

All six of them had crossed it on the forty-first, with the watch on the lip and nothing coming up. Toren had knelt in it on the twenty-fifth with a woman bleeding in the fog. Jab had knelt in its black water that same day, with his hand on the day holder's chest. They went across it now with the fog to their knees, and it was like walking across a floor you know in the dark.

The slabs were tilted. Some had dropped at one edge into the water, and some had risen. The road ran over them in a line of concrete, cracked into blocks, with black water in every crack. The cart went over it a slab at a time, rocking, with the walking wheel singing and knocking and Pell leaning on the high side saying easy.

"Eighty," said Callie. "Eighty-five."

"There's the corner," said Dee.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

The white post was not standing where it had stood. It lay flat in the water on the east side of the road, under the fog, with the 6 on it facing up, and they could see the white of it through the grey. Beside it the slab under the road's east edge had dropped. It had dropped on the twenty-fifth, a hand, and folded the day holder's sheet. It had dropped again since. Now the whole east half of the road sloped down at that slab into the black water, two hands at its low corner, and the water was over the lip of it.

The walking wheel was on the east side.

"Callie," said Toren. "Ground."

She came up past the tail of the cart on the east side. She did not go in front of it. She crouched at the edge of the dropped slab with the hook's end held out flat, and read.

"Soft," she said. "The dropped one's rocking. It's sitting on water." She moved the hook. "The next one's stone. There. Past the corner. It's not moved. It's sitting on the old bed." She looked up at Toren. "Under where the axle'll be when the wheel's in the middle of the drop."

"Set there," said Toren.

"Set there."

"And the ditch side?"

Callie turned her head and looked east. Past the dropped slab and the post in the water, the ground went down in a long shallow slope to the ditch. The fog lay thicker there, heaped over the joints, and it moved.

"That's where they come up," she said. "All of them. Look at it."

"Then that's yours," said Toren.

Callie did not stand.

She knelt on the stone slab past the corner, on the ditch side of the road, on both knees. She put the back of the hook's curve down on the edge of the slab, still, with the bend facing east. Then she did not take the conduit in both hands. She took it in one, her right, by the tail, where it ended. Her left arm stayed across her ribs. She knelt beside the hook, not behind it.

"On the hill it stayed in the steel," she said. She said it to Toren, or to herself. "When my knees went. It held a breath with nothing of me behind it, and I went down onto it. I thought that was the falling." She settled her hand on the tail. "It wasn't the falling. It was the steel. This time I'm putting it there."

"How long?" said Toren.

"The half," said Callie. "And my own. And the ribs." She did not look at him. "Say when the wheel's past, and I'll let it down. Slow. When I say."

Her face went still.

The lee stood up.

It stood up off the outside of the curve, east, toward the ditch and the joints, pale. She did not let it stand straight. She leaned it back over the road, over the dropped slab, like a lean-to. It went back and back: over the place where the cart would be when the wheel was in the drop, over the place where Toren would stand, over Duchess's head.

It was longer than a door. They could all see that. It stood along the edge of the road from the corner past the stone slab, the length of the cart and the horse together, a pale wall with the fog heaped against its outside. It was over all of them at once, cart and horse and people, not a door with her behind it.

"It's a line," said Callie. Her voice was flat. "It's not a door. It's a line. Along the road." She breathed out through her teeth. "It's dear. Holding."

"Bring her on," said Toren.

Dee brought Duchess on. The mare walked into the shelter of the lee with her ears flat and her eyes white, and she did not stop, because Dee was walking in front of her. The cart came on behind. The good wheel rolled along the west side of the road on sound slabs. The walking wheel came to the edge of the dropped slab and went down onto it.

"Set," said Toren.

The strut came up out of the stone slab past the corner, at its slant, under the axle beside the walking wheel. The wheel went down into the drop, down the slope of the slab toward the water, and the weight came onto the strut.

"Holding," said Toren.

It was a wheel. It was not the cart on the arch. It was one wheel on a drop, with Pell on the high side and a load of lead in the middle, and Toren stood soft behind it and paid by the breath.

"Rolling," said Pell.

The wheel went on across the drop.

"Now—" said Jab. He had it late. "Pushing."

Toren could not call it across the Sag. He had a wheel on a strut in a drop, and his stone going under it.

"Pushing!" That was Callie. She said it loud and flat from beside the hook, in the voice she used for a number.

"Everybody back!" said Dessa, from the far lip.

The bottom came up.

It came up all round the dropped slab. The fog on the ditch side heaved against the outside of the lee, and the joints in the ground below the ditch opened in the grey. Things stood up out of them. One. Two. Three. Grey on grey, through the pale of the lee.

They did not turn toward the lamps.

The lamps were far off, up the slope. And here, two paces from them, there was a pale wall standing along the edge of the road, worked. Under the road there was a strut, worked. There was a girl kneeling with her hand on the tail of a hook, and a boy holding a wheel.

They came at the lee.

The first one hit it, and they all felt it. It came through the stone and the strut and up through Toren's boots, with the sound of a sack thrown against a wall. The lee did not move. The husk stood against its outside, pushing, with no face.

"Holding," said Callie.

She did not get up. She knelt with her right hand on the tail of the conduit and her left arm across her ribs, and her eyes were not on the husk. They were on the cart: on Duchess, and Dee at her head, and Pell leaning, and Rook on the canvas, and Jab at the tailboard, and Toren at his strut. She could see every one of them from where she knelt.

The second husk hit the lee beside the first.

"The wheel," said Toren. "It's in the middle. Three more breaths."

"Three," said Callie.

The third husk did not hit the lee. It went along the outside of it, toward the end, where the lee stopped at the tail of the cart.

"End," said Callie. "It's going round the end."

Toren could not move. He had the wheel.

"Mine," said Jab.

He went past the tailboard to the end of the lee with the frame on his back, and the knife came on his left fist, dark. He lit the hook of it and nothing else. The husk came round the end of the pale wall at the worked thing, and met the lit hook, and came apart. Its grey fell on the slab at the end of the lee and slid off into the water.

Something came down across the Sag from the west rim. It came thin and fast, at a long slant over the road, and struck the first husk where it stood against the lee's outside. The husk came apart, and its grey slid down the outside of the pale wall into the fog.

"Ines," said Callie. She had not moved her eyes.

"Past," said Pell. "The wheel's past."

Toren let the strut go. At the end. Not after.

The walking wheel came up off the dropped slab onto sound stone beyond the corner, singing, and the cart came level.

The last husk stood against the lee's outside, pushing. Ines's second arrow came down across the bottom and took it.

"Down," said Dessa, from the far lip.

"Down," said Callie.

She let the lee down. She did not drop it. She brought it in off the road the way you pay a rope back through your hands, the lean-to coming upright, and shorter, and then out. Then she knelt on the slab with the hook lying flat and her right hand still on the tail of it, and breathed out through her teeth, slowly.

"How much?" said Toren.

"All the half," said Callie. "And some of mine." She did not get up yet. "It held on the steel. I put it there, and it held, and I let it down when I said." She looked at her hand on the tail of the conduit. "I didn't have to be the wall."

"No," said Toren.

"On the hill my knees chose it," said Callie. "At the washout I forgot it. I stood behind it, the way I always stand to a door." She got up, one knee and then the other, with the hook for a stick. "I don't have to."

At the tail of the cart Jab nodded, once, as he had nodded at the pump house when she kept the tag.

They came up the south slope in the next quiet.

The lamps were there. The lamp-line stood along the upper edge of the east track, and the made road came up past the end of it to the lip. As the cart came up the last of the slope, the line opened for it.

Otto came down from his place with his big hands out. He took Duchess's rope from Dee without a word, and one of the yard lifters took the other side of her head. They walked the mare up the last of the slope, over the lip and onto the gravel, and the cart came up behind her with the walking wheel knocking. Pell leaned on the high side with his face grey. Rook lay on the canvas with his eyes open. Dee walked beside the mare with her hand still out, as if she had forgotten it was empty.

"Behind the lamps," said Dessa.

They were behind the lamps.

Otto and the yard lifter went back down to their places, and the line closed again below them. Every head on it had turned to the six, except Katori's.

Toren stood on the gravel at the south lip and turned round, and looked back across the Sag. The fog lay in the bottom. The dropped corner lay down there, with the post in the water. The north lip was three hundred paces off, and empty.

He counted them. He could not help it.

"Six," he said. "And a horse."

"I know," said Dessa.

She was on the crate. She had not moved. She sat with her bad leg out straight and the big book in her lap and her eyes shut.

Toren went and stood in front of her.

She opened her eyes.

None of the six had seen her face since the forty-first. It was thinner. It was white, with marks under the eyes, and set, the way Dee's had been set at Caul Hill over the jar. She looked at Toren. She looked at his arm in its cuff, and at his face, and at his coat, which was still grey in the seams.

"You're late," she said.

"Two days," said Toren.

"Not yet," said Toren.

Dessa looked past him at the cart: at Pell, and at Rook on the canvas, at Jab with the frame and Callie with the hook, and at Dee. Then she looked back at Toren, and shut her eyes again.

The table was two boards on trestles behind the lamp-line, with jars on it. They were the watch's jars, Otto's dirty ones, the sweepings from the lip. Then the other one." She did not open her eyes. "The girl's in her arms. Ines is the least. Wyck's been on the lip." She stopped. "I've not been anywhere. I've sat."

"It came up to thirty paces," said Dessa. "It's not come nearer than that all day. I'd have known."

Jab swung the frame off his back onto the table. He took out the lifter's first jar, with its quarter, and Callie's clean one, with seven and a half.

"Dee," he said.

"I'm the watch," said Dee. She stood at his left shoulder with the glass. "Work."

He knelt by the yard lifter on the canvas. He could kneel here. It was the lip. He put his right palm flat on the man's belly, round the white place, with the jar against his left, and shut his eyes.

"Busy," he said. "It's in the belly. He's swallowed it. It's all through the belly and the chest."

He drew. They all watched the yard lifter's face. For a long time it did not change. Then it did.

"Vent," said Dee.

Jab held it high and turned, and put his palm flat on the gravel at the edge of the lip, where the grey from the watch's kills had lain all day.

"Not into my floor," said Callie. She had come to the table and was standing with the hook for a stick. "Into the road's."

"It's the road's," said Jab.

Dee took his leftovers. Jab went back on.

[Warm, intimate narration; hold the feeling lightly]

Toren stood by the table and looked down at the lamp-line.

Otto was in his place in it, grey in the face, with sick down the front of his coat, and there was room beside him for a man with a strut. Toren took a step down the gravel toward it before he had decided anything, the way his hands built a fire.

He stopped. He turned round to the crate.

Dessa did not open her eyes.

Wyck came down the lamp-line from his place on the lip. He had the bar in his left hand. His right arm was strapped across him, and his face was set the way it went on the road when he was doing a thing Keel had told him not to.

"I'm cleared tomorrow," he said, to nobody. "It's one day."

Otto stood there. Jab drew him, and Otto looked down at Jab's hand on his chest the whole time, and went red about nothing.

Taking. Yours. Mine. Letting go. Callie and Toren had learned it in the north yard on the thirty-fourth, with a rack and a sack. None of the six had known that the whole watch was saying it now.

Katori did not come.

She was at the top of the dark lane between the third lamp and the fourth, with her grey blade lit and lying flat along the edge like a stove across a room. She had not moved since the six came over the north lip. None of them thought she had moved since the fourth hour.

"Katori," said Dessa. "Off."

"I don't come off," said Katori. She did not turn her head. "Nobody's got the lane."

They all looked at the lane.

It ran down from the gap between the third lamp and the fourth, dark, toward the ditch. The hounds came up it. That was what it was for. Hounds went for the dark, and the dark was the lane, and at the top of the lane there was Katori with a blade, and nobody else.

"I'll take the lane," said Toren.

Katori turned her head then.

She looked at him: at his arm in its cuff, and his face, and his right fist, which had nothing on it.

Toren knew that look. She had given it to him on the step of eleven, weeks ago, and he had thought then that she was deciding whether he was worth telling something to, and had decided not yet.

"With what?" said Katori.

"A strut," said Toren. "And the spike. Not together."

"How much have you got?"

"A stone," said Toren. "Full. And two turns of my own and a bit. I've held a wheel in the bottom. That was four breaths." He did not look away. "I can hold a hound off a strut. I've held a husk on one at Caul Hill for the whole of a thing I'll tell you about. I can't hold it and kill it. It's one or the other."

Katori looked at him.

"Don't block it," she said.

"What?"

"The lane. Don't put the strut across it." She turned back to the dark. "You block it, they go round. Round the lamp. Into the light, where Otto is. Otto's got a bar and no blade." She was quiet. "Narrow it. Put the strut in at a slant, from this side. Make the lane a pace wide at the top. Then they come one at a time. Or they don't come."

"One at a time," said Toren.

"And when one comes, you don't kill it," said Katori. "You hold it. On the strut. And you say so." She looked at him again. "And somebody else kills it."

"Who?"

"Me," said Katori. "When I've been drawn."

Dessa's voice came across the lip, flat.

"Katori. That's mine to say. You're off."

Katori looked at Toren a moment longer. Then she lifted the blade off the lane, still lit.

"Taking," said Toren.

He stepped into the top of the lane beside her, with the third lamp at his left shoulder and the fourth two paces off at his right.

"Yours," said Katori.

"Mine."

"Letting go," said Katori. She let the blade go dark and stepped back, and walked up the slope to the table with her cap pulled down, and did not look back once.

At the top of the dark lane Toren stood with the fog in the bottom of the Sag below him and nothing on his fist, and waited.

Toren waited a long time.

Behind him, at the table, the work went on. Jab said busy, and after a while clean. Dee said vent, and there was the soft sound of a palm going flat on gravel. Callie said the jar.

"The lifter's first's done," she said. "The quarter. My first's open. Seven and a half."

"It's in my chest," said Katori.

"It's all through you," said Jab. "You've been in it since the fourth hour."

Katori did not answer him.

The fog lay in the bottom. It crept up the lower slope and slid back. It heaved a little, and lay down.

"Pushing," said Jab, from the table. He had caught the gathering that time.

"Everybody back!" said Dessa.

The lamp-line stepped back behind the lamps. Toren did not. He was at the top of the lane, and the lane was the dark, and the dark was where they came.

The bottom heaved. The grey came up the slope toward the lamps, and things stood up in it and went up at the light. Two. Three. The bars met them. The girl came down the lip path with her blade and killed one.

And something came up the dark lane.

It came low and fast, the colour of the dark, with two green points in it where the lamplight caught. It came straight up the lane at the top of it, where Toren was standing.

"Set," said Toren.

He put the foot of the strut down at the top of the lane on the third-lamp side, at a slant, leaning out over the lane toward the fourth. It came up out of the gravel pale and hard, as high as his waist. The lane was a pace wide at the top now: a pace of dark between the end of the strut and the fourth lamp's pole.

The hound hit the strut.

It did not hit it the way a husk hits. It hit it the way a dog hits a gate, all teeth and weight and scrabbling claws, and it fell back and came again. It could not get past the strut. It went along the end of it, into the pace of dark that was left, and came through the pace at him.

"Holding," said Toren. "It's on the strut. It's coming through the end."

There was nobody beside him. He could not kill it. He had the strut.

He let the strut go.

It went out, and the hound came through the whole width of the lane at him, low. He lit the heel and nothing more. He put the lit hook of the spike down across its path, low, and it went into the light, because it was going for him and the light was in the way. He dragged the hook round against the third lamp's pole and put the point in.

It came apart. The grey fell on the gravel at the top of the lane.

He let the heel go dark.

"Set," he said, and put the strut back in.

His breath was going. He could feel it. The stone had paid for the hound on the strut for as long as it was on it, and then for the heel, and it was less than half now.

"That's one," he said.

"Down," said Dessa.

Katori came back.

She came down from the table without being told, with her cap pulled down and her blade dark on her fist. She was not grey in the face any more. She was white. She stood at Toren's right shoulder on the fourth-lamp side of the lane, a pace off.

"I'm drawn," she said.

"You're drawn."

"You let the strut go and killed it," said Katori. "I watched." She did not look at him. "That was right. It was the only thing you could do with nobody else here." She was quiet. "There's somebody else here. You hold. I kill."

"I hold," said Toren.

He understood it all at once, standing at the top of the lane. He had held and killed, held and killed, all the way from the Breach, because there had been nobody else to do the other half. At Caul Hill Callie had held the door with her back to all of them, and he had given her the lean. He had given it away.

He could give this away too.

"I'll hold," he said. "You kill."

"That's the lane," said Katori.

[Focused, grounded narration; make the physical instruction legible]

The big push came at dusk.

By then every one of them had a place. Dessa was on the crate. Otto and the other yard lifter were on the lamp-line with Wyck. The girl was at the rope on the lip path, and Ines was on the west rim. Toren and Katori were at the top of the lane. Jab and Dee were at the table, and Callie stood by them with the counter and Dee's book. Pell and Rook were on the cart.

Jab felt it first. He did not say now this time, or pushing. He said "Dee," and there was a thing in his voice that nobody had heard since the rope by the door at Caul Hill.

"It's all of it," said Jab. "The whole bottom. It's gathering and it's not stopping gathering. It's—"

"Everybody back!" said Dessa.

The whole bottom of the Sag came up.

It came up the way the drifts at the wash had come up in the gust, only there was no gust. The fog heaved up out of the bottom and up the slopes. It came up past the lamp-line on the east track and onto the lip path, and up the made road toward the lip. Things stood up in it everywhere. Toren tried to count them from the top of the lane, and Callie tried from the table, and they both stopped.

The lamp-line was behind the lamps. Nobody was below them. The things came up at the light.

Otto and the yard lifter met them with bars. Wyck stood in Otto's old place with his bar planted and his weight in his heels, and a husk came at him, and he did not strike it. He took it on the bar, low, the way you take a sack, and let it come, and turned it off the end of the bar down the slope, and stepped back into his place.

"Heels," said Wyck, down the line.

Ines was loosing from the west rim. They could hear the bow from the table. The girl was on the lip path with her blade.

And up the made road, toward the lip, toward the table where Jab was drawing, the fog came, with husks in it.

"Callie!" said Dessa.

"I've got the road," said Callie.

She put Dee's book down on the table and went to the top of the made road, where it came up over the lip above the table. She did not stand behind the hook. She knelt beside it, as she had in the bottom, with the curve across the concrete and her right hand on the tail.

"Holding," she said, flat, in the voice for a number.

And the dark lane filled.

They came up it three at a time. Hounds. They came up the lane at the dark top of it, where Toren was, and the first hit the strut, and the second hit the first, and the third went along the end of the strut into the pace of dark.

"Holding," said Toren. "Three. One through the end."

"Mine," said Katori.

She did not step into the lane. She reached across the end of the strut with her blade lit and lying flat, and the hound coming through the pace of dark met the edge of it, and came apart.

"Two on the strut," said Toren.

The strut took them. They hit it, and scrabbled, and fell back, and hit it, and the strut went down into the gravel and did not come up into him, because he was soft. His breath was going under it.

"One coming round," he said. "The end."

"Mine."

Katori killed it.

"One," said Toren.

It came through the pace at the end. Katori was there, and it came apart.

The lane was empty.

Toren stood at the top of it with the strut up and nothing on it. He felt the stone go. It went out from under him the way it had gone at the steel door, like water out of a basin, and he was on his own. He was two turns of his own and a bit, and the strut on that.

"Stone's gone," he said. "I'm on mine."

"How much?" said Katori.

"Two turns."

"Then let it down when it's empty," said Katori. "Not before. I'll say."

He held it. He held a strut with nothing on it at the top of a dark lane while the fog heaved behind the hounds. It was not free. There was no free strut. But it was cheaper than a hound.

At the table the work had not stopped.

"Jar," said Jab. He said it before it was dry.

"The fence's fourth," said Dee. "Not the home three."

"Not the home three," said Callie, from the top of the made road, holding.

Dee put the fence's fourth against Jab's left palm, and Jab went on. He said busy, and kept saying it, and then clean. He said next, and the other yard lifter answered him in his slow voice, and Jab drew him.

Then Jab stopped.

His right palm was still flat on the yard lifter's chest, round the white place, and the man was clean. But the warm was in the wrong place. It was round the mark, past the heel of his hand, where the clean cold should have been holding it off, and it was in his wrist. It was his own hand, hot round the white place, and the hot was going up. On the rope by the door at Caul Hill he had kept his hand where it was, and Dee had had to take his wrist.

He took his hand off.

"Off," said Jab.

Dee looked up from the jar. She had not said it yet.

"I'm warm," said Jab. His voice was very steady. "The palm. Round the mark. It's to the wrist. It's not the draw. It's mine." He breathed. "I'm off. Vent."

"Vent," said Dee.

He put his palm flat on the gravel at the edge of the lip and let it go. He stayed there. Ten breaths. Twenty.

"The girl's not done," said Jab. "Nor Wyck. Nor Ines."

"I know who's not done," said Dee. "You're off. Sit on the crate. I'll draw you."

"Dessa's on the crate."

"Then sit on the ground," said Dee. "It's the lip. You can sit."

He sat on the ground with his back against the trestle, and Dee knelt in front of him and put her palm on his wrist, and drew. He did not ask to go back on.

At the top of the lane Toren could not look round. He had the strut. He had heard all of it behind him: the off, and the vent, and Dee telling Jab where to sit. Then he heard nothing from Jab for a long time, and it was the loudest thing he had ever heard him do.

At the top of the made road Callie was still holding.

"I'm at my floor," she said.

Her voice was thick. There was blood in it.

"I'm at my floor. I'm stopping."

"Down," said Dessa. "Callie. Down."

The hook lay flat on the concrete.

Toren looked down the lane. It was dark, and empty, and below it the fog in the bottom of the Sag was lying down.

It went down the way it had come up, with no count.

The fog sank back down the slopes into the bottom and lay there. It heaved once, a little, and lay down again. Things that had been standing in it came apart on their own, the way the husks in the corridor had come apart when the lifter died, and lay as grey. Or they went back down into the joints. Nobody on the lip could tell which.

"Down," said Dessa. "Stay on the line."

Nobody moved off the line.

"Now," said Katori.

Toren let the strut go. At the end. Not after. He stood at the top of the dark lane with nothing on his fist and his own down to a turn, and his arm aching in its cuff, and did not turn round yet.

"Callie," said Katori, beside him. "Read it."

Callie got up off her knees at the top of the made road with the hook for a stick, and held the counter out over the bowl. Her face was white. There was blood on her lip and down her chin.

Toren turned round.

At the table, Jab was sitting on the ground with his back against the trestle and his right hand held palm up on his knee. Dee was kneeling in front of him with her palm flat on his wrist. The rag was off the white place. The blister had broken, and the skin round the mark was red and wet.

Jab got up. He did it slowly, one knee and then the other.

Dee looked at him, and they watched her do the sum: the one with a price on every line, and the other one.

He drew Ines last. She had come off the west rim with her bow and her empty quiver, and she stood in front of him without a word.

Callie looked at the rack on the cart.

"Not touched," she said.

Dessa counted them.

She did it from the crate, with the big book open on her knee and a lantern the gate crew had brought hung on the trestle beside her. She did it the way she had done the order every night on the road from the old station: out loud, one name at a time, with her eyes open.

Then she stopped, and looked at the six lines, and at the names she had to write in them. She looked down the lip at the lamp-line: at Katori at the top of the dark lane, and at Otto, and the yard lifter with his calf tied up, and the girl.

They went up the made road from the lip toward the yard gate in the last of the light. Otto had Duchess's head. The cart went in the middle with the walking wheel knocking. Pell sat on the high side, leaning. Rook lay on the canvas with his eyes shut, hot. Jab walked at the tailboard with his right hand held palm up and open, cooling in the air. Callie walked beside the cart with her hand on the rail and blood on her chin and the hook for a stick. Dee walked at the wheel. Toren walked at the back, the way he always did.

Behind them the lamps stayed lit along the east track, and the watch stayed on them.

At the yard gate there was a lamp, and under it a man in a white coat, standing with his arms folded. He had the face Dessa had said. Behind him, a long way up, in the long window on the second floor of the yard office, there was a light, and somebody small and square standing in it, not moving.

Toren counted them in through the gate. Out loud.

He did not say out this time. He did not say where to. There was nowhere to.

"In," he said. "Six."

They hosed them at the gate like arrivals.

Callie had known they would. She had thought about it on the road, on the nights when she could not lie down, and she had not minded thinking about it. It was the pen, and the gate, and the grey coats with the hose. It was the first thing Meridian had ever done to her. It was the thing it did to everybody who came in from outside, whoever they were, and she found she wanted it done.

The water was cold. It came out of the hose in a hard grey rope and went over her hair and her face and down the back of her collar, and her ribs took every shiver of it. She stood with her arms out from her sides the way the grey coat told her, the right one out and the left one only a little. She did not make a sound.

"Hook," said the grey coat.

She gave it to him.

He held it up under the lamp by the gate. He read the counter against the curve, and then against the grip, and then he looked at the paper tag tied round the conduit below where the rag had been. pen, 35th.

"Fourth time, miss," he said.

"Third was the pen," said Callie.

"Third was the pen." He took a stub of pencil from behind his ear and wrote on the tag, under the old line, holding it flat against the steel. Then he gave the hook to the other grey coat for the washing.

"When do I get it back?"

"Morning," said the grey coat. "Same as always."

She stood in the lamplight dripping and watched them take it away. She had not been without it since the forty-first. Her right hand did not know what to do.

Behind her, Hallet was at his window with his pen on its string. He was saying things to a young man about the time of night and the distance from the Sag to the north gate. He said them quietly and at length. He had his ledger open, and he was writing them in.

Six. She saw him write it. And then, after a long moment in which he looked at the cart, and a horse.

Doctor Sowerby had Pell off the cart before the cart had stopped.

He did not say anything to Pell. He said a great deal to the two orderlies with the stretcher, and to the lamp, and to the air in general. Most of it was about people who put broken ankles on carts for ten days. Some of it was about the splint, which he looked at without touching.

"Who did this?" he said at last.

"Miss Wren," said Pell.

"With what?"

"The tailboard rail," said Pell. "And the canvas off the cart."

Sowerby looked at the splint a while longer.

"It's not bad," he said, in a voice that meant it was very good and he would not say so. "Take him."

Then he got to Rook.

Rook was lying on the canvas on his side with his eyes open. Sowerby stood over him with his arms folded and his face like a thundercloud.

"Well," said Rook.

"Don't," said Sowerby.

"I've a hole in my back," said Rook. "And a dog in it. And she gave me all four of your papers. One a day. Not twice."

Sowerby knelt on the wet gravel of the gate yard and lifted the pad off Rook's back with two fingers. He looked. He did not say anything. He put the back of his hand against Rook's neck.

"How long?" he said. To Miss Wren.

"Since the forty-seventh," said Miss Wren. "It declared at dawn. The worst was the forty-seventh and the fifty-first. It's not spread since the fifty-first. It's yellow at the foot."

Sowerby put the pad back.

"Take him," he said to the orderlies. And then, to Rook, not looking at him: "You'll lie on your face for a week. You'll eat what I give you. You'll not get up without somebody counting."

"I've been counted for a week," said Rook. "It's the only thing I'm good at now."

The orderlies took him.

Callie looked for Jab.

He was not in the gate yard. The frame was leaning against the cart wheel with its jars in it, and Toren was standing beside it with his hand on the rack, the way you put your hand on a thing so it will not walk off. Jab was not there.

He was walking very fast toward the long building, with his right hand held out a little from his side and his left hand flat on his coat. He was walking the way he had walked out of the room under the hill with the frame on his back, the lantern swinging, when Miss Wren had said out.

She did not call after him.

Her mother was at the weighbridge.

Callie had not expected that. She had thought her mother would be in the hut, at this hour, or in the ward. She came round the end of the berm into the south yard in the dark, wet through, with no hook and her arm across her side, and the weighbridge hut had a lamp in its window.

In the ward, Keel looked at her first. She put her ear to Callie's back, left side and right, and made her breathe, and then cough, which she did not want to do. Then she held the lamp up and looked in her nose.

She noticed that she was not counting it. She noticed it the way you notice that a sound has stopped. Her mother's breath went in and out in the dark on the next bed, slow, with a little catch on the out-breath. Callie lay and let it go in and out, and did not put a number on it. After a while she was asleep.

The technician was waiting at the yellow line in the morning.

He was standing on the far side of it, in the treatment shed, with his left hand at his side and his right hand in a sling. It took all of the morning.

He had been getting ready for it. Callie could see that. There were papers on the bench along the wall, the pages of a book copied out in his hand, in pencil, dozens of them. And on the steel of the rack, beside each box, there were numbers chalked in small figures. He had been writing down what every box ought to say, one by one, while he still knew.

"I did a month's work," he said, when he saw her looking. "Waiting. I didn't sleep much." He looked at the rack. "Now it's a night, maybe two, not a month. It learns the new one off the ones that still tell the truth. It doesn't need me to know, after that."

The rack was the one she had first seen on the tenth day. It was rows of grey boxes behind glass, each one with a small light under it. The lights were green. Most of them. Four along in the third row, one was yellow. The one beside it was a paler green than the rest.

"That's the liar," said the technician. "The fourth. And the fifth, catching it off him."

He had two assistants. They were the two who had made the carrier out of depot sheet, and they had never said a word to Callie in forty days, and they did not say one now. They did what he told them. He told them with his left hand and his voice.

They opened the glass. They took the fourth box out of the third row with the shed's own tongs, long and iron, not your hands. They carried it on the tongs to the bench, where it lay dead and lying. Then they came across the yellow line to the carrier, and the technician came with them, and stood over it.

"The hundred and ten," he said.

The assistant closed the tongs on it and lifted it out of the lead. He carried it on the tongs across the yellow line, slowly, the way you carry a pan too full. They set it in the third row, in the place the liar had been.

It did not go in at once. There were screws, and a plate that went across the back, and the technician did not have the hand for the screws. He stood and told the assistant which, and in what order, and the assistant turned them one at a time. Callie counted them. Eleven.

"There," said the technician. "Now it's in."

The light under it came on yellow.

"Yellow's right," he said, before anybody could ask. "Yellow's learning. It's got to be told what it is by the others. A night. Two." He looked along the row. "If the others agree with it, it goes green. If they don't, it's the hill's box and not ours, and I'll try the other."

"And the other?" said Toren.

"The other goes in that," said the technician. He nodded at a steel cupboard against the back wall, with a lock on it. "In its lead. The Director's said. It's the spare. And it's what she'll show anybody who asks whether six people went to a hill and came back with what they said." He looked at Toren. "It's the proof. You don't spend the proof."

[Measured, compassionate narration; keep the clinical detail clear]

The rack was still open.

Callie was standing at the glass, because the technician had asked her to read the new box once more through it, in its place. She held the counter at a hand and waited ten breaths and said the number. A hundred and ten. The same.

She looked along the rows while she waited.

The first row was at the top. At the end of it, nine along, there was an empty place. That was where the dead box had lived, the one Toren had carried on the eleventh day, the one that had gone into the pen with Miss Wren's arm at its window and come apart. It had gone to the depot after. There was a square of bare steel where it had been.

And beside the empty place, set into the steel of the rack's frame at the end of the row, there was a round thing.

It was a socket. It was a shallow round seat in the steel, not deep, as wide as two of her thumbs laid side by side. It had a rim. And from the middle of it out to the rim there were ribs, fine, raised a little from the steel, like the spokes of a wheel with no wheel on them.

She counted them without deciding to.

Nine.

It was empty. It was clean. It was the only place on the rack that did not have the grey film of seventy years on it. The steel of it was bright, as if nothing had ever sat in it long enough to leave a mark.

"What goes in that?" she said.

The technician looked where she was looking.

"Nothing," he said. "Not in my time. Not in my father's. It came empty."

"Then what's it for?"

"I don't know," said the man. "It's in the book." He went to the bench with his left hand and took down a book from the shelf over it. It was old, thick, the cover gone soft, with the wheel mark stamped into it and worn nearly flat. He opened it at the first page and held it out to her across the yellow line. He did not step over. "The fittings. When it came. The list of everything that was in the rack."

Callie looked.

The page was printed, in the small square letters the plate on the boxes had. A long list, line after line, with numbers. Most of it meant nothing to her.

One line had a pencil line through it.

It was near the bottom. It had a number, and a word she did not know, and after the word the figure 9. The pencil line went through all of it. And beside it, in the margin, in the same pencil, in a small upright hand that was not the technician's and not anybody's she had ever seen, there were three words.

released to bearer

"Released," said the technician. "That's all I know. It was taken out before the machine ever came here. Out of the rack. Whatever it was." He shut the book. "To who, it doesn't say. Bearer. Whoever had it in his hand, that's all that means."

Callie did not say anything.

She had looked up from the book, because that was what she did. She looked at people when a number came, to see what the number did to them.

Toren was standing beside her at the yellow line.

He was not looking at the book. He was looking at the socket in the steel at the end of the first row, the round seat with its nine fine ribs and nothing in it. His face was doing nothing at all. It was so still that Callie looked at it twice.

And his right hand had come up and was lying flat on his shirt. Not his coat. The shirt, under it, where the coat was open. It lay over his breastbone, flat, the way Jab's hand lay over the fish.

He did not seem to know it was there.

"When?" said Toren.

His voice was quite ordinary.

"It doesn't say when," said the technician. "It doesn't say anything. It's a line in a book." He put the book back on the shelf. "There's a lot of lines like that. In a thing this old."

"Yes," said Toren.

He took his hand off his shirt. He did it the way you put a thing down that you did not know you had picked up.

Callie did not ask him. She did not know what she would have asked. She had read ground for fifty-five days and floors for twenty, and she had read that face on a stair and at a door and at the top of a dark lane. She had never seen it do that.

She put it where she put the numbers she did not understand yet. She kept it.

On the fifty-seventh the light under the new box went green.

The technician came to the ward at first light to say so. He stood in the door of the long room with his arm in its sling and did not come in, and said it to the whole ward.

"It's green."

Senna was lying on the fourth bed on the right. She turned her head on the pillow.

"All of it?" she said.

"All of it," said the technician. "It asked itself this morning. Row by row, every one. They all agreed." He was quiet. "I've not seen that since I was twenty-six."

"Then I'll go down," said Senna.

"It's not your day."

"It's not my day," said Senna. "My day was the fifty-fourth, and Sowerby took it out of my arm with a needle and a lot of language." She did not raise her voice. "I'd like the machine to have a look at me now, if it's honest. I'd like to know what it thinks of his needle."

Sowerby was at the end of the ward. He looked at the technician, and the technician looked at him.

"This afternoon," said Sowerby.

Callie was there because her mother was. Her mother sat on the edge of the fourth bed on the left with her stick against her knee. The bruises were still on Senna's arms from the needle on the fifty-fourth, yellow and green down the inside of both elbows. She had had a fever on the fifty-fifth, the night they came back, and had not said so to Toren when he came in.

After noon the two orderlies came and lifted Senna off the bed into the chair.

It took both of them. Callie watched. Senna could not take the step. She could not put her feet where the floor was, because she could not feel the floor. They lifted her the way you lift something you do not want to wake, and set her in the chair, and put her feet on the board, one and then the other. One of them took the handles.

"Mind the camber," said Senna.

"There's no camber in the ward, missus."

"There's camber on the slope," said Senna. "And you never mind it." She turned her head. "Tor."

Toren was at the foot of the bed. He had been there since the gate. Callie did not think he had gone back to eleven at all.

The technician sat at the screen with his left hand. He warmed the machine.

Callie had heard about it for fifty days. The warming, over and over. Seven times on the thirty-second. The sound it made, that Senna told the ceiling was flat. She had never heard it herself.

She heard it now.

It came up out of the machine low and long, a sound like a finger drawn round the rim of a glass. It rose and held. It did not wander. It held.

The lights along the rack went green, row by row, left to right, like somebody going along a row of windows with a candle.

Senna lay on the narrow bed with her eyes shut.

The technician looked at the screen for a long time. Sowerby came and stood behind him and looked too.

The ward was dark except for the lamp at the far end. The fourth bed on the right had Senna in it, asleep, with her hands on the blanket. The fifth had Tonk.

Tonk was asleep on his back with the frame on his leg. The bar went across over the blanket and the four pins went down into the leg through the blanket's tent. One end came out between the first two fingers, and the other between the last two. He was keeping both ends.

There was a chair by the bed. There had always been a chair by the bed.

Jab sat down in it.

He did not wake him. He sat in the chair with his hands in his lap and felt him. He could not help it. He did it the way he had felt the watch across the Sag. Tonk was there. He was small, and warm, and asleep, and not busy. There was nothing in him that was not his.

The leg was the old leaning wall, all down the shin where the pins went in. Done. And near one of the pins, the lowest one, there was something else. A little warm. A little busy. Not grey. Tonk's own, fighting a small thing, the way Rook had fought the dog.

Jab sat and felt it and did not reach.

Jab undid the button on the left side of his coat. He took out the fish and held it out on his palm.

Tonk took it with his left hand. He did not unwind the cord to do it. He held the fish up in the light from the lamp at the far end of the ward and turned it over. He looked at the body. He looked at the tail. He looked at the place where the fin had been. He put his thumb on the place.

Tonk thought about this.

Tonk looked at him for a long time in the dark.

Jab sat in the chair by the fifth bed and did not go back to twelve. After a while Mrs Lask came down the ward and put a blanket over his knees without saying anything, and went away again.

In the morning Tonk did the chair.

The nurse brought the chair to the side of the bed and set the brake and stood back. Jab stood at the foot of the bed with his hands behind his back.

It took six minutes. Jab knew it was six because Senna, in the next bed, counted it out loud. She did it the way she had done it before they went, on the thirty-ninth and the forty-first, because Tonk had asked her to count and she said she knew the numbers after ten.

The Director saw them on the fifty-seventh, in the long room, at the second hour.

It was the same room it had always been. The long window ran the length of the north wall, and through it the yard, and the berm, and the road to the Sag. The slate stood on its easel with a column of numbers down it. At the bottom, in new chalk, 58.

"The sixty-one's the machine's," said the Director. "It's the station's spend. It's not a debt against anybody's household. I'm writing it so." She wrote it. "I lent it against your names so I'd know where it went. I know where it went."

She turned the paper over and put her finger on the back of it, near the middle. On the place she had read twice.

She looked up.

"Say it," she said. "Both of you. In your own words. Not the paper's."

Toren said it first. He said it the way he had said it in the room, Jab thought, with his teeth together. It was the line, and the jar, and the lifter against the strut. Jab was on the push, and Callie was in the door with two turns. And it was nearly done, and if they had come out it had the door and the river.

Dee said it after. She said less.

"It's my line," she said. "I drew it on the thirty-seventh and I drew it again at the pump house. I watched it cross. I said inside two turns, not a breath more, and I turned the glass." She did not look away from the Director. "I'd do it again. The same, in the same room. I'd not do it anywhere else. That's the difference and I don't know how to write it better."

The Director looked at the two of them.

"I've had people break my rules," she said. "Every week of my life. I've had them break it and come home and say nothing. And I've found out, because I always find out. And I've had them off the register and out of the gate the same day, whoever they were." She put her hand flat on the paper. "Not for breaking it. For hiding it. A rule broken in secret is a rule that's gone. There's no rule after that, there's only what people think they can get away with."

She looked at the paper under her hand.

Censured, both names. Not praised. Not a model. The red-call rule and the abort line stand as signed, unchanged." She looked up. "D. For the first time Jab saw Dee's mouth move at the corner.

Jab had thought about it. He had thought about it in the chair by the fifth bed, two nights, and while Tonk did the chair, and on the way up the stair to this room. He had not thought about it in words. He found the words now, standing at the table.

He went to the fifth bed at the supper hour.

He went straight from the east shed, where he had sat at Dee's long table for the first time on the other side of it. He had not taught anybody. Nobody had come. He had sat there for an hour with a jar and a square of paper and nobody on the far bench, and Dee had sat beside him and not drawn anybody, because she was not allowed.

"I'll be here," said Jab.

Mrs Lask was at the ward door. She did not say visiting was over. She looked at his hand, and he showed her the clean dressing, and she stood aside.

Tonk was in the chair by the bed, with a tray on his knee. It was porridge. There was a lump in it you could have built a wall with. Rook's bed was across the ward, the second on the left, and Rook was lying on his face in it with his arm hanging down, and Jab could hear him complaining about the porridge from the door.

Jab sat down in the chair on the other side of the bed and took the second tray on his knee. The fish was on the pillow. The cord was round Tonk's fist, both ends. Jab ate the porridge. "The lady upstairs."

Tonk thought about this for a long time. He ate a spoonful of porridge and looked at the lump in it.

"Good," he said.

Jab finished his porridge. He put the tray on the floor. He sat in the chair by the fifth bed with his hands in his lap, one with a clean dressing on the heel of it, and watched his brother eat. He did not count anything. He did not reach for anything.

He was not asleep.

Chapter 48 — Toren: The First Page After

[Warm, intimate narration; keep emotion earned and restrained]

The weighman put the test weights on before he weighed anything.

Toren had seen him do it on the tenth day, walking past. He had not stood and watched it. He watched it now. The old man in the leather apron came out of the hut with an iron block in each hand and set them down in the middle of the plate one after the other, carefully, as if they might wake. Then he went back into the hut and looked at the beam for a long time. He moved the little weight along it with one finger, and looked again.

"Fifty," said Tilda, from the stool.

"Fifty," said the weighman.

He came out and took the blocks off the plate and carried them back into the hut, one at a time.

"Now it's honest," said Tilda. "Put them on."

[Dry, precise narration; quiet institutional pressure]

It was the fifty-eighth, the third hour, a grey morning, and the whole of the ash was on the gravel beside the plate.

Otto had brought it from the east shed on the barrow, where it had been locked since the fifty-fifth. Toren had walked beside the barrow with the Director's paper in his coat. Jab walked on the other side with his hand an inch off the jars, not touching. Callie walked in front, with the counter.

Three home Flasks, grey to the shoulder, with Tilda's knots on the stoppers. The fence's fifth, whole. The fence's fourth, with three in it. Callie's dirty jar, with four. And the empties, five of them, clinking in the straw.

Otto put the first home Flask on the plate.

"Eight," she said. "Clean. My knot."

"Your knot," said the weighman.

She did it three times. Eight, eight, eight. Each time she leaned forward on the stool and looked at the stopper through the hut window, at the thread round its neck and the knot in the thread. It was a knot Toren did not know, small and hard and folded back on itself.

"My grandfather tied it on grain sacks," said Tilda, when she saw him looking. "At the scale house. So nobody could say a sack had been opened when it hadn't." She wrote the third eight. "Or hadn't when it had."

"They hadn't," said Toren.

"I know they hadn't," said Tilda. "It's my knot. I'm saying it for the board."

The board was on the wall of the hut, painted black, with names down one side in white paint and numbers down the other in chalk. Callie's was on it, and Katori's crew, and a dozen others. Near the bottom there was the line that had been there since the thirty-ninth, in the weighman's chalk:

LENT. CAUL HILL. 12 FLASKS, CLEAN. J., 8, IN THE FRAME. P., 4, ON THE CART. ROAD 1. HOME 3.

The weighman took the chalk off the ledge. He did not rub anything out. He drew a line through the LENT line, straight, with the ruler. Then he wrote under it.

He had it in her hand, not his. She had written it on the fifty-seventh after they left the long room, and sent it down by Hallet to eleven that evening, folded twice. For the board, and the book. "Then I'll believe it," said the weighman. He did not smile. "Once."

He wanted a name.

He said so while Otto was loading the store jars back onto the barrow to go down under the plate. He said it to Toren, with the chalk still in his fingers, looking at the board.

"Whose is it?" he said.

"Whose is what?"

"The crew." The weighman pointed with the chalk at the struck line, and the new block under it. "Every jar on that board goes against a crew. That's how it's kept straight. A crew's got a name. Toren looked at the board.

He knew what it was. He had heard it at a fire on the road, before the gate, with Rook sitting across it. A company, sitting in a yard, hiring. A man behind a table with a box. Sections named off whoever ran them, so the pay was kept straight. A brass chit, stamped with four letters and a number. Tull's sixth.

She was in the barrow. Otto had brought her up in it from the Sag at the end of the night watch, with the big book in her lap and her bad leg out straight. She had been sitting in it at the edge of the plate the whole time, with her eyes shut, listening.

The weighman went into the hut and came out with a pot of white paint and a brush. He painted it on the board, down the side, under Katori's, in square white letters. He took a long time over it. When he had finished he stood back.

And beside it, in chalk, where the numbers went, he wrote D. C.

"Her command," he said. "Not yours."

"Not mine," said Toren.

"Good," said the weighman. He put the brush in the pot. "I don't like crews named after boys. They've no idea what they're doing."

"He's right," said Tilda, from the stool, and wrote nothing, and looked at the board.

Rook was lying on his face in the second bed on the left.

He had been lying on his face for three days. He said it was the longest he had lain still since he was born, and that it was worse than the hole. Sowerby had opened the foot of the stitches on the fifty-sixth and let the yellow out, and put something in it that Rook would not describe, and closed it. The red had not gone further since. It had begun, Sowerby said, to come in. He said it the way he said everything, as if it were bad news.

Toren went to see him on the fifty-ninth. Hallet was already there.

He was standing at the end of the bed in his grey cardigan with his pen on its string, and he had something in his hand. He was saying things, quietly, at length, about the south gate and the fifty-sixth and an arrival party of four, from the east road. He stopped when Toren came in.

"Go on," said Rook, into the pillow. "He's all right. He's heard worse."

Hallet looked at Toren. Then he held out the thing in his hand to Rook, low, by the side of the bed, where Rook could see it without lifting his head.

It was a piece of brass. It was small, flat, the size of a thumbnail, with a hole punched through one end.

"One of the four paid his intake with it," said Hallet. "At my window. On the fifty-sixth. He put it on the ledge and said it was good anywhere on the east road." He was quiet. "The gate doesn't take brass. I told him so. He took it back and paid in the station's coin, which he had. Then he went off to the south huts." He looked at the brass in his hand. "He left it on the ledge after. I don't think by accident. I've kept it since."

"Why?" said Rook.

"Because of the stamp," said Hallet.

Rook put out his hand and took it.

He did not lift his head off the pillow. He held the brass in his fingers in front of his face and turned it over, once, to the stamped side. Toren could see it from where he stood. There were letters stamped in it, and a number. He did not know the letters. They were not four. The number was not six.

Rook looked at it for a long time.

His face did nothing. It did nothing so completely that Toren looked at it twice. He had seen it do that on a gravel bar at midnight, four feet from a disk on a cord. He had seen it at a low fire, across from a girl with a warm stone in her hands.

Rook turned the brass over, face down, on the blanket by his hand. He put his palm flat over it.

"It's the same brass," he said.

Nobody said anything.

"Thank you," said Rook, to Hallet. "I'll keep it now."

"I'd like it back," said Hallet. "For the ledger. It's evidence of a thing."

"It's evidence of a thing," Rook agreed, into the pillow. "You'll have it back. When I can sit up and look at it with the right face on." He shut his eyes. "Not now."

Hallet looked at him for a moment longer. Then he nodded, and went, with his pen swinging on its string.

Toren stood at the end of the bed.

"Don't," said Rook, without opening his eyes.

"I wasn't going to."

"You were going to ask me what it said," said Rook. "It said a name I don't know yet, and a number I don't know yet. That's all it said." His hand lay flat on the brass on the blanket. "It's the same brass. That's all I know. And four men from the east road, in the south huts, since the fifty-sixth."

"Lie on my face," said Rook. "For four more days. Sowerby says." He was quiet. "Then sit up. Then stand. Then I'll ask Hallet where the south huts are, as if I didn't know." He opened his eyes and looked at the wall. "Then we'll see."

Toren did not say anything.

"Go on," said Rook. "You've a lane at the fourth hour. Katori said. You'll be late, and she'll look at you."
